abstract: We propose learning rules for recurrent neural networks with high-order interactions between some or all neurons. The designed networks exhibit the desired associative memory function: perfect storage and retrieval of pieces of information and/or sequences of information of any complexity.
originalAbstract: We propose learning rules for recurrent neural networks with high-order interactions between some or all neurons. The designed networks exhibit the desired associative memory function: perfect storage and retrieval of pieces of information and/or sequences of information of any complexity.

paragraphs: The paper proposes learning rules for recurrent neural networks used as associative memories. In this setting, the goal is to store information and retrieve it through the network's behavior. Recurrence allows activity to feed back through the network, making the organization of its interactions central to how a memory is represented and recalled.

The proposed networks include higher-order interactions involving some or all of their neurons. Such interactions involve groups of neurons, extending the way dependencies can be expressed within the memory. The learning rules are the mechanism for designing these interactions so that the resulting network carries out the intended storage and retrieval function.

The authors state that the designed networks achieve perfect storage and retrieval of individual pieces of information, sequences of information, or both, with information of any complexity. This makes ordered information part of the claimed associative-memory function. The contribution is the connection between higher-order recurrent interactions and learning rules that construct a memory with the desired behavior, including the retrieval of sequences.
summary.tldr: The authors propose higher-order recurrent learning rules and claim perfect associative storage and retrieval of information and sequences of arbitrary complexity.

title: High Order Neural Networks for Efficient Associative Memory Design

abstract: The potential of adaptive networks to learn categorization rules and to model human performance is studied by comparing how natural and artificial systems respond to new inputs, i.e., how they generalize. Like humans, networks can learn a detenninistic categorization task by a variety of alternative individual solutions. An analysis of the con(cid:173) straints imposed by using networks with the minimal number of hidden units shows that this "minimal configuration" constraint is not sufficient to explain and predict human performance; only a few solu(cid:173) tions were found to be shared by both humans and minimal adaptive networks. A further analysis of human and network generalizations indicates that initial conditions may provide important constraints on generalization. A new technique, which we call "reversed learning", is described for finding appropriate initial conditions.
originalAbstract: The potential of adaptive networks to learn categorization rules and to model human performance is studied by comparing how natural and artificial systems respond to new inputs, i.e., how they generalize. Like humans, networks can learn a detenninistic categorization task by a variety of alternative individual solutions. An analysis of the con(cid:173) straints imposed by using networks with the minimal number of hidden units shows that this "minimal configuration" constraint is not sufficient to explain and predict human performance; only a few solu(cid:173) tions were found to be shared by both humans and minimal adaptive networks. A further analysis of human and network generalizations indicates that initial conditions may provide important constraints on generalization. A new technique, which we call "reversed learning", is described for finding appropriate initial conditions.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether adaptive networks can explain how people extend learned categories to unfamiliar inputs. Learning the training task is only part of that question: different solutions can agree on known examples yet classify new examples differently. Both humans and networks were able to learn a deterministic categorization task through several alternative individual solutions.

The authors examine a proposed constraint on those solutions: requiring networks to use the smallest possible number of hidden units. This restriction might seem useful for narrowing the range of behaviors a model can produce. However, only a few solutions were shared by people and these minimally configured networks, so architectural minimality did not adequately explain human generalization.

Further analysis points to initial conditions as another potentially important influence on the eventual solution. The paper introduces a technique called reversed learning for finding suitable starting conditions. The contribution is therefore both diagnostic and methodological: it identifies an insufficient modeling constraint and proposes a way to investigate starting states that may better account for human behavior.
summary.tldr: Minimal network size does not explain human generalization, motivating a method for finding more appropriate learning initial conditions.

title: Constraints on Adaptive Networks for Modeling Human Generalization

abstract: In associative reinforcement learning, an environment generates input vectors, a learning system generates possible output vectors, and a reinforcement function computes feedback signals from the input-output pairs. The task is to discover and remember input-output pairs that generate rewards. Especially difficult cases occur when rewards are rare, since the expected time for any algorithm can grow exponentially with the size of the problem. Nonetheless, if a reinforcement function possesses regularities, and a learning algorithm exploits them, learning time can be reduced below that of non-generalizing algorithms. This paper describes a neural network algorithm called complementary reinforcement back-propagation (CRBP), and reports simulation results on problems designed to offer differing opportunities for generalization.
originalAbstract: In associative reinforcement learning, an environment generates input vectors, a learning system generates possible output vectors, and a reinforcement function computes feedback signals from the input-output pairs. The task is to discover and remember input-output pairs that generate rewards. paragraphs: The paper studies associative reinforcement learning, where a system proposes outputs for given inputs and receives feedback about each pairing. Its job is to discover and retain combinations that earn rewards. Rare rewards make this difficult because useful feedback may be encountered infrequently, and expected learning time can grow exponentially with problem size.

The authors focus on whether structure in the reward function offers a way to reduce that burden. If rewarding input-output relationships contain regularities, a learner that exploits them can improve on algorithms that do not generalize. The potential benefit therefore depends on both the problem's structure and the algorithm's ability to use it.

The paper introduces complementary reinforcement backpropagation, or CRBP, and reports simulations on problems offering different opportunities for generalization. This design makes the availability of useful structure part of the investigation itself. The contribution addresses scaling through transferable regularities in reward, connecting the difficulty of finding successful actions to what a neural learning algorithm can infer across input-output pairs.
summary.tldr: CRBP investigates how generalizing reward regularities can reduce the learning burden in associative reinforcement problems.

title: Generalization and Scaling in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We examine the ability of radial basis functions (RBFs) to generalize. We compare the performance of several types of RBFs. We use the inverse dy(cid:173) namics of an idealized two-joint arm as a test case. We find that without a proper choice of a norm for the inputs, RBFs have poor generalization properties. A simple global scaling of the input variables greatly improves performance. We suggest some efficient methods to approximate this dis(cid:173) tance metric.
originalAbstract: We examine the ability of radial basis functions (RBFs) to generalize. We compare the performance of several types of RBFs. We use the inverse dy(cid:173) namics of an idealized two-joint arm as a test case. We find that without a proper choice of a norm for the inputs, RBFs have poor generalization properties. A simple global scaling of the input variables greatly improves performance. We suggest some efficient methods to approximate this dis(cid:173) tance metric.

paragraphs: The paper studies how well radial basis functions generalize beyond their training examples. It compares several RBF types using the inverse dynamics of an idealized two-joint arm as the test problem. The central issue is how the representation of the inputs affects the model's ability to make useful predictions on new cases.

The authors find poor generalization when the norm used for the inputs is not chosen appropriately. A norm determines how input differences are measured. For a method organized around distances, that choice affects which observations count as close to one another and therefore how the learned approximation extends between examples.

A simple global scaling of the input variables substantially improves performance in the reported study. The authors also suggest efficient ways to approximate the distance metric. The finding makes input geometry a practical modeling decision: choosing an RBF type alone does not settle how the model treats similarity. In this test case, adjusting the scale of the inputs is an effective way to improve generalization.
summary.tldr: RBF generalization depends strongly on the input distance metric, and simple variable scaling greatly improves performance in the studied arm-dynamics task.

title: Generalization Properties of Radial Basis Functions

abstract: A switching between apparently coherent (oscillatory) and stochastic episodes of activity has been observed in responses from cat and monkey visual cortex. We describe the dynamics of these phenomena in two paral(cid:173) lel approaches, a phenomenological and a rather microscopic one. On the one hand we analyze neuronal responses in terms of a hidden state model (HSM). The parameters of this model are extracted directly from exper(cid:173) imental spike trains. They characterize the underlying dynamics as well as the coupling of individual neurons to the network. This phenomenolog(cid:173) ical model thus provides a new framework for the experimental analysis of network dynamics. The application of this method to multi unit ac(cid:173) tivities from the visual cortex of the cat substantiates the existence of oscillatory and stochastic states and quantifies the switching behaviour in the assembly dynamics. On the other hand we start from the single spiking neuron and derive a master equation for the time evolution of the assembly state which we represent by a phase density. This phase density dynamics (PDD) exhibits costability of two attractors, a limit cycle, and a fixed point when synaptic interaction is nonlinear. External fluctuations can switch the bistable system from one state to the other. Finally we show, that the two approaches are mutually consistent and therefore both explain the detailed time structure in the data.

paragraphs: Neuronal responses in cat and monkey visual cortex can alternate between apparently coordinated oscillations and more stochastic activity. This paper investigates whether those episodes reflect switching between underlying collective states. It develops two complementary descriptions: one inferred from recorded spike trains and another derived from a model of interacting spiking neurons.

The data-based approach uses a hidden state model whose parameters describe network dynamics and individual neurons' coupling to the network. Applied to multi-unit recordings from cat visual cortex, it supports the presence of oscillatory and stochastic states and quantifies transitions between them. This turns visible changes in spike activity into an analysis of hidden assembly behavior.

The microscopic approach represents the assembly through a phase density and derives an equation for its evolution. With nonlinear synaptic interactions, a limit cycle and a fixed point can coexist as attractors, and external fluctuations can trigger switching. The authors show consistency between the two approaches, linking the inferred states to a possible dynamical mechanism for the observed temporal structure.
summary.tldr: Two consistent models explain alternating cortical activity as fluctuation-driven switching between coexisting collective states.

title: How Oscillatory Neuronal Responses Reflect Bistability and Switching of the Hidden Assembly Dynamics

paragraphs: This paper proposes learning constraint surfaces: sets of variable combinations that can occur together. A conventional mapping assigns an output to a known input, but many vision, robotics, and control problems do not divide naturally into those roles. A surface instead represents the joint relationships that valid combinations of variables must satisfy.

The authors describe an architecture for learning and manipulating nonlinear surfaces from data. The representation supports different queries, including completion queries in which some variables are supplied and information about the remaining variables is sought. This makes the learned relationship usable with different subsets of known quantities, rather than tying every query to one fixed input-output arrangement.

The technique is demonstrated on low-dimensional synthetic surfaces and compared with nearest-neighbor approaches. It is then used to learn the space of lip images in a lipreading system intended to improve speech recognition. The learned surface improves visual tracking during recognition, showing how a model of allowable image configurations can support the tracking component of a larger recognition process.
summary.tldr: Learning nonlinear constraint surfaces supports flexible queries and improves visual tracking in a lipreading application.

title: Surface Learning with Applications to Lipreading

abstract: A practical method for Bayesian training of feed-forward neural networks using sophisticated Monte Carlo methods is presented and evaluated. In reasonably small amounts of computer time this approach outperforms other state-of-the-art methods on 5 data(cid:173) limited tasks from real world domains.
originalAbstract: A practical method for Bayesian training of feed-forward neural networks using sophisticated Monte Carlo methods is presented and evaluated. In reasonably small amounts of computer time this approach outperforms other state-of-the-art methods on 5 data(cid:173) limited tasks from real world domains.

paragraphs: The paper presents a practical method for training feedforward neural networks using Bayesian learning. The emphasis is on making this approach computationally usable and evaluating whether it helps on real prediction tasks. Its evaluation focuses on settings with limited data, where the training examples provide relatively little evidence about the network's parameters.

The method uses sophisticated Monte Carlo techniques to carry out Bayesian training. Monte Carlo methods use sampling to approximate calculations involving uncertainty. In this setting, they provide a computational route to learning with uncertainty about network parameters. The paper's central contribution is an implementation that makes this approach practical within the reported computing budget.

The abstract reports that the method outperformed other leading methods on five real-world tasks with limited data, while requiring reasonably small amounts of computer time. These findings connect predictive performance with computational feasibility. They provide evidence that Bayesian neural-network training can be useful in practical small-data settings, rather than leaving its value solely at the level of a statistical formulation.
summary.tldr: Monte Carlo methods make Bayesian neural-network training practical and outperform competing methods on five real-world tasks with limited data.

title: A Practical Monte Carlo Implementation of Bayesian Learning

abstract: We present a theoretical framework for population codes which generalizes naturally to the important case where the population provides information about a whole probability distribution over an underlying quantity rather than just a single value. We use the framework to analyze two existing models, and to suggest and evaluate a third model for encoding such probability distributions.
originalAbstract: We present a theoretical framework for population codes which generalizes naturally to the important case where the population provides information about a whole probability distribution over an underlying quantity rather than just a single value. We use the framework to analyze two existing models, and to suggest and evaluate a third model for encoding such probability distributions.

paragraphs: The paper develops a theoretical framework for interpreting population codes, in which information is represented across a collection of neurons. Its key extension is to let the population communicate a probability distribution over an underlying quantity. This expands the interpretation beyond representing just one particular value of that quantity.

A probability distribution can describe how support is spread across possible values. Interpreting a population in this way therefore changes what one asks of the code: the issue becomes how neural activity represents a range of possibilities and their relative probabilities. The framework is designed to make this richer form of representation part of a unified theoretical treatment.

The authors use the framework to analyze two existing models and to propose and evaluate a third model for encoding distributions. This gives the theory a concrete comparative role, as well as a role in constructing a new encoding approach. The contribution is a way to reason about population activity as probabilistic information, supported by analysis of multiple candidate models.
summary.tldr: A theoretical framework interprets neural population activity as encoding probability distributions and uses that view to examine three models.

title: Probabilistic Interpretation of Population Codes

abstract: This paper introduces a method for regularization ofHMM systems that avoids parameter overfitting caused by insufficient training data. Regu(cid:173) larization is done by augmenting the EM training method by a penalty term that favors simple and smooth HMM systems. The penalty term is constructed as a mixture model of negative exponential distributions that is assumed to generate the state dependent emission probabilities of the HMMs. This new method is the successful transfer of a well known regularization approach in neural networks to the HMM domain and can be interpreted as a generalization of traditional state-tying for HMM sys(cid:173) tems. The effect of regularization is demonstrated for continuous speech recognition tasks by improving overfitted triphone models and by speaker adaptation with limited training data.
originalAbstract: This paper introduces a method for regularization ofHMM systems that avoids parameter overfitting caused by insufficient training data. Regu(cid:173) larization is done by augmenting the EM training method by a penalty term that favors simple and smooth HMM systems. The penalty term is constructed as a mixture model of negative exponential distributions that is assumed to generate the state dependent emission probabilities of the HMMs. This new method is the successful transfer of a well known regularization approach in neural networks to the HMM domain and can be interpreted as a generalization of traditional state-tying for HMM sys(cid:173) tems. The effect of regularization is demonstrated for continuous speech recognition tasks by improving overfitted triphone models and by speaker adaptation with limited training data.

paragraphs: Hidden Markov models can fit their training examples too closely when there is too little data to estimate all their parameters reliably. This paper addresses that problem by changing the training objective. Alongside fitting the observations, the model is encouraged to maintain a simpler, smoother system of probabilities.

The method adds a penalty to expectation-maximization training. That penalty comes from a mixture of negative exponential distributions assumed to generate the emission probabilities associated with different states. It provides a probabilistic way to constrain complexity during estimation. The authors interpret the method as a generalization of state tying, which controls complexity by sharing parameters across states.

The approach transfers a regularization idea from neural networks to hidden Markov models and demonstrates it in continuous speech recognition. The reported applications improve overfitted triphone models and support speaker adaptation with limited training data. These findings show how restricting the flexibility of probability estimates can be useful both when building detailed speech models and when adapting them from few examples.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic penalty makes HMM training favor simpler models, improving speech modeling and adaptation when training data is scarce.

title: Controlling the Complexity of HMM Systems by Regularization

abstract: We consider the problem of choosing a kernel suitable for estimation using a Gaussian Process estimator or a Support Vector Machine. A novel solution is presented which involves deﬁning a Reproducing Ker- nel Hilbert Space on the space of kernels itself. By utilizing an analog of the classical representer theorem, the problem of choosing a kernel from a parameterized family of kernels (e.g. of varying width) is reduced to a statistical estimation problem akin to the problem of minimizing a regularized risk functional. Various classical settings for model or kernel selection are special cases of our framework.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of choosing a kernel suitable for estimation using a Gaussian Process estimator or a Support Vector Machine. A novel solution is presented which involves deﬁning a Reproducing Ker- nel Hilbert Space on the space of kernels itself. By utilizing an analog of the classical representer theorem, the problem of choosing a kernel from a parameterized family of kernels (e.g. of varying width) is reduced to a statistical estimation problem akin to the problem of minimizing a regularized risk functional. Various classical settings for model or kernel selection are special cases of our framework.

paragraphs: Gaussian process estimators and support vector machines require a suitable kernel, so selecting that kernel is itself an important estimation problem. This paper develops a framework that treats kernel choice as something to learn systematically. It considers selection from parameterized kernel families, including families whose members differ in width.

The central construction places a reproducing kernel Hilbert space on the space of kernels itself. This gives the possible kernels a mathematical structure in which selection can be formulated as estimation. An analogue of the classical representer theorem then reduces kernel choice to a problem resembling minimization of regularized risk.

The resulting framework connects the choice of a kernel with the same broad kind of fitting-and-regularization problem used in statistical learning. The authors also show that several classical model-selection and kernel-selection settings are special cases. Its significance is this unification: procedures that might otherwise look like separate choices can be expressed within one mathematical approach to learning an appropriate kernel.
summary.tldr: Hyperkernels turn selection from a parameterized kernel family into a regularized statistical estimation problem.

title: Hyperkernels

abstract: We describe a new algorithmic framework for inference in probabilistic models, and apply it to inference for latent Dirichlet allocation. Our framework adopts the methodology of variational inference, but unlike existing variational methods such as mean field and expectation propagation it is not restricted to tractable classes of approximating distributions. Our approach can also be viewed as a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) method, but unlike existing SMC methods there is no need to design the artificial sequence of distributions. Notably, our framework offers a principled means to exchange the variance of an importance sampling estimate for the bias incurred through variational approximation. Experiments on a challenging inference problem in population genetics demonstrate improvements in stability and accuracy over existing methods, and at a comparable cost.
originalAbstract: We describe a new algorithmic framework for inference in probabilistic models, and apply it to inference for latent Dirichlet allocation. Our framework adopts the methodology of variational inference, but unlike existing variational methods such as mean field and expectation propagation it is not restricted to tractable classes of approximating distributions. Our approach can also be viewed as a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) method, but unlike existing SMC methods there is no need to design the artificial sequence of distributions. Notably, our framework offers a principled means to exchange the variance of an importance sampling estimate for the bias incurred through variational approximation. Experiments on a challenging inference problem in population genetics demonstrate improvements in stability and accuracy over existing methods, and at a comparable cost.

paragraphs: Inference in a probabilistic model means working out what its hidden variables imply after observations are available. This paper introduces an algorithmic framework that brings together variational approximation and sampling. It applies the framework to latent Dirichlet allocation and evaluates it on a challenging inference problem in population genetics.

Variational methods approach inference through an approximating distribution. The proposed framework follows that approach without restricting the approximation to the tractable distribution families used by methods such as mean field and expectation propagation. It can also be understood as sequential Monte Carlo, while removing the need to manually construct an artificial sequence of intermediate distributions.

The central contribution is a principled trade between two sources of error: variability in importance sampling estimates and bias from variational approximation. This provides a way to balance sampling and approximation within one framework. In the reported population genetics experiments, the method improves stability and accuracy over existing methods at comparable computational cost.
summary.tldr: A unified inference framework trades sampling variance against variational bias and improves stability and accuracy in reported population genetics experiments.

title: A Stochastic approximation method for inference in probabilistic graphical models

abstract: We introduce a new perspective on approximations to the maximum a posteriori (MAP) task in probabilistic graphical models, that is based on simplifying a given instance, and then tightening the approximation. First, we start with a structural relaxation of the original model. We then infer from the relaxation its deficiencies, and compensate for them. This perspective allows us to identify two distinct classes of approximations. First, we find that max-product belief propagation can be viewed as a way to compensate for a relaxation, based on a particular idealized case for exactness. We identify a second approach to compensation that is based on a more refined idealized case, resulting in a new approximation with distinct properties. We go on to propose a new class of algorithms that, starting with a relaxation, iteratively yields tighter approximations.
originalAbstract: We introduce a new perspective on approximations to the maximum a posteriori (MAP) task in probabilistic graphical models, that is based on simplifying a given instance, and then tightening the approximation. First, we start with a structural relaxation of the original model. We then infer from the relaxation its deficiencies, and compensate for them. This perspective allows us to identify two distinct classes of approximations. First, we find that max-product belief propagation can be viewed as a way to compensate for a relaxation, based on a particular idealized case for exactness. We identify a second approach to compensation that is based on a more refined idealized case, resulting in a new approximation with distinct properties. We go on to propose a new class of algorithms that, starting with a relaxation, iteratively yields tighter approximations.

paragraphs: Maximum a posteriori inference seeks the most probable joint configuration in a probabilistic graphical model. This paper approaches approximation by first simplifying the model’s structure. The simplified model provides a starting point from which the method identifies what the relaxation fails to capture and introduces compensation for those deficiencies.

This perspective separates two kinds of approximation according to the idealized conditions used to guide compensation. The authors show that max-product belief propagation can be understood as compensating for a structural relaxation under one particular idealized case of exactness. A more refined idealized case motivates a second compensation approach, producing a new approximation with different properties.

The paper also proposes a class of algorithms that progressively tighten an initial relaxation. This makes approximation a process of controlled refinement rather than a single fixed simplification. The conceptual contribution is to connect an established inference method and a new alternative through the same relaxation-and-compensation framework. Exactness remains tied to the idealized cases used in the analysis; the general algorithms are presented as producing increasingly tight approximations.
summary.tldr: Viewing MAP approximation as structural simplification followed by compensation connects max-product belief propagation with new, progressively tighter inference methods.

title: Approximating MAP by Compensating for Structural Relaxations

abstract: We present a novel approach to efficiently learn a label tree for large scale classification with many classes. The key contribution of the approach is a technique to simultaneously determine the structure of the tree and learn the classifiers for each node in the tree. This approach also allows fine grained control over the efficiency vs accuracy trade-off in designing a label tree, leading to more balanced trees. Experiments are performed on large scale image classification with 10184 classes and 9 million images. We demonstrate significant improvements in test accuracy and efficiency with less training time and more balanced trees compared to the previous state of the art by Bengio et al.
originalAbstract: We present a novel approach to efficiently learn a label tree for large scale classification with many classes. The key contribution of the approach is a technique to simultaneously determine the structure of the tree and learn the classifiers for each node in the tree. This approach also allows fine grained control over the efficiency vs accuracy trade-off in designing a label tree, leading to more balanced trees. Experiments are performed on large scale image classification with 10184 classes and 9 million images. We demonstrate significant improvements in test accuracy and efficiency with less training time and more balanced trees compared to the previous state of the art by Bengio et al.

paragraphs: Classification becomes computationally demanding when an image may belong to one of many thousands of classes. A label tree organizes those classes into a hierarchy, with classifiers at its nodes guiding the decision. This paper develops a way to learn such a tree efficiently while accounting for both prediction accuracy and computational cost.

The key idea is to learn the tree structure and its node classifiers together. These choices are closely related: the arrangement of classes determines which distinctions a node must make, while the classifiers determine how effectively those distinctions can be resolved. Joint learning allows finer control over the efficiency–accuracy trade-off and leads to more balanced trees.

The authors evaluate the method on image classification involving 10,184 classes and nine million images. Relative to the previous state-of-the-art approach identified in the abstract, they report significant improvements in test accuracy and efficiency, shorter training time, and better tree balance. These results support the practical value of treating hierarchy design and classifier learning as one coordinated problem at large scale.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning a label tree and its node classifiers improves the balance, accuracy, and efficiency of large-scale image classification.

title: Fast and Balanced: Efficient Label Tree Learning for Large Scale Object Recognition

abstract: Most methods for decision-theoretic online learning are based on the Hedge algorithm, which takes a parameter called the learning rate. In most previous analyses the learning rate was carefully tuned to obtain optimal worst-case performance, leading to suboptimal performance on easy instances, for example when there exists an action that is significantly better than all others. We propose a new way of setting the learning rate, which adapts to the difficulty of the learning problem: in the worst case our procedure still guarantees optimal performance, but on easy instances it achieves much smaller regret. In particular, our adaptive method achieves constant regret in a probabilistic setting, when there exists an action that on average obtains strictly smaller loss than all other actions. We also provide a simulation study comparing our approach to existing methods.
originalAbstract: Most methods for decision-theoretic online learning are based on the Hedge algorithm, which takes a parameter called the learning rate. In most previous analyses the learning rate was carefully tuned to obtain optimal worst-case performance, leading to suboptimal performance on easy instances, for example when there exists an action that is significantly better than all others. We propose a new way of setting the learning rate, which adapts to the difficulty of the learning problem: in the worst case our procedure still guarantees optimal performance, but on easy instances it achieves much smaller regret. In particular, our adaptive method achieves constant regret in a probabilistic setting, when there exists an action that on average obtains strictly smaller loss than all other actions. We also provide a simulation study comparing our approach to existing methods.

paragraphs: Online decision making involves choosing actions repeatedly while learning from their losses. Hedge is a common algorithm for this setting, but its behavior depends on a learning rate. The paper identifies a drawback of tuning that rate for the hardest possible situations: the resulting method can fail to exploit easier problems, including those with one clearly superior action.

The proposed method adjusts the learning rate to the difficulty encountered during learning. Its guarantees preserve optimal worst-case performance while allowing much smaller regret on easy instances. Regret measures the accumulated disadvantage relative to a comparison action, so reducing it means paying less for the process of discovering which choices work well.

A particularly strong result applies in a probabilistic setting where one action has strictly lower average loss than every alternative. Under that condition, the adaptive method achieves constant regret, rather than regret that keeps growing with the number of rounds. A simulation study compares the approach with existing methods. Together, the contributions connect conservative worst-case protection with stronger performance when the problem permits it.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Hedge adjusts its learning rate to achieve smaller regret on easy problems while preserving optimal worst-case guarantees.

title: Adaptive Hedge

abstract: We study the problem of reconstructing an unknown matrix M of rank r and dimension d using O(rd polylog d) Pauli measurements. This has applications in quantum state tomography, and is a non-commutative analogue of a well-known problem in compressed sensing: recovering a sparse vector from a few of its Fourier coefficients. We show that almost all sets of O(rd log^6 d) Pauli measurements satisfy the rank-r restricted isometry property (RIP). This implies that M can be recovered from a fixed ("universal") set of Pauli measurements, using nuclear-norm minimization (e.g., the matrix Lasso), with nearly-optimal bounds on the error. A similar result holds for any class of measurements that use an orthonormal operator basis whose elements have small operator norm. Our proof uses Dudley's inequality for Gaussian processes, together with bounds on covering numbers obtained via entropy duality.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of reconstructing an unknown matrix M of rank r and dimension d using O(rd polylog d) Pauli measurements. This has applications in quantum state tomography, and is a non-commutative analogue of a well-known problem in compressed sensing: recovering a sparse vector from a few of its Fourier coefficients. We show that almost all sets of O(rd log^6 d) Pauli measurements satisfy the rank-r restricted isometry property (RIP). This implies that M can be recovered from a fixed ("universal") set of Pauli measurements, using nuclear-norm minimization (e.g., the matrix Lasso), with nearly-optimal bounds on the error. A similar result holds for any class of measurements that use an orthonormal operator basis whose elements have small operator norm. Our proof uses Dudley's inequality for Gaussian processes, together with bounds on covering numbers obtained via entropy duality.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to reconstruct an unknown low-rank matrix from a limited number of Pauli measurements, a problem relevant to quantum state tomography. It relates the task to compressed sensing: low matrix rank plays a role analogous to sparsity when recovering a vector from limited Fourier information.

For a dimension-d matrix of rank r, the authors show that almost all sets of O(rd log⁶ d) Pauli measurements satisfy the rank-r restricted isometry property. This property supports recovery using nuclear-norm minimization, including the matrix Lasso, with nearly optimal error bounds. The measurement set is universal in the sense that a fixed set can support the recovery guarantee.

The result also extends to orthonormal operator bases whose elements have small operator norm. The proof combines an inequality for Gaussian processes with covering-number bounds obtained through entropy duality. The significance is a theoretical route from a limited, fixed measurement collection to reliable low-rank recovery, with the stated measurement-property guarantee holding for almost all such sets.
summary.tldr: Almost all sufficiently large Pauli measurement sets support universal low-rank matrix recovery with nearly optimal error bounds.

title: Universal low-rank matrix recovery from Pauli measurements

abstract: Many machine learning problems can be interpreted as learning for matching two types of objects (e.g., images and captions, users and products, queries and documents). The matching level of two objects is usually measured as the inner product in a certain feature space, while the modeling effort focuses on mapping of objects from the original space to the feature space. This schema, although proven successful on a range of matching tasks, is insufficient for capturing the rich structure in the matching process of more complicated objects. In this paper, we propose a new deep architecture to more effectively model the complicated matching relations between two objects from heterogeneous domains. More specifically, we apply this model to matching tasks in natural language, e.g., finding sensible responses for a tweet, or relevant answers to a given question. This new architecture naturally combines the localness and hierarchy intrinsic to the natural language problems, and therefore greatly improves upon the state-of-the-art models.

paragraphs: Matching short texts involves deciding whether two pieces of language fit together, such as a question and a relevant answer. A common approach maps each object into a feature space and measures the match through an inner product. The paper argues that this arrangement can miss richer relationships involved in matching complicated objects.

The authors propose a deep architecture designed to represent those relationships more effectively. Its central organizing ideas are locality and hierarchy in natural language: matching involves structure at different levels, rather than only a single comparison between overall representations. The architecture brings these properties together when comparing objects from different domains or roles.

The paper applies the approach to language tasks, including finding sensible tweet responses and relevant answers to questions. It reports substantial improvements over the state-of-the-art models. The contribution is therefore an architecture that gives the matching process itself more expressive structure, with reported benefits for the natural-language tasks considered.
summary.tldr: A deep architecture uses locality and hierarchy in language to improve matching between short texts.

title: A Deep Architecture for Matching Short Texts

abstract: Deep learning has recently been introduced to the field of low-level computer vision and image processing. Promising results have been obtained in a number of tasks including super-resolution, inpainting, deconvolution, filtering, etc. However, previously adopted neural network approaches such as convolutional neural networks and sparse auto-encoders are inherently with translation invariant operators. We found this property prevents the deep learning approaches from outperforming the state-of-the-art if the task itself requires translation variant interpolation (TVI). In this paper, we draw on Shepard interpolation and design Shepard Convolutional Neural Networks (ShCNN) which efficiently realizes end-to-end trainable TVI operators in the network. We show that by adding only a few feature maps in the new Shepard layers, the network is able to achieve stronger results than a much deeper architecture. Superior performance on both image inpainting and super-resolution is obtained where our system outperforms previous ones while keeping the running time competitive.

paragraphs: Image restoration tasks can require interpolation rules that change with location. The authors identify the translation-invariant operators used in earlier neural approaches as an obstacle when the task requires this spatial variation. Their focus is therefore on changing the kind of operation the network can perform, rather than relying only on a larger architecture.

Drawing on Shepard interpolation, they introduce Shepard Convolutional Neural Networks. The new layers implement translation-variant interpolation efficiently and can be trained together with the rest of the network from end to end. This makes the required location-dependent interpolation part of the learned image-processing system.

The authors report that adding only a few feature maps in Shepard layers produces stronger results than a much deeper architecture. They also report superior performance over previous systems on image inpainting and super-resolution while retaining competitive running time. These findings support matching a network's operators to the interpolation requirements of the task, showing that an appropriate computational building block can matter more than additional depth in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Shepard layers learn location-dependent interpolation, improving reported inpainting and super-resolution results with competitive runtime.

title: Shepard Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: We propose a new primal-dual algorithmic framework for a prototypical constrained convex optimization template. The algorithmic instances of our framework are universal since they can automatically adapt to the unknown Holder continuity degree and constant within the dual formulation. They are also guaranteed to have optimal convergence rates in the objective residual and the feasibility gap for each Holder smoothness degree. In contrast to existing primal-dual algorithms, our framework avoids the proximity operator of the objective function. We instead leverage computationally cheaper, Fenchel-type operators, which are the main workhorses of the generalized conditional gradient (GCG)-type methods. In contrast to the GCG-type methods, our framework does not require the objective function to be differentiable, and can also process additional general linear inclusion constraints, while guarantees the convergence rate on the primal problem.

paragraphs: Constrained convex optimization requires improving an objective while also satisfying constraints. This paper introduces a primal-dual framework that addresses both requirements while adapting to smoothness properties that need not be known beforehand. Its algorithms automatically adjust to the degree and constant of Hölder continuity in the dual formulation, which describe how smoothly that formulation behaves.

A central computational choice is to avoid the objective function's proximity operator. Instead, the framework uses Fenchel-type operators, described as cheaper computational building blocks and also used in generalized conditional gradient methods. This changes the operations required from the objective while preserving a framework for solving the constrained problem.

The stated guarantees cover both objective error and constraint violation, with optimal convergence rates for each Hölder smoothness degree. The framework also accommodates nondifferentiable objectives and additional general linear inclusion constraints. Its contribution is therefore a combination of automatic adaptation, alternative computational primitives, and guarantees for the primal problem within the constrained convex template studied.
summary.tldr: A primal-dual framework adapts to unknown smoothness and achieves optimal convergence guarantees using cheaper alternatives to proximity operators.

title: A Universal Primal-Dual Convex Optimization Framework

abstract: Spreading processes are often modelled as a stochastic dynamics occurring on top of a given network with edge weights corresponding to the transmission probabilities. Knowledge of veracious transmission probabilities is essential for prediction, optimization, and control of diffusion dynamics. Unfortunately, in most cases the transmission rates are unknown and need to be reconstructed from the spreading data. Moreover, in realistic settings it is impossible to monitor the state of each node at every time, and thus the data is highly incomplete. We introduce an efficient dynamic message-passing algorithm, which is able to reconstruct parameters of the spreading model given only partial information on the activation times of nodes in the network. The method is generalizable to a large class of dynamic models, as well to the case of temporal graphs.

paragraphs: A spreading model describes stochastic activity moving across a network, with edge weights representing transmission probabilities. Those probabilities matter for predicting, optimizing, and controlling the spread. In practice, however, they are often unknown. The task is therefore to reconstruct the model’s parameters from observations of the spreading process.

The paper focuses on incomplete observations, reflecting the difficulty of monitoring every node at every time. Its proposed dynamic message-passing algorithm can reconstruct spreading parameters using only partial information about when nodes become active. The inference problem starts from a given network and seeks the transmission parameters governing dynamics on that network.

The authors describe the algorithm as efficient and state that it can be generalized to a large class of dynamic models and to temporal graphs. Its main contribution is a route from partially observed activation histories to estimates of the underlying spreading parameters. This matters because the information needed for modeling transmission can be recovered without requiring a complete record of every node’s state throughout the process.
summary.tldr: Dynamic message passing reconstructs network spreading parameters from partially observed node activation times.

title: Reconstructing Parameters of Spreading Models from Partial Observations

abstract: A central challenge in neuroscience is understanding how neural system implements computation through its dynamics. We propose a nonlinear time series model aimed at characterizing interpretable dynamics from neural trajectories. Our model assumes low-dimensional continuous dynamics in a finite volume. It incorporates a prior assumption about globally contractional dynamics to avoid overly enthusiastic extrapolation outside of the support of observed trajectories. We show that our model can recover qualitative features of the phase portrait such as attractors, slow points, and bifurcations, while also producing reliable long-term future predictions in a variety of dynamical models and in real neural data.

paragraphs: The paper develops a nonlinear time-series model to explain how neural activity evolves. Its aim is interpretability as well as prediction: the authors want to characterize the structure of the dynamics underlying observed neural trajectories. The model assumes that these dynamics are continuous, low-dimensional, and confined to a finite volume.

A central design choice is a prior favoring globally contracting dynamics. This constrains how the model behaves beyond the region supported by observed trajectories, reducing overly aggressive extrapolation. The assumption matters because predicting a trajectory far into the future requires specifying behavior at states that may have little direct support in the observations.

The authors show that the model can recover qualitative features of the phase portrait, including attractors, slow points, and bifurcations. These describe where trajectories tend to settle, linger, or change their overall behavior. They also report reliable long-term predictions across several dynamical models and real neural data. The findings connect an explicit dynamical assumption with both interpretable structure and demonstrated forecasting performance.
summary.tldr: A nonlinear neural-trajectory model uses a contraction prior to recover interpretable dynamics and support reliable long-term predictions.

title: Interpretable Nonlinear Dynamic Modeling of Neural Trajectories

abstract: Gaussian processes are rich distributions over functions, with generalization properties determined by a kernel function. When used for long-range extrapolation, predictions are particularly sensitive to the choice of kernel parameters. It is therefore critical to account for kernel uncertainty in our predictive distributions. We propose a distribution over kernels formed by modelling a spectral mixture density with a Levy process. The resulting distribution has support for all stationary covariances---including the popular RBF, periodic, and Matern kernels---combined with inductive biases which enable automatic and data efficient learning, long-range extrapolation, and state of the art predictive performance. The proposed model also presents an approach to spectral regularization, as the Levy process introduces a sparsity-inducing prior over mixture components, allowing automatic selection over model order and pruning of extraneous components. We exploit the algebraic structure of the proposed process for O(n) training and O(1) predictions. We perform extrapolations having reasonable uncertainty estimates on several benchmarks, show that the proposed model can recover flexible ground truth covariances and that it is robust to errors in initialization.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process predictions depend on the kernel describing relationships between function values. For long-range extrapolation, uncertainty about the kernel’s parameters can strongly affect predictions. This paper models that uncertainty through a distribution over kernels, constructed by placing a Lévy process over a spectral mixture density.

The resulting distribution supports all stationary covariance functions, including RBF, periodic, and Matérn kernels. Its prior favors sparse mixtures, allowing the model to select its complexity automatically and remove unnecessary components. This links flexible kernel learning with spectral regularization: the representation can accommodate varied covariance patterns while discouraging extraneous mixture terms.

The authors exploit the process’s algebraic structure to obtain O(n) training and O(1) prediction costs. Their benchmarks demonstrate long-range extrapolation with reasonable uncertainty estimates, recovery of flexible ground-truth covariances, and robustness to initialization errors. They also report state-of-the-art predictive performance. These findings support the proposed combination of kernel uncertainty, automatic complexity selection, and computational scalability for the evaluated prediction problems.
summary.tldr: A Lévy-process prior learns flexible stationary kernels with uncertainty and automatic complexity selection, supporting scalable Gaussian-process extrapolation.

title: Scalable Levy Process Priors for Spectral Kernel Learning

abstract: The collection and analysis of telemetry data from user's devices is routinely performed by many software companies. Telemetry collection leads to improved user experience but poses significant risks to users' privacy. Locally differentially private (LDP) algorithms have recently emerged as the main tool that allows data collectors to estimate various population statistics, while preserving privacy. The guarantees provided by such algorithms are typically very strong for a single round of telemetry collection, but degrade rapidly when telemetry is collected regularly. In particular, existing LDP algorithms are not suitable for repeated collection of counter data such as daily app usage statistics. In this paper, we develop new LDP mechanisms geared towards repeated collection of counter data, with formal privacy guarantees even after being executed for an arbitrarily long period of time. For two basic analytical tasks, mean estimation and histogram estimation, our LDP mechanisms for repeated data collection provide estimates with comparable or even the same accuracy as existing single-round LDP collection mechanisms. We conduct empirical evaluation on real-world counter datasets to verify our theoretical results. Our mechanisms have been deployed by Microsoft to collect telemetry across millions of devices.

paragraphs: Software telemetry helps companies understand device usage, but repeatedly collecting it creates a privacy problem. Locally differentially private methods can provide strong protection for a single collection round while losing protection rapidly across repeated rounds. Counter data, such as daily application usage, makes this issue especially relevant because the same kind of measurement is collected regularly.

The paper develops local differential privacy mechanisms specifically for repeated counter collection. Their formal privacy guarantees continue to apply over arbitrarily long execution periods. The design therefore treats repeated reporting as part of the problem itself, rather than relying on the privacy guarantee of an isolated report.

For estimating population means and histograms, the mechanisms achieve accuracy comparable to, or even the same as, existing single-round methods. The authors evaluate them on real counter datasets to check the theoretical findings and report deployment by Microsoft across millions of devices. Together, these results indicate that continuing telemetry collection can retain useful aggregate accuracy while supporting the stated long-term privacy guarantees.
summary.tldr: New local differential privacy mechanisms support repeated counter telemetry with long-term privacy guarantees and accuracy comparable to single-round methods.

title: Collecting Telemetry Data Privately

abstract: In this paper, we investigate Dimensionality reduction (DR) maps in an information retrieval setting from a quantitative topology point of view. In particular, we show that no DR maps can achieve perfect precision and perfect recall simultaneously. Thus a continuous DR map must have imperfect precision. We further prove an upper bound on the precision of Lipschitz continuous DR maps. While precision is a natural measure in an information retrieval setting, it does not measure `how' wrong the retrieved data is. We therefore propose a new measure based on Wasserstein distance that comes with similar theoretical guarantee. A key technical step in our proofs is a particular optimization problem of the $L_2$-Wasserstein distance over a constrained set of distributions. We provide a complete solution to this optimization problem, which can be of independent interest on the technical side.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction represents data in fewer dimensions, but the paper asks what this compression necessarily loses when the representation is used for information retrieval. It studies the question through quantitative topology, focusing on precision and recall as measures of how faithfully retrieval preserves the original relationships.

Within the studied setting, the authors prove that no dimensionality-reduction map can achieve perfect precision and perfect recall together. They establish that a continuous map must have imperfect precision and derive an upper bound on precision for Lipschitz continuous maps. These results quantify geometric restrictions on retrieval quality rather than attributing all errors to a particular learning algorithm.

Precision alone does not describe the severity of an incorrect retrieval. The authors therefore introduce a measure based on Wasserstein distance with a similar theoretical guarantee. Their proofs require optimizing the L2-Wasserstein distance over a constrained collection of distributions, and they provide a complete solution to that problem. The work supplies both limits on retrieval fidelity and a way to account for how wrong retrieved results are.
summary.tldr: The paper proves geometric limits on dimensionality-reduction retrieval quality and introduces a Wasserstein-based measure of retrieval error.

title: Dimensionality Reduction has Quantifiable Imperfections: Two Geometric Bounds

abstract: The state-of-the-art hardware platforms for training deep neural networks are moving from traditional single precision (32-bit) computations towards 16 bits of precision - in large part due to the high energy efficiency and smaller bit storage associated with using reduced-precision representations. However, unlike inference, training with numbers represented with less than 16 bits has been challenging due to the need to maintain fidelity of the gradient computations during back-propagation. Here we demonstrate, for the first time, the successful training of deep neural networks using 8-bit floating point numbers while fully maintaining the accuracy on a spectrum of deep learning models and datasets. In addition to reducing the data and computation precision to 8 bits, we also successfully reduce the arithmetic precision for additions (used in partial product accumulation and weight updates) from 32 bits to 16 bits through the introduction of a number of key ideas including chunk-based accumulation and floating point stochastic rounding. The use of these novel techniques lays the foundation for a new generation of hardware training platforms with the potential for 2-4 times improved throughput over today's systems.

paragraphs: Lower-precision arithmetic reduces storage needs and can improve energy efficiency, but training places demanding requirements on gradient accuracy. This paper demonstrates training deep neural networks with eight-bit floating-point data and computation while maintaining accuracy across a range of models and datasets. The challenge extends beyond representing the forward computation compactly.

The authors also reduce the precision of additions used in partial-product accumulation and weight updates from 32 bits to 16 bits. Their techniques include chunk-based accumulation and floating-point stochastic rounding. These changes address arithmetic operations that remain important even when the main data representation uses eight bits, making the precision reduction broader than a change to stored values alone.

The reported training results establish that this combination can preserve accuracy in the evaluated settings. The hardware implication is prospective: the authors describe a foundation for training platforms with the potential to improve throughput by a factor of two to four. That projected hardware benefit is distinct from the demonstrated ability to train the tested networks accurately at reduced precision.
summary.tldr: Eight-bit floating-point training with specialized accumulation and rounding preserves tested model accuracy and supports potential hardware throughput gains.

title: Training Deep Neural Networks with 8-bit Floating Point Numbers

abstract: An Euler discretization of the Langevin diffusion is known to converge to the global minimizers of certain convex and non-convex optimization problems. We show that this property holds for any suitably smooth diffusion and that different diffusions are suitable for optimizing different classes of convex and non-convex functions. This allows us to design diffusions suitable for globally optimizing convex and non-convex functions not covered by the existing Langevin theory. Our non-asymptotic analysis delivers computable optimization and integration error bounds based on easily accessed properties of the objective and chosen diffusion. Central to our approach are new explicit Stein factor bounds on the solutions of Poisson equations. We complement these results with improved optimization guarantees for targets other than the standard Gibbs measure.

paragraphs: Diffusion processes provide a route to optimization through dynamics that combine movement with randomness. Earlier theory established that an Euler discretization of Langevin diffusion can converge to global minimizers for certain convex and non-convex objectives. This paper broadens that perspective to suitably smooth diffusions and studies how the choice of diffusion relates to the objective being optimized.

Different diffusions are suitable for different classes of functions. The authors use that flexibility to design processes for convex and non-convex objectives outside the coverage of existing Langevin theory. Their analysis is non-asymptotic: it gives computable optimization and integration error bounds using accessible properties of both the objective and the selected diffusion.

The technical foundation includes new explicit Stein factor bounds for solutions of Poisson equations. These support the error analysis behind the optimization framework. The paper also improves guarantees for target distributions beyond the standard Gibbs measure, expanding the choices available when connecting diffusion dynamics to global optimization. The results retain the smoothness and objective-dependent qualifications of the framework.
summary.tldr: The paper extends diffusion-based global optimization beyond Langevin dynamics, with computable finite-time error bounds for suitable objectives and smooth diffusions.

title: Global Non-convex Optimization with Discretized Diffusions

abstract: Recent developments in differentially private (DP) machine learning and DP Bayesian learning have enabled learning under strong privacy guarantees for the training data subjects. In this paper, we further extend the applicability of DP Bayesian learning by presenting the first general DP Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm whose privacy-guarantees are not subject to unrealistic assumptions on Markov chain convergence and that is applicable to posterior inference in arbitrary models. Our algorithm is based on a decomposition of the Barker acceptance test that allows evaluating the Rényi DP privacy cost of the accept-reject choice. We further show how to improve the DP guarantee through data subsampling and approximate acceptance tests.

Our algorithm is based on a decomposition of the Barker acceptance test that allows evaluating the Rényi DP privacy cost of the accept-reject choice. paragraphs: Bayesian learning uses posterior inference to reason about unknown model quantities from data. When those data describe people, the inference procedure may also need formal privacy protections. This paper extends differentially private Bayesian learning with a general Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that applies to posterior inference in arbitrary models.

The central contribution concerns the privacy of the sampling procedure's accept-or-reject decision. The authors decompose the Barker acceptance test in a way that makes this decision's Rényi differential privacy cost possible to evaluate. This provides a basis for privacy accounting without relying on the unrealistic assumptions about Markov chain convergence that the paper identifies in earlier approaches.

The authors additionally show how data subsampling and approximate acceptance tests can strengthen the differential privacy guarantee. These results broaden the applicability of private posterior inference by addressing privacy within the sampling mechanism itself. The stated advance is a general algorithm and its privacy analysis; the convergence-related claim concerns the assumptions required for that privacy guarantee.
summary.tldr: A general private MCMC algorithm accounts for accept-or-reject privacy costs without unrealistic assumptions about chain convergence.

title: Differentially Private Markov Chain Monte Carlo

abstract: In this paper, we provide a method to learn the directed structure of a Bayesian network using data. The data is accessed by making conditional probability queries to a black-box model. We introduce a notion of simplicity of representation of conditional probability tables for the nodes in the Bayesian network, that we call ` low rankness''. We connect this notion to the Fourier transformation of real valued set functions and propose a method which learns the exact directed structure of a low rank` Bayesian network using very few queries. We formally prove that our method correctly recovers the true directed structure, runs in polynomial time and only needs polynomial samples with respect to the number of nodes. We also provide further improvements in efficiency if we have access to some observational data.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover the directed structure of a Bayesian network from data accessed through a black-box model. The algorithm obtains information by asking conditional-probability queries. Its central assumption is a form of simplicity in the conditional probability tables associated with network nodes, which the authors call low rankness.

The authors connect this representation property to the Fourier transformation of real-valued set functions. That connection supports a method for learning the exact directed structure of a low-rank Bayesian network using few queries. The contribution links a constraint on how local probabilities are represented to the larger problem of recovering the network’s directed relationships.

The paper formally proves correct recovery, polynomial running time, and polynomial sample requirements as a function of the number of nodes. It also describes further efficiency improvements when observational data are available. These guarantees apply to the stated low-rank setting and query-based access model, making the representation assumption an essential part of why efficient exact recovery is possible.
summary.tldr: A query-based method exactly recovers low-rank Bayesian network structure with polynomial time and sample requirements.

title: Learning Bayesian Networks with Low Rank Conditional Probability Tables

abstract: Differential Privacy is a popular and well-studied notion of privacy. In the era ofbig data that we are in, privacy concerns are becoming ever more prevalent and thusdifferential privacy is being turned to as one such solution. A popular method forensuring differential privacy of a classifier is known as subsample-and-aggregate,in which the dataset is divided into distinct chunks and a model is learned on eachchunk, after which it is aggregated. This approach allows for easy analysis of themodel on the data and thus differential privacy can be easily applied. In this paper,we extend this approach by dividing the data several times (rather than just once)and learning models on each chunk within each division. The first benefit of thisapproach is the natural improvement of utility by aggregating models trained ona more diverse range of subsets of the data (as demonstrated by the well-knownbagging technique). The second benefit is that, through analysis that we provide inthe paper, we can derive tighter differential privacy guarantees when several queriesare made to this mechanism. In order to derive these guarantees, we introducethe upwards and downwards moments accountants and derive bounds for thesemoments accountants in a data-driven fashion. We demonstrate the improvementsour model makes over standard subsample-and-aggregate in two datasets (HeartFailure (private) and UCI Adult (public)).

paragraphs: Subsample-and-aggregate builds a private classifier by dividing training data into separate chunks, training a model on each chunk, and combining their outputs. This paper extends the approach by partitioning the dataset several times and training models within every partition. Aggregation therefore draws on models trained on a more varied collection of data subsets.

That diversity provides the utility benefit associated with bagging. The paper also develops a privacy analysis that yields tighter differential privacy guarantees when the mechanism answers multiple queries. This second contribution concerns how privacy costs accumulate across uses, making the accounting method part of the improvement alongside the enlarged collection of models.

To obtain those guarantees, the authors introduce upwards and downwards moments accountants and bound them using the data. They evaluate the method on a private Heart Failure dataset and the public UCI Adult dataset, demonstrating improvements over standard subsample-and-aggregate. The work thus connects repeated partitioning with both better predictive utility and a more favorable analysis of privacy under repeated querying.
summary.tldr: Repeated data partitioning improves private ensemble utility and enables tighter privacy accounting for multiple queries.

title: Differentially Private Bagging: Improved utility and cheaper privacy than subsample-and-aggregate

abstract: Recent studies have demonstrated the efficiency of generative pretraining for English natural language understanding. In this work, we extend this approach to multiple languages and show the effectiveness of cross-lingual pretraining. We propose two methods to learn cross-lingual language models (XLMs): one unsupervised that only relies on monolingual data, and one supervised that leverages parallel data with a new cross-lingual language model objective. We obtain state-of-the-art results on cross-lingual classification, unsupervised and supervised machine translation. On XNLI, our approach pushes the state of the art by an absolute gain of 4.9% accuracy. On unsupervised machine translation, we obtain 34.3 BLEU on WMT'16 German-English, improving the previous state of the art by more than 9 BLEU. On supervised machine translation, we obtain a new state of the art of 38.5 BLEU on WMT'16 Romanian-English, outperforming the previous best approach by more than 4 BLEU. Our code and pretrained models will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Language model pretraining had shown strong results for English language understanding. This paper extends that approach across languages, investigating whether pretraining can support both cross-lingual classification and machine translation. The aim is to learn language models whose usefulness spans multiple languages and different kinds of downstream tasks.

The authors propose two ways to train cross-lingual language models. The unsupervised method uses only monolingual text, so it does not depend on paired translations. The supervised method uses parallel data through a new cross-lingual language modeling objective. These alternatives address settings with different forms of available language data.

The reported results improve the state of the art in cross-lingual classification and both unsupervised and supervised translation. On XNLI, the accuracy gain is 4.9 absolute percentage points. Unsupervised German-English translation reaches 34.3 BLEU, more than nine points above the previous best, while supervised Romanian-English translation reaches 38.5 BLEU, improving by more than four points. Together, these findings demonstrate the effectiveness of cross-lingual pretraining across the evaluated tasks and data settings.
summary.tldr: Cross-lingual language model pretraining improves classification and translation using either monolingual text or parallel language data.

title: Cross-lingual Language Model Pretraining

abstract: In recent years, neural backdoor attack has been considered to be a potential security threat to deep learning systems. Such systems, while achieving the state-of-the-art performance on clean data, perform abnormally on inputs with predefined triggers. Current backdoor techniques, however, rely on uniform trigger patterns, which are easily detected and mitigated by current defense methods. In this work, we propose a novel backdoor attack technique in which the triggers vary from input to input. To achieve this goal, we implement an input-aware trigger generator driven by diversity loss. A novel cross-trigger test is applied to enforce trigger nonreusablity, making backdoor verification impossible. Experiments show that our method is efficient in various attack scenarios as well as multiple datasets. We further demonstrate that our backdoor can bypass the state of the art defense methods. An analysis with a famous neural network inspector again proves the stealthiness of the proposed attack. Our code is publicly available.

paragraphs: A neural backdoor makes a model behave abnormally on triggered inputs even when it performs well on clean data. This paper targets a common feature of earlier backdoors: the same trigger pattern is reused across inputs. Such uniformity gives defenses a recurring pattern to detect and mitigate, motivating the authors to investigate triggers that depend on the input.

The proposed method uses an input-aware generator and a diversity loss to produce varying triggers. It also introduces a cross-trigger test to enforce nonreusability across inputs. The authors describe this as preventing backdoor verification through trigger reuse, making the relationship between a trigger and its particular input central to the attack.

Experiments across multiple datasets and attack scenarios report an efficient attack that bypasses the state-of-the-art defenses evaluated. Analysis with a neural network inspection tool further supports its stealthiness. The security finding is that defenses built around a shared trigger can be challenged by input-dependent patterns whose behavior does not transfer in the same way.
summary.tldr: Input-dependent, nonreusable triggers let the proposed backdoor evade the defenses and inspection methods evaluated in the paper.

title: Input-Aware Dynamic Backdoor Attack

abstract: We formalize and attack the problem of generating new images from old ones that are as diverse as possible, only allowing them to change without restrictions in certain parts of the image while remaining globally consistent. This encompasses the typical situation found in generative modelling, where we are happy with parts of the generated data, but would like to resample others (``I like this generated castle overall, but this tower looks unrealistic, I would like a new one''). In order to attack this problem we build from the best conditional and unconditional generative models to introduce a new network architecture, training procedure, and a new algorithm for resampling parts of the image as desired.
