This encompasses the typical situation found in generative modelling, where we are happy with parts of the generated data, but would like to resample others (``I like this generated castle overall, but this tower looks unrealistic, I would like a new one''). In order to attack this problem we build from the best conditional and unconditional generative models to introduce a new network architecture, training procedure, and a new algorithm for resampling parts of the image as desired.

paragraphs: A generated image may be satisfactory overall while containing one region that needs another attempt. This paper formalizes the problem of generating diverse alternatives within selected parts of an existing image while keeping the whole image coherent. The aim is to give local freedom without abandoning the surrounding content that already works.

The formulation combines several demands. Selected regions should be allowed to change freely, alternatives should be as diverse as possible, and the resulting image should remain globally consistent. These requirements make the task more specific than generating another complete image: the user is choosing where new variation is wanted.

To address the problem, the authors build on conditional and unconditional generative models and introduce a network architecture, a training procedure, and an algorithm for resampling requested image regions. The contribution spans both the definition of the editing problem and a proposed system for carrying it out. Its practical significance is the ability to revisit part of a generated result while preserving the overall image as a coherent starting point.
summary.tldr: The paper defines and addresses selective image resampling, seeking diverse local changes that remain consistent with the overall image.

title: Low Distortion Block-Resampling with Spatially Stochastic Networks

abstract: We study an online linear optimization (OLO) problem in which the learner is provided access to $K$ ``hint'' vectors in each round prior to making a decision. In this setting, we devise an algorithm that obtains logarithmic regret whenever there exists a convex combination of the $K$ hints that has positive correlation with the cost vectors. This significantly extends prior work that considered only the case $K=1$. To accomplish this, we develop a way to combine many arbitrary OLO algorithms to obtain regret only a logarithmically worse factor than the minimum regret of the original algorithms in hindsight; this result is of independent interest.

In this setting, we devise an algorithm that obtains logarithmic regret whenever there exists a convex combination of the $K$ hints that has positive correlation with the cost vectors. This significantly extends prior work that considered only the case $K=1$. paragraphs: In online linear optimization, a learner repeatedly chooses an action before encountering its cost. This paper studies a setting where K hint vectors arrive before each decision. The challenge is to benefit from several sources of advice when their usefulness may emerge through a combination, rather than through a single hint considered alone.

The authors develop an algorithm with logarithmic regret whenever some convex combination of the hints positively correlates with the cost vectors. A convex combination blends the hints using nonnegative weights that sum to one. The guarantee is conditional on the existence of this useful blend, extending earlier work restricted to one hint.

To obtain the result, the paper introduces a broader method for combining arbitrary online linear optimization algorithms. The combined learner's regret is within a logarithmic factor of the smallest regret achieved by those algorithms in hindsight. This gives the work a second contribution beyond advice vectors: a general way to assemble online algorithms while retaining performance close to the best constituent.
summary.tldr: An online optimization algorithm achieves logarithmic regret when a convex combination of available hints positively correlates with costs.

title: Online Linear Optimization with Many Hints

abstract: Applying differentiable programming techniques and machine learning algorithms to foreign programs requires developers to either rewrite their code in a machine learning framework, or otherwise provide derivatives of the foreign code. This paper presents Enzyme, a high-performance automatic differentiation (AD) compiler plugin for the LLVM compiler framework capable of synthesizing gradients of statically analyzable programs expressed in the LLVM intermediate representation (IR). Enzyme synthesizes gradients for programs written in any language whose compiler targets LLVM IR including C, C++, Fortran, Julia, Rust, Swift, MLIR, etc., thereby providing native AD capabilities in these languages. Unlike traditional source-to-source and operator-overloading tools, Enzyme performs AD on optimized IR. On a machine-learning focused benchmark suite including Microsoft's ADBench, AD on optimized IR achieves a geometric mean speedup of 4.2 times over AD on IR before optimization allowing Enzyme to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Packaging Enzyme for PyTorch and TensorFlow provides convenient access to gradients of foreign code with state-of-the-art performance, enabling foreign code to be directly incorporated into existing machine learning workflows.

paragraphs: Using existing programs inside differentiable machine-learning workflows often requires rewriting them in a framework or supplying derivatives manually. Enzyme addresses this integration problem through an automatic differentiation plugin for LLVM. It synthesizes gradients for statically analyzable programs expressed in LLVM's intermediate representation, making the compiler representation the common point of access.

Because multiple languages compile to LLVM IR, the approach supports programs originating in languages such as C, C++, Fortran, Julia, Rust, and Swift. A central design choice is to differentiate optimized intermediate code. This lets differentiation operate after compiler optimization, rather than restricting it to source-level transformations or operator overloading.

On a machine-learning-focused benchmark suite that includes Microsoft's ADBench, differentiating optimized IR achieves a geometric mean speedup of 4.2 times over differentiating IR before optimization. The authors report state-of-the-art performance and package Enzyme for PyTorch and TensorFlow. This makes gradients of eligible existing code accessible within established workflows, reducing the need to reimplement that code solely to make it differentiable.
summary.tldr: Enzyme generates fast gradients from optimized LLVM code, enabling eligible programs from multiple languages to participate directly in machine-learning workflows.

title: Instead of Rewriting Foreign Code for Machine Learning, Automatically Synthesize Fast Gradients

abstract: Training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) on low-dimensional tasks has been widely used to model functional biological networks. However, the solutions found by learning and the effect of initial connectivity are not well understood. Here, we examine RNNs trained using gradient descent on different tasks inspired by the neuroscience literature. We find that the changes in recurrent connectivity can be described by low-rank matrices. This observation holds even in the presence of random initial connectivity, although this initial connectivity has full rank and significantly accelerates training. To understand the origin of these observations, we turn to an analytically tractable setting: training a linear RNN on a simpler task. We show how the low-dimensional task structure leads to low-rank changes to connectivity, and how random initial connectivity facilitates learning. Altogether, our study opens a new perspective to understand learning in RNNs in light of low-rank connectivity changes and the synergistic role of random initialization.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks trained on low-dimensional tasks are used to study biological network function, but it is less clear how training changes their connections. This paper examines networks trained by gradient descent on neuroscience-inspired tasks, asking how task structure and the network's initial random connectivity jointly shape learning.

The authors find that changes to recurrent connectivity can be described by low-rank matrices. This remains true when the initial connectivity is random and full rank. The distinction matters: learning can add a relatively low-dimensional modification to a much richer starting network. In the experiments, that random starting connectivity also substantially speeds training.

To explain these observations, the paper analyzes a simpler task with a linear recurrent network. This tractable setting shows how low-dimensional task structure produces low-rank connectivity changes and how random initial connections facilitate learning. Together, the empirical and analytical results suggest that structured changes and random initialization can work cooperatively, offering a perspective on learning that focuses on modifications to connectivity rather than only the final network.
summary.tldr: RNNs trained on low-dimensional tasks develop low-rank connectivity changes, while full-rank random initialization can accelerate learning.

title: The interplay between randomness and structure during learning in RNNs

abstract: We consider the problem of obtaining dense 3D reconstructions of deformable objects from single and partially occluded views. In such cases, the visual evidence is usually insufficient to identify a 3D reconstruction uniquely, so we aim at recovering several plausible reconstructions compatible with the input data. We suggest that ambiguities can be modeled more effectively by parametrizing the possible body shapes and poses via a suitable 3D model, such as SMPL for humans. We propose to learn a multi-hypothesis neural network regressor using a best-of-M loss, where each of the M hypotheses is constrained to lie on a manifold of plausible human poses by means of a generative model. We show that our method outperforms alternative approaches in ambiguous pose recovery on standard benchmarks for 3D humans, and in heavily occluded versions of these benchmarks.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a human body in three dimensions from one image can leave several answers consistent with the evidence. Occlusion makes this ambiguity more pronounced because parts of the body are hidden. This paper treats that uncertainty as part of the reconstruction problem: the goal is to produce several plausible bodies instead of committing to a single interpretation.

The method uses a neural network that predicts M candidate reconstructions and trains with a best-of-M loss. Body shape and pose are expressed through a suitable parametric 3D model, such as SMPL. A generative model also constrains each candidate to a space of plausible human poses, so producing multiple answers remains tied to realistic body configurations.

The authors report better ambiguous-pose recovery than alternative approaches on standard human reconstruction benchmarks and heavily occluded versions of those benchmarks. These findings support representing ambiguity explicitly through several constrained hypotheses. The contribution is a way to recover plausible alternatives when the image itself cannot uniquely determine the underlying body.
summary.tldr: A neural network predicts several plausible 3D human bodies to handle ambiguity and occlusion in single-image reconstruction.

title: 3D Multi-bodies: Fitting Sets of Plausible 3D Human Models to Ambiguous Image Data

abstract: We present a novel discriminator for GANs that improves realness and diversity of generated samples by learning a structured hypersphere embedding space using spherical circles. The proposed discriminator learns to populate realistic samples around the longest spherical circle, i.e., a great circle, while pushing unrealistic samples toward the poles perpendicular to the great circle. Since longer circles occupy larger area on the hypersphere, they encourage more diversity in representation learning, and vice versa. Discriminating samples based on their corresponding spherical circles can thus naturally induce diversity to generated samples. We also extend the proposed method for conditional settings with class labels by creating a hypersphere for each category and performing class-wise discrimination and update. In experiments, we validate the effectiveness for both unconditional and conditional generation on standard benchmarks, achieving the state of the art.

The proposed discriminator learns to populate realistic samples around the longest spherical circle, i.e., a great circle, while pushing unrealistic samples toward the poles perpendicular to the great circle. Since longer circles occupy larger area on the hypersphere, they encourage more diversity in representation learning, and vice versa. Discriminating samples based on their corresponding spherical circles can thus naturally induce diversity to generated samples. We also extend the proposed method for conditional settings with class labels by creating a hypersphere for each category and performing class-wise discrimination and update. In experiments, we validate the effectiveness for both unconditional and conditional generation on standard benchmarks, achieving the state of the art.

paragraphs: CircleGAN changes the discriminator in a generative adversarial network to encourage both realistic and diverse samples. Its central idea is to organize learned representations on a hypersphere, using positions relative to spherical circles to distinguish realistic examples from unrealistic ones. This gives the discriminator a geometric structure for judging generated data.

The discriminator places realistic samples around a great circle, the sphere’s longest circle, and pushes unrealistic samples toward the perpendicular poles. Longer circles offer more room for representations to spread out. The method uses this relationship between circle size and representational diversity to encourage the generator to produce varied samples as it learns to make them realistic.

For generation conditioned on class labels, the method assigns a separate hypersphere to each category and performs discrimination and updates within each class. Experiments support the approach for both conditional and unconditional generation, with state-of-the-art results on the reported standard benchmarks. The contribution is a discriminator whose representation geometry explicitly connects judgments of realism with encouragement of diversity.
summary.tldr: CircleGAN organizes discriminator representations on spherical circles to encourage realistic, diverse generation.

title: CircleGAN: Generative Adversarial Learning across Spherical Circles

abstract: Nonparametric regression on complex domains has been a challenging task as most existing methods, such as ensemble models based on binary decision trees, are not designed to account for intrinsic geometries and domain boundaries. This article proposes a Bayesian additive regression spanning trees (BAST) model for nonparametric regression on manifolds, with an emphasis on complex constrained domains or irregularly shaped spaces embedded in Euclidean spaces. Our model is built upon a random spanning tree manifold partition model as each weak learner, which is capable of capturing any irregularly shaped spatially contiguous partitions while respecting intrinsic geometries and domain boundary constraints. Utilizing many nice properties of spanning tree structures, we design an efficient Bayesian inference algorithm. Equipped with a soft prediction scheme, BAST is demonstrated to significantly outperform other competing methods in simulation experiments and in an application to the chlorophyll data in Aral Sea, due to its strong local adaptivity to different levels of smoothness.

paragraphs: Regression on an irregularly shaped domain needs to account for the domain’s geometry and boundaries. Many existing approaches, including ensembles of binary decision trees, are not designed to do this. BAST addresses the problem with a Bayesian regression model for manifolds, emphasizing constrained or irregular spaces embedded in Euclidean space.

Each weak learner partitions the manifold using a random spanning tree. These partitions can take irregular shapes while remaining spatially contiguous and respecting the domain’s intrinsic geometry and boundary constraints. Combining these learners gives the model a way to adapt its predictions to the structure of the space. The authors also use properties of spanning trees to construct an efficient Bayesian inference algorithm.

Together with a soft prediction scheme, BAST significantly outperforms competing methods in the reported simulations and an application involving chlorophyll data from the Aral Sea. The abstract attributes this performance to strong local adaptability across regions with different levels of smoothness. The findings support geometry-aware partitioning when regression must follow an irregular domain.
summary.tldr: BAST combines spanning-tree partitions in a Bayesian regression model that respects irregular domain geometry and adapts to local smoothness.

title: BAST: Bayesian Additive Regression Spanning Trees for Complex Constrained Domain

abstract: The invariance principle from causality is at the heart of notable approaches such as invariant risk minimization (IRM) that seek to address out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization failures. Despite the promising theory, invariance principle-based approaches fail in common classification tasks, where invariant (causal) features capture all the information about the label. Are these failures due to the methods failing to capture the invariance? Or is the invariance principle itself insufficient? To answer these questions, we revisit the fundamental assumptions in linear regression tasks, where invariance-based approaches were shown to provably generalize OOD. In contrast to the linear regression tasks, we show that for linear classification tasks we need much stronger restrictions on the distribution shifts, or otherwise OOD generalization is impossible. Furthermore, even with appropriate restrictions on distribution shifts in place, we show that the invariance principle alone is insufficient. We prove that a form of the information bottleneck constraint along with invariance helps address the key failures when invariant features capture all the information about the label and also retains the existing success when they do not. We propose an approach that incorporates both of these principles and demonstrate its effectiveness in several experiments.

paragraphs: Learning features whose predictive relationships remain stable across environments is a major strategy for handling distribution shifts. Yet invariance-based methods can fail in classification even when invariant features contain all the information needed to determine the label. This paper asks whether those failures arise from imperfect methods or from limits of invariance itself.

The authors revisit assumptions that support generalisation guarantees in linear regression and compare them with linear classification. They show that classification requires substantially stronger restrictions on distribution shifts; without suitable restrictions, out-of-distribution generalisation is impossible. They also establish that invariance alone remains insufficient even when appropriate shift restrictions are imposed.

The proposed remedy combines invariance with a form of information bottleneck constraint, which limits information retained in the representation. The theory shows that this combination addresses key failures when invariant features fully determine labels while preserving existing successes when they do not. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of an approach built from both principles, supporting a more qualified account of when invariance can help.
summary.tldr: Combining invariance with an information bottleneck addresses classification failures that invariance alone cannot resolve under suitable shift restrictions.

title: Invariance Principle Meets Information Bottleneck for Out-of-Distribution Generalization

abstract: We study a multi-armed bandit problem where the rewards exhibit regime switching. Specifically, the distributions of the random rewards generated from all arms are modulated by a common underlying state modeled as a finite-state Markov chain. The agent does not observe the underlying state and has to learn the transition matrix and the reward distributions. We propose a learning algorithm for this problem, building on spectral method-of-moments estimations for hidden Markov models, belief error control in partially observable Markov decision processes and upper-confidence-bound methods for online learning. We also establish an upper bound $O(T^{2/3}\sqrt{\log T})$ for the proposed learning algorithm where $T$ is the learning horizon. Finally, we conduct proof-of-concept experiments to illustrate the performance of the learning algorithm.
originalAbstract: We study a multi-armed bandit problem where the rewards exhibit regime switching. Specifically, the distributions of the random rewards generated from all arms are modulated by a common underlying state modeled as a finite-state Markov chain. The agent does not observe the underlying state and has to learn the transition matrix and the reward distributions. We propose a learning algorithm for this problem, building on spectral method-of-moments estimations for hidden Markov models, belief error control in partially observable Markov decision processes and upper-confidence-bound methods for online learning. We also establish an upper bound $O(T^{2/3}\sqrt{\log T})$ for the proposed learning algorithm where $T$ is the learning horizon. Finally, we conduct proof-of-concept experiments to illustrate the performance of the learning algorithm.

paragraphs: In this bandit problem, the reward distributions of all available actions change with a shared hidden regime. That regime follows a finite-state Markov chain, so the environment's changes have temporal structure. The learner observes neither the underlying state nor the transition and reward distributions, making action selection a problem of learning under partial observability.

The proposed algorithm combines three tools. Spectral method-of-moments estimation learns hidden Markov model quantities, belief-error control addresses uncertainty about the unobserved state, and upper-confidence-bound methods guide online learning. These components connect estimating the environment's dynamics with making decisions while those estimates are still imperfect.

The paper establishes an upper bound of O(T^(2/3) sqrt(log T)) for its learning algorithm, where T is the learning horizon, and supplies proof-of-concept experiments. The bound grows sublinearly with the horizon. The central contribution is an analyzed learning approach for the specified shared-regime model, with experiments illustrating its behavior rather than establishing performance across arbitrary forms of environmental change.
summary.tldr: The paper develops and analyzes a bandit algorithm for rewards governed by an unobserved shared Markov regime.

title: Regime Switching Bandits

abstract: The plug-and-play priors (PnP) and regularization by denoising (RED) methods have become widely used for solving inverse problems by leveraging pre-trained deep denoisers as image priors. While the empirical imaging performance and the theoretical convergence properties of these algorithms have been widely investigated, their recovery properties have not previously been theoretically analyzed. We address this gap by showing how to establish theoretical recovery guarantees for PnP/RED by assuming that the solution of these methods lies near the fixed-points of a deep neural network. We also present numerical results comparing the recovery performance of PnP/RED in compressive sensing against that of recent compressive sensing algorithms based on generative models. Our numerical results suggest that PnP with a pre-trained artifact removal network provides significantly better results compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods.

Their empirical performance and convergence behavior had already received substantial attention. This paper focuses on a different question: what can theoretically be said about the quality of the recovered solution, beyond whether an algorithm converges?

The authors establish a route to recovery guarantees by assuming that the methods' solution lies near fixed points of a deep neural network. A fixed point is an input that the network leaves unchanged. This assumption links the recovered solution to the network's behavior and supports the theoretical recovery analysis. The guarantees therefore depend on a stated relationship between the solution and those fixed points.

The paper also evaluates recovery in compressive sensing against recent methods based on generative models. Its numerical results suggest that plug-and-play reconstruction with a pretrained artifact-removal network gives significantly better results than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The work combines conditional theoretical guarantees with empirical evidence about a specific reconstruction setting.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional recovery guarantees for denoiser-based inverse methods and reports promising compressive-sensing results.

title: Recovery Analysis for Plug-and-Play Priors using the Restricted Eigenvalue Condition

abstract: Transductive inference is widely used in few-shot learning, as it leverages the statistics of the unlabeled query set of a few-shot task, typically yielding substantially better performances than its inductive counterpart. The current few-shot benchmarks use perfectly class-balanced tasks at inference. We argue that such an artificial regularity is unrealistic, as it assumes that the marginal label probability of the testing samples is known and fixed to the uniform distribution. In fact, in realistic scenarios, the unlabeled query sets come with arbitrary and unknown label marginals. We introduce and study the effect of arbitrary class distributions within the query sets of few-shot tasks at inference, removing the class-balance artefact. Specifically, we model the marginal probabilities of the classes as Dirichlet-distributed random variables, which yields a principled and realistic sampling within the simplex. This leverages the current few-shot benchmarks, building testing tasks with arbitrary class distributions. We evaluate experimentally state-of-the-art transductive methods over 3 widely used data sets, and observe, surprisingly, substantial performance drops, even below inductive methods in some cases. Furthermore, we propose a generalization of the mutual-information loss, based on α-divergences, which can handle effectively class-distribution variations. Empirically, we show that our transductive α-divergence optimization outperforms state-of-the-art methods across several data sets, models and few-shot settings.

paragraphs: Transductive few-shot methods use the unlabeled query set's collective statistics to improve predictions from a small labeled set. The paper questions evaluations that make every query set perfectly class-balanced. That arrangement fixes class proportions to a uniform distribution, whereas practical query sets can have unknown and unequal proportions.

The authors construct evaluation tasks with class probabilities sampled from a Dirichlet distribution, allowing varying class mixtures within existing benchmarks. Across three widely used datasets, leading transductive methods experience substantial performance drops. Some even fall below inductive methods, showing that their apparent advantage can depend strongly on the balance built into the evaluation.

The paper also proposes an alpha-divergence generalization of the mutual-information loss to handle changing class distributions. Its optimization method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across the evaluated datasets, models, and few-shot settings. The contribution combines a more varied testing protocol with an objective designed for that variation, making class proportions an explicit part of assessing few-shot performance.
summary.tldr: Unequal query-class proportions expose weaknesses in transductive few-shot methods, while an alpha-divergence objective improves performance under this variation.

title: Realistic evaluation of transductive few-shot learning

abstract: Modern approaches typically formulate semantic segmentation as a per-pixel classification task, while instance-level segmentation is handled with an alternative mask classification. Our key insight: mask classification is sufficiently general to solve both semantic- and instance-level segmentation tasks in a unified manner using the exact same model, loss, and training procedure. Following this observation, we propose MaskFormer, a simple mask classification model which predicts a set of binary masks, each associated with a single global class label prediction. Overall, the proposed mask classification-based method simplifies the landscape of effective approaches to semantic and panoptic segmentation tasks and shows excellent empirical results. In particular, we observe that MaskFormer outperforms per-pixel classification baselines when the number of classes is large. Our mask classification-based method outperforms both current state-of-the-art semantic (55.6 mIoU on ADE20K) and panoptic segmentation (52.7 PQ on COCO) models.

This formulation simplifies the range of approaches needed for semantic and panoptic segmentation, and the authors observe a particular advantage over per-pixel classification baselines when the class vocabulary is large.

The reported results surpass the semantic and panoptic state-of-the-art models used in the paper's comparisons. MaskFormer reaches 55.6 mIoU on ADE20K for semantic segmentation and 52.7 PQ on COCO for panoptic segmentation. These findings support mask classification as an effective unified approach. The central claim is that it is sufficiently general for both task types, with the empirical comparisons showing that this unification can also deliver strong performance.
summary.tldr: MaskFormer unifies segmentation through labeled mask predictions and achieves strong semantic and panoptic results, especially relative to per-pixel baselines with many classes.

title: Per-Pixel Classification is Not All You Need for Semantic Segmentation

abstract: We consider robust variants of the standard optimal transport, named robust optimal transport, where marginal constraints are relaxed via Kullback-Leibler divergence. We show that Sinkhorn-based algorithms can approximate the optimal cost of robust optimal transport in $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{n^2}{\varepsilon})$ time, in which $n$ is the number of supports of the probability distributions and $\varepsilon$ is the desired error. Furthermore, we investigate a fixed-support robust barycenter problem between $m$ discrete probability distributions with at most $n$ number of supports and develop an approximating algorithm based on iterative Bregman projections (IBP). For the specific case $m = 2$, we show that this algorithm can approximate the optimal barycenter value in $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{mn^2}{\varepsilon})$ time, thus being better than the previous complexity $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{mn^2}{\varepsilon^2})$ of the IBP algorithm for approximating the Wasserstein barycenter.

paragraphs: This paper studies robust optimal transport formulations that relax the usual marginal constraints using Kullback–Leibler divergence. Its focus is computational: how much work is needed to approximate the optimal cost to a desired accuracy? The authors analyze Sinkhorn-based algorithms for this relaxed transport problem.

They show that the optimal cost can be approximated in Õ(n²/ε) time, where n counts distribution support points and ε is the desired error. They also investigate a fixed-support robust barycenter problem for m discrete distributions, each with at most n support points. For this problem, they develop an approximation algorithm based on iterative Bregman projections.

For the specific case of two distributions, the barycenter algorithm approximates the optimal value in Õ(mn²/ε) time. Its dependence on accuracy improves on the cited Õ(mn²/ε²) complexity for iterative Bregman projections applied to Wasserstein barycenters. The two-distribution qualification is essential to that stated bound. The contribution establishes computational guarantees for both robust transport costs and this particular robust barycenter setting.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes efficient approximation bounds for KL-relaxed optimal transport and, with two distributions, robust barycenter computation.

title: On Robust Optimal Transport: Computational Complexity and Barycenter Computation

abstract: An overarching goal in machine learning is to build a generalizable model with few samples. To this end, overparameterization has been the subject of immense interest to explain the generalization ability of deep nets even when the size of the dataset is smaller than that of the model. While the prior literature focuses on the classical supervised setting, this paper aims to demystify overparameterization for meta-learning. Here we have a sequence of linear-regression tasks and we ask: (1) Given earlier tasks, what is the optimal linear representation of features for a new downstream task? and (2) How many samples do we need to build this representation? This work shows that surprisingly, overparameterization arises as a natural answer to these fundamental meta-learning questions. Specifically, for (1), we first show that learning the optimal representation coincides with the problem of designing a task-aware regularization to promote inductive bias. We leverage this inductive bias to explain how the downstream task actually benefits from overparameterization, in contrast to prior works on few-shot learning. For (2), we develop a theory to explain how feature covariance can implicitly help reduce the sample complexity well below the degrees of freedom and lead to small estimation error. We then integrate these findings to obtain an overall performance guarantee for our meta-learning algorithm. Numerical experiments on real and synthetic data verify our insights on overparameterized meta-learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies why a model with more parameters than available examples can still be useful in meta-learning. Its setting is a sequence of linear regression tasks. The authors ask what linear feature representation earlier tasks should provide for a new task, and how much data is needed to learn that representation.

They show that finding the optimal representation coincides with designing task-aware regularization. This connection explains the representation through the inductive bias it promotes: knowledge from earlier tasks shapes how the downstream problem is solved. Within this analysis, overparameterization emerges as beneficial for the new task rather than simply as excess model capacity.

The authors combine these findings into an overall performance guarantee for their meta-learning algorithm. Experiments on real and synthetic data support the analysis. The contribution ties together representation learning, task-aware regularization, and covariance structure in the stated linear-regression setting.
summary.tldr: For linear-regression meta-learning, task-aware regularization and feature covariance explain how overparameterization can help downstream learning with few samples.

title: Towards Sample-efficient Overparameterized Meta-learning

abstract: The training of sparse neural networks is becoming an increasingly important tool for reducing the computational footprint of models at training and evaluation, as well enabling the effective scaling up of models. Whereas much work over the years has been dedicated to specialised pruning techniques, little attention has been paid to the inherent effect of gradient based training on model sparsity. Inthis work, we introduce Powerpropagation, a new weight-parameterisation for neural networks that leads to inherently sparse models. Exploiting the behaviour of gradient descent, our method gives rise to weight updates exhibiting a “rich get richer” dynamic, leaving low-magnitude parameters largely unaffected by learning. Models trained in this manner exhibit similar performance, but have a distributionwith markedly higher density at zero, allowing more parameters to be pruned safely. Powerpropagation is general, intuitive, cheap and straight-forward to implement and can readily be combined with various other techniques. To highlight its versatility, we explore it in two very different settings: Firstly, following a recent line of work, we investigate its effect on sparse training for resource-constrained settings. Here, we combine Powerpropagation with a traditional weight-pruning technique as well as recent state-of-the-art sparse-to-sparse algorithms, showing superior performance on the ImageNet benchmark. Secondly, we advocate the useof sparsity in overcoming catastrophic forgetting, where compressed representations allow accommodating a large number of tasks at fixed model capacity. In all cases our reparameterisation considerably increases the efficacy of the off-the-shelf methods.

paragraphs: Sparse neural networks reduce the number of active parameters, helping lower computational demands and accommodate larger models. This paper asks how the training process itself can encourage sparsity. Powerpropagation changes the parameterization of network weights so that ordinary gradient-based learning produces a different pattern of weight updates.

The resulting dynamics favor parameters that already have larger magnitudes, while small parameters change relatively little. Trained models retain similar performance but have substantially more weight mass at zero, allowing more parameters to be removed safely. The method is described as inexpensive and straightforward to implement, and it can be combined with other sparsity techniques.

The authors explore two applications. For resource-constrained training, they combine Powerpropagation with traditional pruning and sparse-to-sparse algorithms, reporting improved ImageNet performance. They also investigate sparsity for reducing catastrophic forgetting, using compressed representations to fit more tasks within fixed model capacity. Across the settings studied, the reparameterization strengthens the off-the-shelf methods it accompanies. The main idea is that a change to weight representation can make existing sparsification approaches more effective.
summary.tldr: Powerpropagation changes weight parameterization to encourage sparsity during training and improve existing pruning and continual-learning methods.

title: Powerpropagation: A sparsity inducing weight reparameterisation

abstract: We study the learnability of linear threshold functions (LTFs) in the learning from label proportions (LLP) framework. In this, the feature-vector classifier is learnt from bags of feature-vectors and their corresponding observed label proportions which are satisfied by (i.e., consistent with) some unknown LTF. This problem has been investigated in recent work (Saket21) which gave an algorithm to produce an LTF that satisfies at least $(2/5)$-fraction of a satisfiable collection of bags, each of size $\leq 2$, by solving and rounding a natural SDP relaxation. However, this SDP relaxation is specific to at most $2$-sized bags and does not apply to bags of larger size. In this work we provide a fairly non-trivial SDP relaxation of a non-quadratic formulation for bags of size $3$. We analyze its rounding procedure using novel matrix decomposition techniques to obtain an algorithm which outputs an LTF satisfying at least $(1/12)$-fraction of the bags of size $\leq 3$. We also apply our techniques to bags of size $q \geq 4$ to provide a $\Omega\left(1/q\right)$-approximation guarantee for a weaker notion of satisfiability. We include comparative experiments on simulated data demonstrating the applicability of our algorithmic techniques. From the complexity side we provide a hardness reduction to produce instances with bags of any constant size $q$. Our reduction proves the NP-hardness of satisfying more than $({1}/{q}) + o(1)$ fraction of a satisfiable collection of such bags using as hypothesis any function of constantly many LTFs, showing thereby that the problem is harder to approximate as the bag size $q$ increases. Using a strengthened analysis, for $q=2$ we obtain a $({4}/{9}) +o(1)$ hardness factor for this problem, improving upon the $({1}/{2}) + o(1)$ factor shown by Saket21.

paragraphs: Learning from label proportions replaces individual training labels with the proportions observed in groups, called bags. This paper studies linear threshold classifiers when some unknown classifier satisfies every supplied bag. The challenge is to recover a classifier that matches many of those proportions despite lacking individual labels.

The authors develop a semidefinite relaxation and a rounding procedure for bags containing at most three examples. Their algorithm guarantees satisfaction of at least one twelfth of the bags. For bags of size q at least four, their techniques give an approximation guarantee proportional to 1/q under a weaker definition of satisfaction. Simulated-data experiments also demonstrate the applicability of the techniques.

The paper complements these algorithms with computational hardness results. For any constant bag size q, satisfying more than approximately a 1/q fraction is NP-hard even when predictions may combine constantly many linear threshold functions. For size two, the hardness threshold improves to approximately 4/9. Together, the results show how larger bags make approximation harder and distinguish achievable guarantees from computational barriers.
summary.tldr: The paper gives approximation algorithms and hardness bounds for learning linear thresholds from grouped label proportions, exposing increasing difficulty with larger bags.

title: Algorithms and Hardness for Learning Linear Thresholds from Label Proportions

abstract: Labeled data often comes at a high cost as it may require recruiting human labelers or running costly experiments. At the same time, in many practical scenarios, one already has access to a partially labeled, potentially biased dataset that can help with the learning task at hand. Motivated by such settings, we formally initiate a study of ``semi-supervised active learning'' through the frame of linear regression. Here, the learner has access to a dataset $X \in \mathbb{R}^{(n_{\text{un}}+n_{\text{lab}}) \times d}$ composed of $n_{\text{un}}$ unlabeled examples that a learner can actively query, and $n_{\text{lab}}$ examples labeled a priori. Denoting the true labels by $Y \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{un}} + n_{\text{lab}}}$, the learner's objective is to find $\widehat{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that,$$\| X \widehat{\beta} - Y \|_2^2 \le (1 + \epsilon) \min_{\beta \in \mathbb{R}^d} \| X \beta - Y \|_2^2$$while querying the labels of as few unlabeled points as possible. In this paper, we introduce an instance dependent parameter called the reduced rank, denoted $\text{R}_X$, and propose an efficient algorithm with query complexity $O(\text{R}_X/\epsilon)$. This result directly implies improved upper bounds for two important special cases: $(i)$ active ridge regression, and $(ii)$ active kernel ridge regression, where the reduced-rank equates to the ``statistical dimension'', $\textsf{sd}_\lambda$ and ``effective dimension'', $d_\lambda$ of the problem respectively, where $\lambda \ge 0$ denotes the regularization parameter. Finally, we introduce a distributional version of the problem as a special case of the agnostic formulation we consider earlier; here, for every $X$, we prove a matching instance-wise lower bound of $\Omega (\text{R}_X / \epsilon)$ on the query complexity of any algorithm.

paragraphs: Obtaining labels can be expensive, while some labels may already be available from a potentially biased collection process. This paper studies linear regression with both previously labeled examples and unlabeled examples whose labels can be actively requested. The aim is to approach the best full-data regression fit while making as few new queries as possible.

The authors introduce an instance-dependent quantity called reduced rank. Their efficient algorithm needs O(R_X/epsilon) label queries to achieve squared error within a factor of 1 + epsilon of the best linear fit. The query bound therefore reflects this property of the particular problem, while also making the cost of demanding greater accuracy explicit.

The result yields improved upper bounds for active ridge regression and active kernel ridge regression, where reduced rank corresponds to established dimension measures. For a distributional special case, the paper proves a matching instance-wise lower bound for every design matrix. In that setting, the dependence on reduced rank and accuracy captures both what the algorithm achieves and what any algorithm must pay.
summary.tldr: Reduced rank characterizes label-query complexity for semi-supervised active linear regression, with a matching lower bound in a distributional special case.

title: Semi-supervised Active Linear Regression

abstract: We present a framework to statistically audit the privacy guarantee conferred by a differentially private machine learner in practice. While previous works have taken steps toward evaluating privacy loss through poisoning attacks or membership inference, they have been tailored to specific models or have demonstrated low statistical power. Our work develops a general methodology to empirically evaluate the privacy of differentially private machine learning implementations, combining improved privacy search and verification methods with a toolkit of influence-based poisoning attacks. We demonstrate significantly improved auditing power over previous approaches on a variety of models including logistic regression, Naive Bayes, and random forest. Our method can be used to detect privacy violations due to implementation errors or misuse. When violations are not present, it can aid in understanding the amount of information that can be leaked from a given dataset, algorithm, and privacy specification.

We demonstrate significantly improved auditing power over previous approaches on a variety of models including logistic regression, Naive Bayes, and random forest. Our method can be used to detect privacy violations due to implementation errors or misuse. When violations are not present, it can aid in understanding the amount of information that can be leaked from a given dataset, algorithm, and privacy specification.

paragraphs: A privacy guarantee is useful only if the implemented learning system actually provides it. This paper develops a statistical framework for auditing the privacy behavior of machine learning implementations that claim differential privacy. Its focus is empirical evaluation: examining how much information a particular combination of data, learning algorithm, and privacy specification can reveal.

The framework combines improved methods for searching for privacy leakage and verifying it statistically with poisoning attacks based on influence. These attacks help probe the learner's response to changes in its training data. The combined approach addresses two shortcomings identified in earlier audits: methods tailored to particular models and tests with limited power to detect privacy loss.

The authors report substantially stronger auditing power on logistic regression, Naive Bayes, and random forests. The framework can expose privacy violations caused by implementation mistakes or misuse. When such violations are absent, its measurements can still help characterize information leakage, giving developers an empirical view of the privacy behavior of the system they actually run.
summary.tldr: A statistical auditing framework uses stronger privacy searches and poisoning attacks to detect privacy leakage across multiple machine learning models.

title: A General Framework for Auditing Differentially Private Machine Learning

abstract: We consider streaming principal component analysis when the stochastic data-generating model is subject to perturbations. While existing models assume a fixed covariance, we adopt a robust perspective where the covariance matrix belongs to a temporal uncertainty set. Under this setting, we provide fundamental limits on any algorithm recovering principal components. We analyze the convergence of the noisy power method and Oja’s algorithm, both studied for the stationary data generating model, and argue that the noisy power method is rate-optimal in our setting. Finally, we demonstrate the validity of our analysis through numerical experiments.

While existing models assume a fixed covariance, we adopt a robust perspective where the covariance matrix belongs to a temporal uncertainty set. Under this setting, we provide fundamental limits on any algorithm recovering principal components. Finally, we demonstrate the validity of our analysis through numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Streaming principal component analysis seeks principal directions from data arriving over time. Standard analyses assume that the data-generating covariance stays fixed. This paper instead considers a perturbed stochastic model in which the covariance belongs to an uncertainty set that varies over time, making uncertainty in the evolving data distribution part of the problem.

Within this setting, the authors derive fundamental limits on recovering principal components. Such limits establish what any algorithm can achieve under the model, providing a reference for judging particular methods. They then analyze the convergence of the noisy power method and Oja's algorithm, both of which have also been studied under stationary data generation.

The authors argue that the noisy power method achieves an optimal rate in their robust setting and present numerical experiments supporting the analysis. The significance is that performance is assessed against the difficulty imposed by temporal covariance uncertainty itself. This gives both a characterization of the recovery problem and an analysis of established algorithms when the fixed-covariance assumption is relaxed.
summary.tldr: The paper derives recovery limits for streaming PCA with time-varying covariance uncertainty and argues that the noisy power method is rate-optimal.

title: Robust Streaming PCA

abstract: We propose the Nesterov neural ordinary differential equations (NesterovNODEs), whose layers solve the second-order ordinary differential equations (ODEs) limit of Nesterov's accelerated gradient (NAG) method, and a generalization called GNesterovNODEs. Taking the advantage of the convergence rate $\mathcal{O}(1/k^{2})$ of the NAG scheme, GNesterovNODEs speed up training and inference by reducing the number of function evaluations (NFEs) needed to solve the ODEs. We also prove that the adjoint state of a GNesterovNODEs also satisfies a GNesterovNODEs, thus accelerating both forward and backward ODE solvers and allowing the model to be scaled up for large-scale tasks. We empirically corroborate the advantage of GNesterovNODEs on a wide range of practical applications, including point cloud separation, image classification, and sequence modeling. Compared to NODEs, GNesterovNODEs require a significantly smaller number of NFEs while achieving better accuracy across our experiments.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equation models compute their transformations by solving differential equations. This paper proposes NesterovNODEs, whose layers solve second-order equations arising as a continuous limit of Nesterov's accelerated gradient method. It also introduces a generalized version, GNesterovNODEs, aimed at reducing the work needed by the equation solvers.

The approach draws on the accelerated method's O(1/k²) convergence rate. Its computational target is the number of function evaluations required to solve the differential equations, which affects both training and inference. The authors also prove that the adjoint state of a GNesterovNODE satisfies an equation of the same generalized form. This extends the acceleration mechanism to the backward solver as well as the forward solver.

Experiments cover point-cloud separation, image classification, and sequence modeling. Across the reported experiments, GNesterovNODEs use significantly fewer function evaluations than NODEs while achieving better accuracy. These findings support the proposed dynamics as a way to make continuous-depth models more computationally efficient, with the adjoint result helping the approach address the cost of training as well as prediction.
summary.tldr: Nesterov-inspired neural differential equations reduce solver evaluations and improve accuracy across the reported experiments.

title: Improving Neural Ordinary Differential Equations with Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Method

abstract: When machine learning training is outsourced to third parties, $backdoor$ $attacks$ become practical as the third party who trains the model may act maliciously to inject hidden behaviors into the otherwise accurate model. Until now, the mechanism to inject backdoors has been limited to $poisoning$. We argue that a supply-chain attacker has more attack techniques available by introducing a $handcrafted$ attack that directly manipulates a model's weights. This direct modification gives our attacker more degrees of freedom compared to poisoning, and we show it can be used to evade many backdoor detection or removal defenses effectively. Across four datasets and four network architectures our backdoor attacks maintain an attack success rate above 96%. Our results suggest that further research is needed for understanding the complete space of supply-chain backdoor attacks.

paragraphs: When a third party trains a machine-learning model, that party may be able to embed hidden behavior while leaving the model otherwise accurate. This paper examines that supply-chain threat beyond attacks based on poisoning training data. It asks what becomes possible when an attacker directly manipulates the model’s weights.

The authors introduce handcrafted backdoors built through such direct modification. Their central argument is that weight access gives an attacker more freedom than influencing the model indirectly through poisoned examples. That broader control matters for defenses: the paper demonstrates that these attacks can effectively evade many techniques intended to detect or remove backdoors.

Across four datasets and four network architectures, the reported attack success rate remains above 96%. Those experiments support the claim that direct weight manipulation is a consequential part of the supply-chain attack space. The authors call for further research into that wider space. The findings concern the evaluated attacks and defenses; they establish a broader threat model without claiming that every backdoor defense can be defeated.
summary.tldr: Direct weight manipulation enables handcrafted backdoors that evade many evaluated defenses and exceed 96% attack success in the reported experiments.

title: Handcrafted Backdoors in Deep Neural Networks

abstract: We study the generalisation properties of majority voting on finite ensembles of classifiers, proving margin-based generalisation bounds via the PAC-Bayes theory. These provide state-of-the-art guarantees on a number of classification tasks. Our central results leverage the Dirichlet posteriors studied recently by Zantedeschi et al. (2021) for training voting classifiers; in contrast to that work our bounds apply to non-randomised votes via the use of margins. Our contributions add perspective to the debate on the ``margins theory'' proposed by Schapire et al. (1998) for the generalisation of ensemble classifiers.

paragraphs: A voting classifier combines predictions from a finite collection of classifiers into one decision. The paper asks how well that combined decision should perform beyond its training examples. Its analysis focuses on margins, which describe how strongly a vote favors a classification, providing more information than whether the final prediction is simply correct.

The authors use PAC-Bayes theory to prove margin-based generalization bounds. Their central construction draws on Dirichlet posterior distributions previously studied for training voting classifiers. The key distinction is that margins allow the resulting bounds to apply to non-randomized votes. This connects a probabilistic analytical framework to classifiers that make a fixed voting decision.

Across a number of classification tasks, the bounds provide state-of-the-art guarantees. These findings concern the strength of generalization guarantees for ensembles, rather than a reported universal improvement in prediction accuracy. They also contribute to the debate over margin-based explanations of ensemble generalization by showing how margins can support strong guarantees for finite, non-randomized voting classifiers.
summary.tldr: Margin-based PAC-Bayes bounds provide strong generalization guarantees for finite ensembles that use non-randomized voting.

title: On Margins and Generalisation for Voting Classifiers

abstract: Creating fast and accurate force fields is a long-standing challenge in computational chemistry and materials science. Recently, Equivariant Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for building machine learning interatomic potentials, outperforming other approaches in terms of accuracy. However, they suffer from high computational cost and poor scalability. Moreover, most MPNNs only pass two-body messages leading to an intricate relationship between the number of layers and the expressivity of the features. This work introduces MACE, a new equivariant MPNN model that uses higher order messages, and demonstrates that this leads to an improved learning law. We show that by using four-body messages, the required number of message passing iterations reduces to just one, resulting in a fast and highly parallelizable model, reaching or exceeding state of the art accuracy on the rMD17 and 3BPA benchmark tasks. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ACEsuit/mace.

paragraphs: Machine learning force fields aim to describe atomic interactions accurately while remaining fast enough for computational chemistry and materials science. Equivariant message-passing networks have achieved strong accuracy, but their computational cost and scalability remain challenges. Many pass only two-body messages, tying the richness of their features closely to the number of message-passing layers.

MACE introduces higher-order messages into an equivariant network. These messages represent interactions involving more atoms within a single exchange of information. The authors demonstrate an improved learning law and show that using four-body messages reduces the required message-passing iterations to one. This changes how the network obtains expressive features without requiring repeated rounds of message passing.

The resulting model is described as fast and highly parallelizable. On the rMD17 and 3BPA benchmarks, it reaches or exceeds state-of-the-art accuracy. Those results connect the architectural choice to both predictive quality and computational practicality. The central contribution is to enrich the content of individual messages so that accurate interatomic modeling can be achieved with fewer sequential exchanges.
summary.tldr: MACE uses higher-order atomic messages to achieve strong force-field accuracy with a single message-passing iteration.

title: MACE: Higher Order Equivariant Message Passing Neural Networks for Fast and Accurate Force Fields

abstract: Recent work has shown that augmenting environments with language descriptions improves policy learning. However, for environments with complex language abstractions, learning how to ground language to observations is difficult due to sparse, delayed rewards. We propose Language Dynamics Distillation (LDD), which pretrains a model to predict environment dynamics given demonstrations with language descriptions, and then fine-tunes these language-aware pretrained representations via reinforcement learning (RL). In this way, the model is trained to both maximize expected reward and retain knowledge about how language relates to environment dynamics. On SILG, a benchmark of five tasks with language descriptions that evaluate distinct generalization challenges on unseen environments (NetHack, ALFWorld, RTFM, Messenger, and Touchdown), LDD outperforms tabula-rasa RL, VAE pretraining, and methods that learn from unlabeled demonstrations in inverse RL and reward shaping with pretrained experts. In our analyses, we show that language descriptions in demonstrations improve sample-efficiency and generalization across environments, and that dynamics modeling with expert demonstrations is more effective than with non-experts.

paragraphs: Language descriptions can help an agent learn what to do, but connecting complex descriptions to observations is difficult when rewards arrive rarely or late. Language Dynamics Distillation addresses this grounding problem by learning from demonstrations before reinforcement learning begins. Its pretraining task predicts environment dynamics from demonstrations accompanied by language.

The resulting language-aware representations are then fine-tuned through reinforcement learning. Training aims both to increase expected reward and to retain knowledge of how language relates to changes in the environment. This makes the connection between descriptions and dynamics part of the representation the policy learns to use, rather than leaving that connection entirely dependent on delayed task rewards.

On SILG's five tasks, which assess different generalization challenges in unseen environments, LDD outperforms learning from scratch, VAE pretraining, and the compared methods using unlabeled demonstrations. Additional analyses find that language in demonstrations improves sample efficiency and generalization across environments. They also find expert demonstrations more effective than non-expert demonstrations for dynamics modeling.
summary.tldr: LDD pretrains language-aware dynamics representations from demonstrations and improves policy learning and generalization on the SILG benchmark.

title: Improving Policy Learning via Language Dynamics Distillation

abstract: In machine teaching, a concept is represented by (and inferred from) a small number of labeled examples. Various teaching models in the literature cast the interaction between teacher and learner in a way to obtain a small complexity (in terms of the number of examples required for teaching a concept) while obeying certain constraints that are meant to prevent unfair collusion between teacher and learner. In recent years, one major research goal has been to show interesting relationships between teaching complexity and the VC-dimension (VCD). So far, the only interesting relationship known from batch teaching settings is an upper bound quadratic in the VCD, on a parameter called recursive teaching dimension. The only known upper bound on teaching complexity that is linear in VCD was obtained in a model of teaching with sequences rather than batches.This paper is the first to provide an upper bound of VCD on a batch teaching complexity parameter. This parameter, called STDmin, is introduced here as a model of teaching that intuitively incorporates a notion of ``importance'' of an example for a concept. In designing the STDmin teaching model, we argue that the standard notion of collusion-freeness from the literature may be inadequate for certain applications; we hence propose three desirable properties of teaching complexity and demonstrate that they are satisfied by STDmin.

paragraphs: Machine teaching studies how a teacher can convey a concept through a small set of labeled examples. The number needed depends on the rules governing how teacher and learner interact. This paper investigates batch teaching, where examples are supplied as a collection, and its relationship to VC-dimension, a measure of concept-class complexity.

The authors introduce a teaching-complexity parameter called STDmin, whose model incorporates an intuitive notion of how important an example is for a concept. They prove an upper bound equal to the VC-dimension. Earlier batch-teaching work had established a quadratic upper bound for recursive teaching dimension, while a known linear bound applied to teaching with sequences.

The result depends on the newly proposed teaching model. In developing it, the authors argue that the customary criterion intended to prevent unfair teacher-learner collusion may be inadequate for some applications. They propose three desirable properties of teaching complexity and show that STDmin satisfies them. The contribution combines a sharper bound with a reconsideration of what a useful batch-teaching framework should require.
summary.tldr: A new batch-teaching model, STDmin, has teaching complexity bounded above by VC-dimension and satisfies three proposed desirable properties.

title: On Batch Teaching with Sample Complexity Bounded by VCD

abstract: In recent years, federated learning (FL) has emerged as an important distributed machine learning paradigm to collaboratively learn a global model with multiple clients, while keeping data local and private. However, a key assumption in most existing works on FL algorithms' convergence analysis is that the noise in stochastic first-order information has a finite variance. Although this assumption covers all light-tailed (i.e., sub-exponential) and some heavy-tailed noise distributions (e.g., log-normal, Weibull, and some Pareto distributions), it fails for many fat-tailed noise distributions (i.e., ``heavier-tailed'' with potentially infinite variance) that have been empirically observed in the FL literature. To date, it remains unclear whether one can design convergent algorithms for FL systems that experience fat-tailed noise. This motivates us to fill this gap in this paper by proposing an algorithmic framework called $\mathsf{FAT}$-$\mathsf{Clipping}~$ (\ul{f}ederated \ul{a}veraging with \ul{t}wo-sided learning rates and \ul{clipping}), which contains two variants: $\mathsf{FAT}$-$\mathsf{Clipping}~$ per-round ($\mathsf{FAT}$-$\mathsf{Clipping}$-$\mathsf{PR}$) and $\mathsf{FAT}$-$\mathsf{Clipping}~$ per-iteration ($\mathsf{FAT}$-$\mathsf{Clipping}$-$\mathsf{PI}$). Specifically, for the largest $\alpha \in (1,2]$ such that the fat-tailed noise in FL still has a bounded $\alpha$-moment, we show that both variants achieve $\mathcal{O}((mT)^{\frac{2-\alpha}{\alpha}})$ and $\mathcal{O}((mT)^{\frac{1-\alpha}{3\alpha-2}})$ convergence rates in the strongly-convex and general non-convex settings, respectively, where $m$ and $T$ are the numbers of clients and communication rounds. Moreover, at the expense of more clipping operations compared to $\mathsf{FAT}$-$\mathsf{Clipping}$-$\mathsf{PR}$, $\mathsf{FAT}$-$\mathsf{Clipping}$-$\mathsf{PI}~$ further enjoys a linear speedup effect with respect to the number of local updates at each client and being lower-bound-matching (i.e., order-optimal). Collectively, our results advance the understanding of designing efficient algorithms for FL systems that exhibit fat-tailed first-order oracle information.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines updates from multiple clients while leaving their data local. Many convergence analyses assume that noise in gradient information has finite variance. This paper addresses heavier-tailed noise that can violate that assumption, a situation reported in federated-learning research and one that falls outside many existing guarantees.

The proposed FAT-Clipping framework combines federated averaging, two-sided learning rates, and clipping. It has per-round and per-iteration variants, distinguished by how frequently clipping is performed. The analysis assumes a bounded alpha-moment for an alpha between one and two, allowing treatment of some noise distributions whose variance need not be finite. The authors derive rates for strongly convex and general nonconvex settings.

The per-iteration variant requires more clipping operations, but the paper establishes additional benefits: linear speedup with the number of local client updates and rates matching a lower bound in order. These results clarify a tradeoff between clipping effort and theoretical efficiency. The contribution extends convergence analysis beyond finite-variance noise while retaining an explicit moment condition on the noise.
summary.tldr: FAT-Clipping provides federated-learning convergence results under bounded-moment noise assumptions that can allow infinite variance, with extra efficiency guarantees for per-iteration clipping.

title: Taming Fat-Tailed (“Heavier-Tailed” with Potentially Infinite Variance) Noise in Federated Learning

abstract: For the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) in high risk settings, such as healthcare, methods that provide interpretability/explainability or allow fine-grained error analysis are critical. Many recent methods for interpretability/explainability and fine-grained error analysis use concepts, which are meta-labels which are semantically meaningful to humans. However, there are only a few datasets that include concept-level meta-labels and most of these meta-labels are relevant for natural images that do not require domain expertise. Previous densely annotated datasets in medicine focused on meta-labels that are relevant to a single disease such as osteoarthritis or melanoma. In dermatology, skin disease is described using an established clinical lexicon that allow clinicians to describe physical exam findings to one another. To provide the first medical dataset densely annotated by domain experts to provide annotations useful across multiple disease processes, we developed SkinCon: a skin disease dataset densely annotated by dermatologists. SkinCon includes 3230 images from the Fitzpatrick 17k skin disease dataset densely annotated with 48 clinical concepts, 22 of which have at least 50 images representing the concept. The concepts used were chosen by two dermatologists considering the clinical descriptor terms used to describe skin lesions. Examples include "plaque", "scale", and "erosion". These same concepts were also used to label 656 skin disease images from the Diverse Dermatology Images dataset, providing an additional external dataset with diverse skin tone representations. We review the potential applications for the SkinCon dataset, such as probing models, concept-based explanations, concept bottlenecks, error analysis, and slice discovery. Furthermore, we use SkinCon to demonstrate two of these use cases: debugging mistakes of an existing dermatology AI model with concepts and developing interpretable models with post-hoc concept bottleneck models.

title: SkinCon: A skin disease dataset densely annotated by domain experts for fine-grained debugging and analysis

abstract: In image segmentation, the classic approach of learning a deterministic segmentation neither accounts for noise and ambiguity in the data nor for expert disagreements about the correct segmentation. This has been addressed by architectures that predict heteroscedastic (input-dependent) segmentation uncertainty, which indicates regions of segmentations that should be treated with care. What is missing are structural insights into the uncertainty, which would be desirable for interpretability and systematic adjustments. In the context of state-of-the-art stochastic segmentation networks (SSNs), we solve this issue by dismantling the overall predicted uncertainty into smaller uncertainty components. We obtain them directly from the low-rank Gaussian distribution for the logits in the network head of SSNs, based on a previously unconsidered view of this distribution as a factor model. The rank subsequently encodes a number of latent variables, each of which controls an individual uncertainty component. Hence, we can use the latent variables (called factors) for fine-grained sample control, thereby solving an open problem from previous work. There is one caveat though--factors are only unique up to orthogonal rotations. Factor rotations allow us to structure the uncertainty in a way that endorses simplicity, non-redundancy, and separation among the individual uncertainty components. To make the overall and factor-specific uncertainties at play comprehensible, we introduce flow probabilities that quantify deviations from the mean prediction and can also be used for uncertainty visualization. We show on medical-imaging, earth-observation, and traffic-scene data that rotation criteria based on factor-specific flow probabilities consistently yield the best factors for fine-grained sampling.

paragraphs: Image segmentation can be ambiguous because of noise or expert disagreement. Stochastic segmentation networks represent uncertainty, but an overall uncertainty prediction does not explain its individual components. This paper seeks to separate those components so that users can understand the variation and control which aspects change when sampling alternative segmentations.

The authors reinterpret the network head's low-rank Gaussian distribution over logits as a factor model. Its latent factors control individual uncertainty components. However, these factors are only identifiable up to orthogonal rotations, so their interpretation is not unique. The method uses rotations to encourage simpler, less redundant, and more separated components.

The paper introduces flow probabilities to quantify departures from the mean prediction, both overall and for individual factors. These quantities support visualization and help select rotations. Experiments on medical images, earth observation, and traffic scenes find that rotation criteria based on factor-specific flow probabilities consistently produce the best factors for fine-grained sampling. The contribution makes predicted uncertainty more structured and controllable, rather than merely reporting its magnitude.
summary.tldr: A factor-model interpretation separates segmentation uncertainty into components that can be rotated, visualized, and controlled during sampling.

title: Structuring Uncertainty for Fine-Grained Sampling in Stochastic Segmentation Networks

abstract: Graphical models such as Gaussian graphical models have been widely applied for direct interaction inference in many different areas. In many modern applications, such as single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies, the observed data are counts and often contain many small counts. Traditional graphical models for continuous data are inappropriate for network inference of count data. We consider the Poisson log-normal (PLN) graphical model for count data and the precision matrix of the latent normal distribution represents the network. We propose a two-step method PLNet to estimate the precision matrix. PLNet first estimates the latent covariance matrix using the maximum marginal likelihood estimator (MMLE) and then estimates the precision matrix by minimizing the lasso-penalized D-trace loss function. We establish the convergence rate of the MMLE of the covariance matrix and further establish the convergence rate and the sign consistency of the proposed PLNet estimator of the precision matrix in the high dimensional setting. Importantly, although the PLN model is not sub-Gaussian, we show that the PLNet estimator is consistent even if the model dimension goes to infinity exponentially as the sample size increases. The performance of PLNet is evaluated and compared with available methods using simulation and gene regulatory network analysis of real scRNA-seq data.
originalAbstract: Graphical models such as Gaussian graphical models have been widely applied for direct interaction inference in many different areas. In many modern applications, such as single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies, the observed data are counts and often contain many small counts.
