We consider the Poisson log-normal (PLN) graphical model for count data and the precision matrix of the latent normal distribution represents the network. We propose a two-step method PLNet to estimate the precision matrix. PLNet first estimates the latent covariance matrix using the maximum marginal likelihood estimator (MMLE) and then estimates the precision matrix by minimizing the lasso-penalized D-trace loss function. We establish the convergence rate of the MMLE of the covariance matrix and further establish the convergence rate and the sign consistency of the proposed PLNet estimator of the precision matrix in the high dimensional setting. Importantly, although the PLN model is not sub-Gaussian, we show that the PLNet estimator is consistent even if the model dimension goes to infinity exponentially as the sample size increases. The performance of PLNet is evaluated and compared with available methods using simulation and gene regulatory network analysis of real scRNA-seq data.

paragraphs: Single-cell RNA sequencing produces count data, often with many small values. Graphical models designed for continuous measurements can therefore be inappropriate for inferring networks from these observations. This paper uses a Poisson log-normal model, where the network is represented by the precision matrix of an underlying normal distribution associated with the observed counts.

The proposed estimator, PLNet, works in two stages. It first estimates the latent covariance matrix through maximum marginal likelihood. It then estimates the precision matrix using a lasso-penalized D-trace loss. Separating these stages provides a route from count observations to an estimate of the matrix that encodes the model's network relationships.

The authors establish convergence rates for both stages and sign consistency for the precision estimator in high dimensions. They also show consistency even when model dimension grows exponentially with sample size, despite the Poisson log-normal model lacking sub-Gaussian behavior. Simulations and analyses of real single-cell gene regulatory networks evaluate PLNet against available methods, connecting the statistical theory to its intended count-data application.
summary.tldr: PLNet estimates networks from count data through a two-stage Poisson log-normal approach with high-dimensional consistency guarantees.

title: Estimating graphical models for count data with applications to single-cell gene network

abstract: We propose a general framework to design posterior sampling methods for model-based RL. We show that the proposed algorithms can be analyzed by reducing regret to Hellinger distance in conditional probability estimation. We further show that optimistic posterior sampling can control this Hellinger distance, when we measure model error via data likelihood. This technique allows us to design and analyze unified posterior sampling algorithms with state-of-the-art sample complexity guarantees for many model-based RL settings. We illustrate our general result in many special cases, demonstrating the versatility of our framework.

We show that the proposed algorithms can be analyzed by reducing regret to Hellinger distance in conditional probability estimation. We further show that optimistic posterior sampling can control this Hellinger distance, when we measure model error via data likelihood. This technique allows us to design and analyze unified posterior sampling algorithms with state-of-the-art sample complexity guarantees for many model-based RL settings. We illustrate our general result in many special cases, demonstrating the versatility of our framework.

paragraphs: The paper develops a general framework for posterior sampling in model-based reinforcement learning. The central aim is to design and analyze learning algorithms through a shared mathematical approach. Its guarantees concern sample complexity: how much interaction data an algorithm needs to achieve the learning performance covered by the analysis.

The key step translates regret analysis into a problem of conditional probability estimation. Specifically, the authors bound regret through Hellinger distance, a measure of discrepancy between probability distributions. They then show that optimistic posterior sampling can control this distance when model error is measured using data likelihood. This provides a connection between estimating an environment model and controlling the cost of learning to act.

Using that connection, the framework yields unified posterior sampling algorithms with state-of-the-art sample complexity guarantees for many model-based reinforcement learning settings. The authors illustrate the general result through numerous special cases. The significance is the reusable route from likelihood-based model estimation to regret analysis, together with guarantees that apply across the settings covered by their framework.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis connects optimistic posterior sampling, likelihood-based model estimation, and strong sample complexity guarantees in model-based reinforcement learning.

title: Model-based RL with Optimistic Posterior Sampling: Structural Conditions and Sample Complexity

abstract: We study the regret of Thompson sampling (TS) algorithms for exponential family bandits, where the reward distribution is from a one-dimensional exponential family, which covers many common reward distributions including Bernoulli, Gaussian, Gamma, Exponential, etc. We propose a Thompson sampling algorithm, termed ExpTS, which uses a novel sampling distribution to avoid the under-estimation of the optimal arm. We provide a tight regret analysis for ExpTS, which simultaneously yields both the finite-time regret bound as well as the asymptotic regret bound. In particular, for a $K$-armed bandit with exponential family rewards, ExpTS over a horizon $T$ is sub-UCB (a strong criterion for the finite-time regret that is problem-dependent), minimax optimal up to a factor $\sqrt{\log K}$, and asymptotically optimal, for exponential family rewards. Moreover, we propose ExpTS$^+$, by adding a greedy exploitation step in addition to the sampling distribution used in ExpTS, to avoid the over-estimation of sub-optimal arms. ExpTS$^+$ is an anytime bandit algorithm and achieves the minimax optimality and asymptotic optimality simultaneously for exponential family reward distributions. Our proof techniques are general and conceptually simple and can be easily applied to analyze standard Thompson sampling with specific reward distributions.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling addresses the problem of choosing among options whose rewards are initially uncertain. This paper studies its regret for rewards from one-dimensional exponential families, which include Bernoulli, Gaussian, Gamma, and Exponential distributions. Regret measures the accumulated cost of choosing less rewarding options while learning.

The first proposed algorithm, ExpTS, uses a new sampling distribution to avoid underestimating the best option. Its analysis covers both finite-time performance and behavior as the horizon grows. ExpTS satisfies the problem-dependent sub-UCB criterion, is asymptotically optimal, and is minimax optimal up to a factor equal to the square root of log K, where K is the number of options.

The second algorithm, ExpTS+, adds a greedy exploitation step to address overestimation of inferior options. It is an anytime algorithm and achieves both minimax and asymptotic optimality for the stated reward family. Together, the results connect two sources of estimation error to sampling design and establish guarantees across finite and long horizons.
summary.tldr: New Thompson sampling variants achieve strong finite-time and asymptotic regret guarantees for one-dimensional exponential-family rewards.

title: Finite-Time Regret of Thompson Sampling Algorithms for Exponential Family Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: We present a novel actor-critic algorithm for an environment with delayed feedback, which addresses the state-space explosion problem of conventional approaches. Conventional approaches use an augmented state constructed from the last observed state and actions executed since visiting the last observed state. Using the augmented state space, the correct Markov decision process for delayed environments can be constructed; however, this causes the state space to explode as the number of delayed timesteps increases, leading to slow convergence. Our proposed algorithm, called Belief-Projection-Based Q-learning (BPQL), addresses the state-space explosion problem by evaluating the values of the critic for which the input state size is equal to the original state-space size rather than that of the augmented one. We compare BPQL to traditional approaches in continuous control tasks and demonstrate that it significantly outperforms other algorithms in terms of asymptotic performance and sample efficiency. We also show that BPQL solves long-delayed environments, which conventional approaches are unable to do.

paragraphs: Delayed feedback complicates reinforcement learning because the latest observed state may describe the environment several actions ago. Conventional methods handle this by combining that observation with all actions taken since then. This augmented state supports a correct Markov decision process, but its size expands as delays grow and can make learning converge slowly.

The paper introduces Belief-Projection-Based Q-learning, or BPQL, as an actor-critic approach to this problem. Its central distinction concerns the critic, which evaluates values using a state input the size of the original state space. This avoids making the critic operate directly on the much larger augmented state used by conventional approaches.

In continuous control comparisons, BPQL significantly improves both final performance and sample efficiency over the other tested algorithms. It also solves tested environments with long delays that the conventional approaches cannot solve. These findings connect the representation choice to a practical learning benefit: handling delayed information without requiring the critic’s state input to grow with the full action history.
summary.tldr: BPQL improves learning with delayed feedback by keeping the critic’s state input at the original state-space size.

title: Belief Projection-Based Reinforcement Learning for Environments with Delayed Feedback

abstract: Message passing neural networks (MPNNs) have emerged as the most popular framework of graph neural networks (GNNs) in recent years. However, their expressive power is limited by the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman (1-WL) test. Some works are inspired by $k$-WL/FWL (Folklore WL) and design the corresponding neural versions. Despite the high expressive power, there are serious limitations in this line of research. In particular, (1) $k$-WL/FWL requires at least $O(n^k)$ space complexity, which is impractical for large graphs even when $k=3$; (2) The design space of $k$-WL/FWL is rigid, with the only adjustable hyper-parameter being $k$. To tackle the first limitation, we propose an extension, $(k, t)$-FWL. We theoretically prove that even if we fix the space complexity to $O(n^k)$ (for any $k \geq 2$) in $(k, t)$-FWL, we can construct an expressiveness hierarchy up to solving the graph isomorphism problem. To tackle the second problem, we propose $k$-FWL+, which considers any equivariant set as neighbors instead of all nodes, thereby greatly expanding the design space of $k$-FWL. Combining these two modifications results in a flexible and powerful framework $(k, t)$-FWL+. We demonstrate $(k, t)$-FWL+ can implement most existing models with matching expressiveness. We then introduce an instance of $(k,t)$-FWL+ called Neighborhood$^2$-FWL (N$^2$-FWL), which is practically and theoretically sound. We prove that N$^2$-FWL is no less powerful than 3-WL, and can encode many substructures while only requiring $O(n^2)$ space. Finally, we design its neural version named **N$^2$-GNN** and evaluate its performance on various tasks. N$^2$-GNN achieves record-breaking results on ZINC-Subset (**0.059**), outperforming previous SOTA results by 10.6\%. Moreover, N$^2$-GNN achieves new SOTA results on the BREC dataset (**71.8\%**) among all existing high-expressive GNN methods.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks differ in their ability to distinguish graph structures. Standard message-passing networks are limited by the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman test. Higher-order versions offer more expressive power, but require substantial storage and traditionally provide a rigid design choice centered on the order k.

The paper introduces two extensions. The first, (k, t)-FWL, creates an expressiveness hierarchy reaching graph isomorphism while keeping space complexity at O(n^k) for any fixed k of at least two. The second, k-FWL+, allows equivariant neighbor sets, expanding which relationships the procedure can consider. Together they form a framework that can reproduce most existing models with matching expressiveness. The fixed-space result concerns storage, rather than a claim that all such computations are cheap.

A concrete instance, Neighborhood²-FWL, is proved at least as powerful as 3-WL while requiring O(n²) space and encoding many substructures. Its neural version, N²-GNN, reports record results of 0.059 on ZINC-Subset and 71.8% on BREC. These results connect the broader theoretical design space to an empirically effective architecture.
summary.tldr: Extensions of Folklore Weisfeiler-Lehman enable more flexible graph models, including a quadratic-space model with at least 3-WL expressiveness.

title: Extending the Design Space of Graph Neural Networks by Rethinking Folklore Weisfeiler-Lehman

abstract: Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) is a collaborative machine learning paradigm that enables multiple participants to jointly train a model on their private data without sharing it.To make VFL practical, privacy security and communication efficiency should both be satisfied. Recent research has shown that Zero-Order Optimization (ZOO) in VFL can effectively conceal the internal information of the model without adding costly privacy protective add-ons, making it a promising approach for privacy and efficiency.However, there are still two key problems that have yet to be resolved. First, the convergence rate of ZOO-based VFL is significantly slower compared to gradient-based VFL, resulting in low efficiency in model training and more communication round, which hinders its application on large neural networks. Second, although ZOO-based VFL has demonstrated resistance to state-of-the-art (SOTA) attacks, its privacy guarantee lacks a theoretical explanation.To address these challenges, we propose a novel cascaded hybrid optimization approach that employs a zeroth-order (ZO) gradient on the most critical output layer of the clients, with other parts utilizing the first-order (FO) gradient. This approach preserves the privacy protection of ZOO while significantly enhancing convergence.Moreover, we theoretically prove that applying ZOO to the VFL is equivalent to adding Gaussian Mechanism to the gradient information, which offers an implicit differential privacy guarantee. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves similar utility as the Gaussian mechanism under the same privacy budget, while also having significantly lower communication costs compared with SOTA communication-efficient VFL frameworks.

paragraphs: Vertical federated learning lets participants jointly train a model while retaining their private data. Zeroth-order optimization offers a way to conceal internal model information without expensive additional privacy mechanisms, but its slower convergence can require more communication. This paper addresses both that efficiency problem and the lack of a theoretical explanation for its privacy protection.

The proposed approach combines two optimization methods within the training process. It applies a zeroth-order gradient at clients’ output layers, identified as especially important for privacy, while using first-order gradients elsewhere. This selective arrangement preserves the privacy protection attributed to zeroth-order optimization while improving convergence, rather than applying the slower approach throughout the model.

The authors also prove an equivalence between applying zeroth-order optimization in their VFL analysis and adding a Gaussian mechanism to gradient information, providing an implicit differential privacy guarantee. Experiments report utility similar to the Gaussian mechanism at the same privacy budget, alongside substantially lower communication costs than the compared communication-efficient VFL frameworks. The contribution therefore connects an optimization design with both privacy analysis and practical communication savings.
summary.tldr: Hybrid optimization concentrates zeroth-order updates at client outputs to improve federated training efficiency while supporting an implicit differential privacy guarantee.

title: A Unified Solution for Privacy and Communication Efficiency in Vertical Federated Learning

abstract: Representation learning has significantly driven the field to develop pretrained models that can act as a valuable starting point when transferring to new datasets. With the rising demand for reliable machine learning and uncertainty quantification, there is a need for pretrained models that not only provide embeddings but also transferable uncertainty estimates. To guide the development of such models, we propose the Uncertainty-aware Representation Learning (URL) benchmark. Besides the transferability of the representations, it also measures the zero-shot transferability of the uncertainty estimate using a novel metric. We apply URL to evaluate ten uncertainty quantifiers that are pretrained on ImageNet and transferred to eight downstream datasets. We find that approaches that focus on the uncertainty of the representation itself or estimate the prediction risk directly outperform those that are based on the probabilities of upstream classes. Yet, achieving transferable uncertainty quantification remains an open challenge. Our findings indicate that it is not necessarily in conflict with traditional representation learning goals. Code is available at [https://github.com/mkirchhof/url](https://github.com/mkirchhof/url).

paragraphs: Pretrained representations can be useful on new datasets, but their usefulness does not establish whether accompanying uncertainty estimates also transfer. The Uncertainty-aware Representation Learning benchmark, or URL, evaluates both properties. It introduces a metric for measuring zero-shot transfer of uncertainty alongside the transferability of the representations themselves.

The authors apply the benchmark to ten uncertainty quantification methods pretrained on ImageNet and transferred to eight downstream datasets. This setup tests whether uncertainty remains informative when the model is used beyond its original training setting. It therefore adds a reliability dimension to evaluation of pretrained features.

The reported comparison favors methods that model uncertainty in the representation itself or directly estimate prediction risk over methods based on probabilities for the original training classes. Transferable uncertainty nevertheless remains an open challenge. The findings also suggest that improving it need not conflict with conventional representation learning goals. URL provides a way to evaluate that relationship explicitly and guide development of pretrained models with useful features and uncertainty estimates.
summary.tldr: URL benchmarks transferable representations and uncertainty, finding advantages for representation-based uncertainty and direct risk estimates.

title: URL: A Representation Learning Benchmark for Transferable Uncertainty Estimates

abstract: We propose EB-TC$\varepsilon$, a novel sampling rule for $\varepsilon$-best arm identification in stochastic bandits.It is the first instance of Top Two algorithm analyzed for approximate best arm identification. EB-TC$\varepsilon$ is an *anytime* sampling rule that can therefore be employed without modification for fixed confidence or fixed budget identification (without prior knowledge of the budget).We provide three types of theoretical guarantees for EB-TC$\varepsilon$.First, we prove bounds on its expected sample complexity in the fixed confidence setting, notably showing its asymptotic optimality in combination with an adaptive tuning of its exploration parameter.We complement these findings with upper bounds on its probability of error at any time and for any slack parameter, which further yield upper bounds on its simple regret at any time.Finally, we show through numerical simulations that EB-TC$\varepsilon$ performs favorably compared to existing algorithms for different approximate best arm identification tasks.

EB-TC$\varepsilon$ is an *anytime* sampling rule that can therefore be employed without modification for fixed confidence or fixed budget identification (without prior knowledge of the budget).We provide three types of theoretical guarantees for EB-TC$\varepsilon$.First, we prove bounds on its expected sample complexity in the fixed confidence setting, notably showing its asymptotic optimality in combination with an adaptive tuning of its exploration parameter.We complement these findings with upper bounds on its probability of error at any time and for any slack parameter, which further yield upper bounds on its simple regret at any time.Finally, we show through numerical simulations that EB-TC$\varepsilon$ performs favorably compared to existing algorithms for different approximate best arm identification tasks.

paragraphs: In stochastic bandits, an algorithm samples options with uncertain rewards to identify a good choice. Approximate best-arm identification allows a tolerance, epsilon, rather than demanding the exact best option. This paper introduces EB-TCε, a sampling rule from the Top Two family, and provides the first analysis of that family for approximate identification.

The rule is anytime: it can keep sampling without knowing the eventual budget. The same sampling procedure therefore supports both a fixed-confidence setting, where reliability determines when to stop, and a fixed-budget setting. The authors bound expected sample requirements for fixed confidence and establish asymptotic optimality when the exploration parameter is tuned adaptively. That tuning is part of the stated optimality result.

The analysis also bounds error probabilities at any time and for any slack parameter. These results yield bounds on simple regret, which measures the reward shortfall of the recommended option. Numerical simulations show favorable performance against existing algorithms across different approximate identification tasks, complementing the theoretical guarantees with empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: EB-TCε provides an anytime sampling rule for approximately identifying the best bandit option, with sample-complexity, error, and regret guarantees.

title: An $\varepsilon$-Best-Arm Identification Algorithm for Fixed-Confidence and Beyond

abstract: Generative modeling has recently undergone remarkable advancements, primarily propelled by the transformative implications of Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DPMs). The impressive capability of these models, however, often entails significant computational overhead during both training and inference. To tackle this challenge, we present Diff-Pruning, an efficient compression method tailored for learning lightweight diffusion models from pre-existing ones, without the need for extensive re-training. The essence of Diff-Pruning is encapsulated in a Taylor expansion over pruned timesteps, a process that disregards non-contributory diffusion steps and ensembles informative gradients to identify important weights. Our empirical assessment, undertaken across several datasets highlights two primary benefits of our proposed method: 1) Efficiency: it enables approximately a 50\% reduction in FLOPs at a mere 10% to 20% of the original training expenditure; 2) Consistency: the pruned diffusion models inherently preserve generative behavior congruent with their pre-trained models.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can produce impressive outputs but require substantial computation during training and inference. Diff-Pruning aims to obtain a lightweight model from an existing pretrained diffusion model without extensive retraining. The challenge is identifying which parts can be removed while retaining the generative behavior already learned.

The method uses a Taylor-expansion-based assessment over selected diffusion timesteps. It disregards steps that do not contribute useful information to this assessment and combines informative gradients to identify important weights. This makes information from the diffusion process part of the pruning decision, rather than treating weight importance as independent of the model’s progression across timesteps.

Across several datasets, the authors report approximately a 50% reduction in floating-point operations at a cost of 10% to 20% of the original training expenditure. They also find that the pruned models preserve generative behavior consistent with their pretrained counterparts. These results support compression as a way to reuse an existing model’s learned capabilities while reducing its computational requirements.
summary.tldr: Diff-Pruning uses informative timestep gradients to compress pretrained diffusion models, roughly halving FLOPs in the reported experiments.

title: Structural Pruning for Diffusion Models

abstract: Deep regression models typically learn in an end-to-end fashion without explicitly emphasizing a regression-aware representation. Consequently, the learned representations exhibit fragmentation and fail to capture the continuous nature of sample orders, inducing suboptimal results across a wide range of regression tasks. To fill the gap, we propose Rank-N-Contrast (RNC), a framework that learns continuous representations for regression by contrasting samples against each other based on their rankings in the target space. We demonstrate, theoretically and empirically, that RNC guarantees the desired order of learned representations in accordance with the target orders, enjoying not only better performance but also significantly improved robustness, efficiency, and generalization. Extensive experiments using five real-world regression datasets that span computer vision, human-computer interaction, and healthcare verify that RNC achieves state-of-the-art performance, highlighting its intriguing properties including better data efficiency, robustness to spurious targets and data corruptions, and generalization to distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Regression predicts continuously varying targets, yet ordinary end-to-end training does not explicitly require internal representations to reflect that continuity. The paper argues that representations can consequently become fragmented and fail to preserve sample ordering. Rank-N-Contrast addresses this by making the structure of the target space part of representation learning itself.

The framework contrasts samples according to their rankings in target space. This gives training a direct signal about how examples should be ordered in the learned representation. The authors provide theoretical and empirical support for the resulting alignment, including a guarantee that the desired representation ordering follows the target ordering.

Experiments span five real-world regression datasets in computer vision, human-computer interaction, and healthcare. They report state-of-the-art performance together with improved data efficiency, robustness to spurious targets and corrupted data, and generalization under distribution shifts. These findings support the paper's central argument that explicitly learning a regression-aware representation can improve both prediction quality and behavior under challenging data conditions.
summary.tldr: Rank-N-Contrast uses target rankings to learn ordered regression representations, improving accuracy and robustness in the reported evaluations.

title: Rank-N-Contrast: Learning Continuous Representations for Regression

abstract: Motivated by alternating game-play in two-player games, we study an altenating variant of the \textit{Online Linear Optimization} (OLO). In alternating OLO, a \textit{learner} at each round $t \in [n]$ selects a vector $x^t$ and then an \textit{adversary} selects a cost-vector $c^t \in [-1,1]^n$. The learner then experiences cost $(c^t + c^{t-1})^\top x^t$ instead of $(c^t)^\top x^t$ as in standard OLO. We establish that under this small twist, the $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ lower bound on the regret is no longer valid. More precisely, we present two online learning algorithms for alternating OLO that respectively admit $\mathcal{O}((\log n)^{4/3} T^{1/3})$ regret for the $n$-dimensional simplex and $\mathcal{O}(\rho \log T)$ regret for the ball of radius $\rho>0$. Our results imply that in alternating game-play, an agent can always guarantee $\mathcal{\tilde{O}}((\log n)^{4/3} T^{1/3})$ regardless the strategies of the other agent while the regret bound improves to $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$ in case the agent admits only two actions.
originalAbstract: Motivated by alternating game-play in two-player games, we study an altenating variant of the \textit{Online Linear Optimization} (OLO). In alternating OLO, a \textit{learner} at each round $t \in [n]$ selects a vector $x^t$ and then an \textit{adversary} selects a cost-vector $c^t \in [-1,1]^n$. The learner then experiences cost $(c^t + c^{t-1})^\top x^t$ instead of $(c^t)^\top x^t$ as in standard OLO. We establish that under this small twist, the $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ lower bound on the regret is no longer valid. More precisely, we present two online learning algorithms for alternating OLO that respectively admit $\mathcal{O}((\log n)^{4/3} T^{1/3})$ regret for the $n$-dimensional simplex and $\mathcal{O}(\rho \log T)$ regret for the ball of radius $\rho>0$. Our results imply that in alternating game-play, an agent can always guarantee $\mathcal{\tilde{O}}((\log n)^{4/3} T^{1/3})$ regardless the strategies of the other agent while the regret bound improves to $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$ in case the agent admits only two actions.

paragraphs: Online linear optimization studies repeated decisions against changing costs. This paper considers a variation motivated by alternating moves in two-player games: after the learner chooses an action vector, the adversary chooses a cost vector, and the learner's cost depends on both the current and previous cost vectors. That small change alters the achievable guarantees.

The authors show that the usual square-root dependence on the number of rounds in the regret lower bound no longer applies to this setting. They construct algorithms with regret bounded by O((log n)^(4/3) T^(1/3)) on the n-dimensional simplex and O(ρ log T) on a ball of radius ρ, where T counts rounds.

Regret measures accumulated cost relative to a fixed comparison decision. Thus, these results describe how quickly the learner can limit its disadvantage despite adversarial choices. For alternating gameplay, the derived guarantee holds regardless of the other player's strategy, with a logarithmic regret bound when the learner has only two actions. The improvement depends on the specific alternating cost structure analyzed in the paper.
summary.tldr: A specific alternating cost structure permits stronger regret guarantees than standard online linear optimization.

title: Alternation makes the adversary weaker in two-player games

abstract: Learning curve extrapolation aims to predict model performance in later epochs of training, based on the performance in earlier epochs.In this work, we argue that, while the inherent uncertainty in the extrapolation of learning curves warrants a Bayesian approach, existing methods are (i) overly restrictive, and/or (ii) computationally expensive. We describe the first application of prior-data fitted neural networks (PFNs) in this context. A PFN is a transformer, pre-trained on data generated from a prior, to perform approximate Bayesian inference in a single forward pass. We propose LC-PFN, a PFN trained to extrapolate 10 million artificial right-censored learning curves generated from a parametric prior proposed in prior art using MCMC. We demonstrate that LC-PFN can approximate the posterior predictive distribution more accurately than MCMC, while being over 10 000 times faster. We also show that the same LC-PFN achieves competitive performance extrapolating a total of 20 000 real learning curves from four learning curve benchmarks (LCBench, NAS-Bench-201, Taskset, and PD1) that stem from training a wide range of model architectures (MLPs, CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers) on 53 different datasets with varying input modalities (tabular, image, text, and protein data). Finally, we investigate its potential in the context of model selection and find that a simple LC-PFN based predictive early stopping criterion obtains 2 - 6x speed-ups on 45 of these datasets, at virtually no overhead.

paragraphs: Learning-curve extrapolation predicts a model's later performance from its early training results. Because many futures can fit the same early observations, the paper argues for predicting a distribution of outcomes. It introduces LC-PFN, a transformer pretrained to approximate Bayesian inference in one forward pass, avoiding repeated expensive inference for each new learning curve.

LC-PFN learns from 10 million artificial curves generated from a parametric prior. These curves are right-censored, meaning their later portions are unobserved in the extrapolation task. The authors report that LC-PFN approximates the posterior predictive distribution more accurately than the compared MCMC approach while running more than 10,000 times faster.

The same model also performs competitively on 20,000 real learning curves spanning four benchmarks, multiple neural architectures, and 53 datasets with different input modalities. In model-selection experiments, a simple predictive early-stopping rule based on LC-PFN produces two- to six-fold speedups on 45 datasets with virtually no overhead. These results connect fast uncertainty-aware extrapolation to a concrete use: deciding when further model training is unlikely to be worthwhile.
summary.tldr: LC-PFN predicts learning-curve futures with fast approximate Bayesian inference and enables substantial early-stopping speedups in reported experiments.

title: Efficient Bayesian Learning Curve Extrapolation using Prior-Data Fitted Networks

abstract: Temporal graphs are widely used to model dynamic systems with time-varying interactions. In real-world scenarios, the underlying mechanisms of generating future interactions in dynamic systems are typically governed by a set of recurring substructures within the graph, known as temporal motifs. Despite the success and prevalence of current temporal graph neural networks (TGNN), it remains uncertain which temporal motifs are recognized as the significant indications that trigger a certain prediction from the model, which is a critical challenge for advancing the explainability and trustworthiness of current TGNNs. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach, called **Temp**oral **M**otifs **E**xplainer (**TempME**), which uncovers the most pivotal temporal motifs guiding the prediction of TGNNs. Derived from the information bottleneck principle, TempME extracts the most interaction-related motifs while minimizing the amount of contained information to preserve the sparsity and succinctness of the explanation. Events in the explanations generated by TempME are verified to be more spatiotemporally correlated than those of existing approaches, providing more understandable insights. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of TempME, with up to 8.21% increase in terms of explanation accuracy across six real-world datasets and up to 22.96% increase in boosting the prediction Average Precision of current TGNNs.

paragraphs: Temporal graph neural networks predict interactions in systems whose connections change over time. Understanding these predictions requires identifying which patterns in the interaction history matter to the model. TempME focuses on temporal motifs: recurring arrangements of interactions that can provide a meaningful unit for explaining a prediction.

The method uses the information bottleneck principle to select motifs strongly related to the interaction being predicted while limiting the amount of information retained. This balances relevance with concise explanations. Instead of returning an unnecessarily large collection of events, it aims to identify a sparse set of patterns that captures the model's key predictive evidence.

The authors find that events selected by TempME are more closely connected in space and time than those selected by existing approaches. Across six real-world datasets, they report explanation accuracy improvements of up to 8.21% and increases of up to 22.96% in prediction Average Precision for current temporal graph models. These are reported maximum gains, supporting both the explanatory usefulness and potential predictive value of motif discovery.
summary.tldr: TempME explains temporal graph predictions by selecting compact, relevant recurring interaction patterns.

title: TempME: Towards the Explainability of Temporal Graph Neural Networks via Motif Discovery

abstract: Masked image modeling (MIM) has become a prevalent pre-training setup for vision foundation models and attains promising performance. Despite its success, existing MIM methods discard the decoder network during downstream applica- tions, resulting in inconsistent representations between pre-training and fine-tuning and can hamper downstream task performance. In this paper, we propose a new architecture, RevColV2, which tackles this issue by keeping the entire autoen- coder architecture during both pre-training and fine-tuning. The main body of RevColV2 contains bottom-up columns and top-down columns, between which information is reversibly propagated and gradually disentangled. Such design enables our architecture with the nice property: maintaining disentangled low-level and semantic information at the end of the network in MIM pre-training. Our experimental results suggest that a foundation model with decoupled features can achieve competitive performance across multiple downstream vision tasks such as image classification, semantic segmentation and object detection. For exam- ple, after intermediate fine-tuning on ImageNet-22K dataset, RevColV2-L attains 88.4\% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K classification and 58.6 mIoU on ADE20K semantic segmentation. With extra teacher and large scale dataset, RevColv2-L achieves 62.1 APbox on COCO detection and 60.4 mIoU on ADE20K semantic segmentation.

RevColV2 addresses this by retaining the entire autoencoder during both stages.

Those results come from different training conditions and illustrate the architecture's performance across several vision tasks.
summary.tldr: RevColV2 retains the full autoencoder through fine-tuning and separates low-level from semantic information for competitive downstream vision performance.

title: RevColV2: Exploring Disentangled Representations in Masked Image Modeling

abstract: Meta-learning has demonstrated promising results in few-shot classification (FSC) by learning to solve new problems using prior knowledge. Bayesian methods are effective at characterizing uncertainty in FSC, which is crucial in high-risk fields. In this context, the logistic-softmax likelihood is often employed as an alternative to the softmax likelihood in multi-class Gaussian process classification due to its conditional conjugacy property. However, the theoretical property of logistic-softmax is not clear and previous research indicated that the inherent uncertainty of logistic-softmax leads to suboptimal performance. To mitigate these issues, we revisit and redesign the logistic-softmax likelihood, which enables control of the \textit{a priori} confidence level through a temperature parameter. Furthermore, we theoretically and empirically show that softmax can be viewed as a special case of logistic-softmax and logistic-softmax induces a larger family of data distribution than softmax. Utilizing modified logistic-softmax, we integrate the data augmentation technique into the deep kernel based Gaussian process meta-learning framework, and derive an analytical mean-field approximation for task-specific updates. Our approach yields well-calibrated uncertainty estimates and achieves comparable or superior results on standard benchmark datasets. Code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/keanson/revisit-logistic-softmax}.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification uses prior learning to solve new classification tasks from limited examples. Bayesian approaches also characterize uncertainty, but the likelihood used to connect a model to class labels affects its confidence behavior. This paper revisits logistic-softmax, whose conditional conjugacy makes it useful in multiclass Gaussian process classification.

The authors redesign the likelihood with a temperature parameter that controls confidence before observing task data. They show theoretically and empirically that softmax is a special case of logistic-softmax, with logistic-softmax supporting a broader family of data distributions. This clarifies the relationship between the alternatives and provides a mechanism for adjusting prior confidence.

The modified likelihood is incorporated into a deep-kernel Gaussian process meta-learning framework using data augmentation. The authors derive an analytical mean-field approximation for task-specific updates. Their approach produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates and comparable or better results on standard benchmarks. The contribution combines a more flexible likelihood with an analytical adaptation procedure, addressing predictive performance and uncertainty together.
summary.tldr: A temperature-controlled logistic-softmax likelihood broadens Bayesian few-shot classification while supporting calibrated uncertainty and analytical task updates.

title: Revisiting Logistic-softmax Likelihood in Bayesian Meta-Learning for Few-Shot Classification

abstract: We study offline reinforcement learning (RL) which seeks to learn a good policy based on a fixed, pre-collected dataset. A fundamental challenge behind this task is the distributional shift due to the dataset lacking sufficient exploration, especially under function approximation. To tackle this issue, we propose a bi-level structured policy optimization algorithm that models a hierarchical interaction between the policy (upper-level) and the value function (lower-level). The lower level focuses on constructing a confidence set of value estimates that maintain sufficiently small weighted average Bellman errors, while controlling uncertainty arising from distribution mismatch. Subsequently, at the upper level, the policy aims to maximize a conservative value estimate from the confidence set formed at the lower level. This novel formulation preserves the maximum flexibility of the implicitly induced exploratory data distribution, enabling the power of model extrapolation. In practice, it can be solved through a computationally efficient, penalized adversarial estimation procedure. Our theoretical regret guarantees do not rely on any data-coverage and completeness-type assumptions, only requiring realizability. These guarantees also demonstrate that the learned policy represents the ``best effort'' among all policies, as no other policies can outperform it. We evaluate our model using a blend of synthetic, benchmark, and real-world datasets for offline RL, showing that it performs competitively with state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must choose actions using a fixed collection of past experience. When that collection explores only a limited part of the environment, a learned policy can encounter situations poorly represented in its training data. This paper addresses the resulting distribution mismatch through a two-level interaction between policy learning and value estimation.

The lower level constructs a confidence set of value estimates. These estimates must have sufficiently small weighted average Bellman errors while accounting for uncertainty caused by distribution mismatch. The upper level then chooses a policy by maximizing a conservative value from that set. A penalized adversarial estimation procedure makes this formulation computationally practical while preserving flexibility in the exploratory distribution it implicitly uses.

The theoretical regret guarantees require realizability but do not require data-coverage or completeness assumptions. Within the proposed theoretical setting, the authors characterize the learned policy as a best-effort solution among the available policies. Experiments spanning synthetic, benchmark, and real-world datasets show competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods, connecting the theoretical formulation with practical offline learning.
summary.tldr: A two-level offline reinforcement learning method optimizes conservative value estimates and provides regret guarantees requiring realizability without coverage or completeness assumptions.

title: Bi-Level Offline Policy Optimization with Limited Exploration

abstract: Simulation with realistic, interactive agents represents a key task for autonomous vehicle software development. In this work, we introduce the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC). WOSAC is the first public challenge to tackle this task and propose corresponding metrics. The goal of the challenge is to stimulate the design of realistic simulators that can be used to evaluate and train a behavior model for autonomous driving. We outline our evaluation methodology, present results for a number of different baseline simulation agent methods, and analyze several submissions to the 2023 competition which ran from March 16, 2023 to May 23, 2023. The WOSAC evaluation server remains open for submissions and we discuss open problems for the task.

paragraphs: Autonomous-driving development needs simulations populated by agents that behave realistically and interact with one another. The Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge focuses on this problem as a public research task. Its goal is to encourage simulators that can support both evaluating driving behavior models and training those models.

The paper introduces the challenge together with metrics and an evaluation methodology. This makes the contribution more than a call to build simulation agents: it also provides a shared way to assess proposed methods. The authors present results for several baseline agent approaches and examine submissions from the competition, giving concrete examples of methods evaluated within that framework.

The paper also discusses open problems, positioning realistic interactive simulation as an ongoing research challenge. Its central contribution is evaluation infrastructure and comparative analysis rather than a single new simulator. By bringing task definition, metrics, baseline results, and competition submissions together, it creates a common setting for studying how well simulated agents support the needs of autonomous-driving research.
summary.tldr: WOSAC establishes a public challenge and evaluation framework for realistic, interactive simulation agents in autonomous driving.

title: The Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge

abstract: We present the ilLumination-Aware conditional Image Repainting (LuminAIRe) task to address the unrealistic lighting effects in recent conditional image repainting (CIR) methods. The environment lighting and 3D geometry conditions are explicitly estimated from given background images and parsing masks using a parametric lighting representation and learning-based priors. These 3D conditions are then converted into illumination images through the proposed physically-based illumination rendering and illumination attention module. With the injection of illumination images, physically-correct lighting information is fed into the lighting-realistic generation process and repainted images with harmonized lighting effects in both foreground and background regions can be acquired, whose superiority over the results of state-of-the-art methods is confirmed through extensive experiments. For facilitating and validating the LuminAIRe task, a new dataset Car-LuminAIRe with lighting annotations and rich appearance variants is collected.

paragraphs: Conditional image repainting can produce unrealistic lighting, making the repainted content inconsistent with its surroundings. LuminAIRe introduces an illumination-aware version of this task. The approach explicitly incorporates estimates of the scene’s lighting and three-dimensional geometry into image generation so that the foreground and background can have harmonized lighting effects.

The method begins with a background image and parsing masks. It estimates environmental lighting and geometry using a parametric lighting representation together with learned priors. A physically based illumination-rendering process and an illumination attention module then turn those estimates into illumination images. These images supply lighting information to the generation process.

Experiments report superior results to state-of-the-art conditional repainting methods, supporting the value of making illumination an explicit condition for generation. The authors also collect Car-LuminAIRe, a dataset with lighting annotations and varied appearances, to support development and evaluation of the task. The work combines a lighting-aware generation pipeline with data intended to make lighting realism a directly studied part of repainting.
summary.tldr: LuminAIRe uses estimated lighting and geometry to guide image repainting toward consistent foreground and background illumination.

title: LuminAIRe: Illumination-Aware Conditional Image Repainting for Lighting-Realistic Generation

abstract: As there exist competitive subnetworks within a dense network in concert with Lottery Ticket Hypothesis, we introduce a novel neuron-wise task incremental learning method, namely Data-free Subnetworks (DSN), which attempts to enhance the elastic knowledge transfer across the tasks that sequentially arrive. Specifically, DSN primarily seeks to transfer knowledge to the new coming task from the learned tasks by selecting the affiliated weights of a small set of neurons to be activated, including the reused neurons from prior tasks via neuron-wise masks. And it also transfers possibly valuable knowledge to the earlier tasks via data-free replay. Especially, DSN inherently relieves the catastrophic forgetting and the unavailability of past data or possible privacy concerns. The comprehensive experiments conducted on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DSN in the context of task-incremental learning by comparing it to several state-of-the-art baselines. In particular, DSN enables the knowledge transfer to the earlier tasks, which is often overlooked by prior efforts.

paragraphs: Learning tasks sequentially raises two connected problems: retaining earlier knowledge and using that knowledge to help with new tasks. Data-free Subnetworks, or DSN, approaches both through small groups of neurons inside a larger network. Its motivation is that competitive smaller networks can exist within a dense network, as suggested by the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis.

For an arriving task, DSN activates weights associated with a small selection of neurons. Neuron-level masks allow that selection to include neurons already used by earlier tasks, providing a route for transferring existing knowledge forward. The method also uses data-free replay to transfer potentially useful knowledge back to previous tasks without requiring their original data.

Experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness against several leading task-incremental learning baselines. The authors emphasize backward transfer, which earlier approaches often overlook. DSN therefore treats continual learning as an opportunity to improve earlier tasks as well as preserve them, while alleviating forgetting and difficulties caused by unavailable past data.
summary.tldr: DSN uses neuron-level subnetworks and data-free replay to transfer knowledge both to new tasks and back to earlier ones.

title: Enhancing Knowledge Transfer for Task Incremental Learning with Data-free Subnetwork

abstract: Intent learning, which aims to learn users' intents for user understanding and item recommendation, has become a hot research spot in recent years. However, existing methods suffer from complex and cumbersome alternating optimization, limiting performance and scalability. To this end, we propose a novel intent learning method termed \underline{ELCRec}, by unifying behavior representation learning into an \underline{E}nd-to-end \underline{L}earnable \underline{C}lustering framework, for effective and efficient \underline{Rec}ommendation. Concretely, we encode user behavior sequences and initialize the cluster centers (latent intents) as learnable neurons. Then, we design a novel learnable clustering module to separate different cluster centers, thus decoupling users' complex intents. Meanwhile, it guides the network to learn intents from behaviors by forcing behavior embeddings close to cluster centers. This allows simultaneous optimization of recommendation and clustering via mini-batch data. Moreover, we propose intent-assisted contrastive learning by using cluster centers as self-supervision signals, further enhancing mutual promotion. Both experimental results and theoretical analyses demonstrate the superiority of ELCRec from six perspectives. Compared to the runner-up, ELCRec improves NDCG@5 by 8.9\% and reduces computational costs by 22.5\% on the Beauty dataset. Furthermore, due to the scalability and universal applicability, we deploy this method on the industrial recommendation system with 130 million page views and achieve promising results. The codes are available on GitHub\footnote{https://github.com/yueliu1999/ELCRec}. A collection (papers, codes, datasets) of deep group recommendation/intent learning methods is available on GitHub\footnote{https://github.com/yueliu1999/Awesome-Deep-Group-Recommendation}.

ELCRec combines behavior representation and intent clustering in one trainable framework, allowing both to improve together using mini-batches of user data.

These two pressures aim to distinguish different intents and connect observed behavior to the corresponding intent representations. An additional contrastive-learning component uses the cluster centers as self-supervision signals to strengthen this interaction.

They also report promising results from deployment in an industrial recommendation system with 130 million page views. Together, the reported findings connect the unified training design to improvements in recommendation performance and computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: ELCRec jointly learns user behavior representations and intent clusters, improving recommendation performance and reducing computational costs in reported experiments.

title: End-to-end Learnable Clustering for Intent Learning in Recommendation

abstract: Online Budgeted Matching (OBM) is a classic problem with important applications in online advertising, online service matching, revenue management, and beyond. Traditional online algorithms typically assume a small bid setting, where the maximum bid-to-budget ratio ($\kappa$) is infinitesimally small. While recent algorithms have tried to address scenarios with non-small or general bids, they often rely on the Fractional Last Matching (FLM) assumption, which allows for accepting partial bids when the remaining budget is insufficient. This assumption, however, does not hold for many applications with indivisible bids. In this paper, we remove the FLM assumption and tackle the open problem of OBM with general bids. We first establish an upper bound of $1-\kappa$ on the competitive ratio for any deterministic online algorithm. We then propose a novel meta algorithm, called MetaAd, which reduces to different algorithms with first known provable competitive ratios parameterized by the maximum bid-to-budget ratio $\kappa\in [0,1]$. As a by-product, we extend MetaAd to the FLM setting and get provable competitive algorithms. Finally, we apply our competitive analysis to the design learning- augmented algorithms.

paragraphs: Online budgeted matching concerns decisions made as opportunities arrive under limited budgets, with applications including advertising and service matching. Many algorithms assume each bid is tiny relative to a budget. Methods allowing larger bids often rely on fractional last matching, which permits accepting part of a bid when the remaining budget cannot cover it.

This paper removes that fractional acceptance assumption to handle indivisible bids. It characterizes bid size using kappa, the largest bid-to-budget ratio. The authors prove that any deterministic online algorithm has a competitive ratio no greater than 1 minus kappa. This establishes a ceiling on worst-case performance guarantees as bids become larger relative to budgets.

The proposed MetaAd framework produces different algorithms with provable competitive ratios parameterized by kappa throughout the interval from zero to one. The authors describe these as the first known such guarantees for the general-bid problem without fractional last matching. They also extend the framework to the fractional setting and use its competitive analysis to design learning-augmented algorithms.
summary.tldr: MetaAd provides competitive guarantees for online budgeted matching with general, indivisible bids.

title: Online Budgeted Matching with General Bids

abstract: Binary analysis is a core component of many critical security tasks, including reverse engineering, malware analysis, and vulnerability detection. Manual analysis is often time-consuming, but identifying commonly-used or previously-seen functions can reduce the time it takes to understand a new file. However, given the complexity of assembly, and the NP-hard nature of determining function equivalence, this task is extremely difficult. Common approaches often use sophisticated disassembly and decompilation tools, graph analysis, and other expensive pre-processing steps to perform function similarity searches over some corpus. In this work, we identify a number of discrepancies between the current research environment and the underlying application need. To remedy this, we build a new benchmark, REFuSe-Bench, for binary function similarity detection consisting of high-quality datasets and tests that better reflect real-world use cases. In doing so, we address issues like data duplication and accurate labeling, experiment with real malware, and perform the first serious evaluation of ML binary function similarity models on Windows data. Our benchmark reveals that a new, simple baseline — one which looks at only the raw bytes of a function, and requires no disassembly or other pre-processing --- is able to achieve state-of-the-art performance in multiple settings. Our findings challenge conventional assumptions that complex models with highly-engineered features are being used to their full potential, and demonstrate that simpler approaches can provide significant value.

The result challenges assumptions about how much existing methods gain from sophisticated features and complex processing. It shows that simple representations can be highly competitive under these evaluations, providing a useful reference point for assessing more elaborate methods.
summary.tldr: REFuSe-Bench improves binary function similarity evaluation and finds that a simple raw-byte baseline reaches state-of-the-art performance in multiple settings.

title: Is Function Similarity Over-Engineered? Building a Benchmark

abstract: Given an unconditional diffusion model and a predictor for a target property of interest (e.g., a classifier), the goal of training-free guidance is to generate samples with desirable target properties without additional training. Existing methods, though effective in various individual applications, often lack theoretical grounding and rigorous testing on extensive benchmarks. As a result, they could even fail on simple tasks, and applying them to a new problem becomes unavoidably difficult. This paper introduces a novel algorithmic framework encompassing existing methods as special cases, unifying the study of training-free guidance into the analysis of an algorithm-agnostic design space. Via theoretical and empirical investigation, we propose an efficient and effective hyper-parameter searching strategy that can be readily applied to any downstream task. We systematically benchmark across 7 diffusion models on 16 tasks with 40 targets, and improve performance by 8.5% on average. Our framework and benchmark offer a solid foundation for conditional generation in a training-free manner.

paragraphs: Training-free guidance aims to steer an existing unconditional diffusion model toward desired properties using a predictor, such as a classifier, without additional training. Existing techniques can work well in particular applications, yet their limited theoretical grounding and broad evaluation make choosing an approach for a new task difficult.

TFG introduces a common algorithmic framework that includes existing guidance methods as special cases. This turns separate methods into choices within a shared design space, allowing their behavior to be studied in a unified way. The authors combine theoretical and empirical investigation to develop an efficient hyperparameter-search strategy intended for use across downstream tasks.

The evaluation spans seven diffusion models, 16 tasks, and 40 targets, with an average reported performance improvement of 8.5%. This breadth makes systematic testing a substantial part of the contribution alongside the framework itself. The findings support a more organized approach to conditional generation without retraining: characterize the available guidance choices, search their settings efficiently, and assess them across varied target properties rather than relying only on isolated applications.
summary.tldr: TFG unifies training-free diffusion guidance and supplies a hyperparameter-search strategy, reporting an average 8.5% improvement across a broad benchmark.

title: TFG: Unified Training-Free Guidance for Diffusion Models

abstract: This work presents BAdam, an optimization method that leverages the block coordinate descent (BCD) framework with Adam's update rule. BAdam offers a memory efficient approach to the full parameter finetuning of large language models. We conduct a theoretical convergence analysis for BAdam in the deterministic case. Experimentally, we apply BAdam to finetune the Llama 3-8B and Llama 3-70B models using a single RTX3090-24GB GPU and 4 A100-80GB GPUs, respectively. The results confirm BAdam's efficiency in terms of memory usage, running time, and optimization capability. Furthermore, the downstream performance evaluation based on MT-bench and math benchmarks shows that BAdam outperforms existing memory efficient baselines such as LoRA. It also demonstrates that BAdam can achieve comparable or even superior performance compared to Adam. Finally, the ablation study using SGD's update rule illustrates the suitability of BCD for finetuning LLMs. Our code can be easily integrated into any PyTorch-based codebase and is available at https://github.com/Ledzy/BAdam.

paragraphs: BAdam is an optimizer designed to make full-parameter fine-tuning of large language models more memory efficient. It combines block coordinate descent, which organizes optimization around blocks of parameters, with Adam's update rule. This gives the method a way to adapt the full model while changing how parameter updates are organized.

The paper provides a convergence analysis for the deterministic case and evaluates practical fine-tuning on two model sizes. The authors fine-tune Llama 3-8B on one RTX3090 with 24 GB of memory and Llama 3-70B on four A100 GPUs with 80 GB each. The reported results support efficiency in memory use, running time, and optimization capability.

On MT-bench and math benchmarks, BAdam outperforms evaluated memory-efficient alternatives such as LoRA and achieves performance comparable to or better than Adam. An ablation using SGD updates also supports the suitability of block coordinate descent for this application. These results suggest that restructuring optimization can make full-model adaptation practical under the demonstrated hardware budgets.
summary.tldr: BAdam combines block coordinate descent with Adam updates to enable memory-efficient full-parameter language-model fine-tuning.

title: BAdam: A Memory Efficient Full Parameter Optimization Method for Large Language Models

abstract: Recent research has shown that representation learning models may accidentally memorize their training data. For example, the déjà vu method shows that for certain representation learning models and training images, it is sometimes possible to correctly predict the foreground label given only the representation of he background – better than through dataset-level correlations. However, their measurement method requires training two models – one to estimate dataset-level correlations and the other to estimate memorization. This multiple model setup becomes infeasible for large open-source models. In this work, we propose alter native simple methods to estimate dataset-level correlations, and show that these can be used to approximate an off-the-shelf model’s memorization ability without any retraining. This enables, for the first time, the measurement of memorization in pre-trained open-source image representation and vision-language models. Our results show that different ways of measuring memorization yield very similar aggregate results. We also find that open-source models typically have lower aggregate memorization than similar models trained on a subset of the data. The code is available both for vision (https://github.com/facebookresearch/DejaVuOSS) and vision language (https://github.com/facebookresearch/VLMDejaVu) models.

paragraphs: A representation model can sometimes reveal information about a training image’s foreground even when given only its background. The déjà vu memorization test looks for predictive ability beyond what ordinary correlations in the dataset would explain. This distinction is essential: a background can legitimately correlate with a foreground category without implying that a particular training example was memorized.

Earlier measurement required training two models, one to estimate dataset correlations and another to estimate memorization. That makes the procedure impractical for large released models. This paper proposes simpler ways to estimate the correlation component, allowing memorization in an existing model to be approximated without retraining it.

The approach enables evaluation of pretrained open-source image representation and vision-language models. Different measurement methods produce very similar aggregate results, supporting the usefulness of the cheaper estimates at that level. The authors also find that open-source models typically exhibit less aggregate memorization than comparable models trained on a data subset. These are aggregate comparisons, rather than claims that every example or every released model behaves identically.
summary.tldr: The paper estimates déjà vu memorization in existing vision models without retraining by simplifying the measurement of dataset-level correlations.

title: Measuring Dejavu Memorization Efficiently

abstract: Test-time adaptation, which enables models to generalize to diverse data with unlabeled test samples, holds significant value in real-world scenarios. Recently, researchers have applied this setting to advanced pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs), developing approaches such as test-time prompt tuning to further extend their practical applicability. However, these methods typically focus solely on adapting VLMs from a single modality and fail to accumulate task-specific knowledge as more samples are processed. To address this, we introduce Dual Prototype Evolving (DPE), a novel test-time adaptation approach for VLMs that effectively accumulates task-specific knowledge from multi-modalities. Specifically, we create and evolve two sets of prototypes—textual and visual—to progressively capture more accurate multi-modal representations for target classes during test time. Moreover, to promote consistent multi-modal representations, we introduce and optimize learnable residuals for each test sample to align the prototypes from both modalities. Extensive experimental results on 15 benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed DPE consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods while also exhibiting competitive computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation lets a pretrained model adjust to incoming data without needing labels for those examples. For vision-language models, existing approaches often adapt only one modality and do not retain task knowledge as more examples arrive. Dual Prototype Evolving addresses both issues by maintaining class representations in text and image form.

The method creates two sets of prototypes, which serve as representative descriptions of the target classes. Both sets evolve during testing, allowing information from successive samples to improve the representations. It also learns residual adjustments for each test sample to bring the textual and visual prototypes into closer alignment.

This design combines accumulated task information with coordination between the two modalities. Across 15 benchmark datasets, the authors report consistent improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods while retaining competitive computational efficiency. The findings support adapting both sides of a vision-language model and carrying useful information forward through the test sequence, rather than treating adaptation solely as an isolated adjustment to each incoming example.
summary.tldr: DPE adapts vision-language models using evolving text and image class prototypes that accumulate knowledge from unlabeled test samples.

title: Dual Prototype Evolving for Test-Time Generalization of Vision-Language Models

abstract: *Do we fully leverage the potential of visual encoder in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs)?* The recent outstanding performance of MLLMs in multimodal understanding has garnered broad attention from both academia and industry. In the current MLLM rat race, the focus seems to be predominantly on the linguistic side. We witness the rise of larger and higher-quality instruction datasets, as well as the involvement of larger-sized LLMs. Yet, scant attention has been directed towards the visual signals utilized by MLLMs, often assumed to be the final high-level features extracted by a frozen visual encoder. In this paper, we introduce the **Dense Connector** - a simple, effective, and plug-and-play vision-language connector that significantly enhances existing MLLMs by leveraging multi-layer visual features, with minimal additional computational overhead. Building on this, we also propose the Efficient Dense Connector, which achieves performance comparable to LLaVA-v1.5 with only 25% of the visual tokens. Furthermore, our model, trained solely on images, showcases remarkable zero-shot capabilities in video understanding as well. Experimental results across various vision encoders, image resolutions, training dataset scales, varying sizes of LLMs (2.7B→70B), and diverse architectures of MLLMs (e.g., LLaVA-v1.5, LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini) validate the versatility and scalability of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 19 image and video benchmarks. We hope that this work will provide valuable experience and serve as a basic module for future MLLM development. Code is available at https://github.com/HJYao00/DenseConnector.

paragraphs: Dense Connector focuses on the visual information supplied to multimodal language models. Many systems use only the final high-level features from a frozen image encoder. The paper asks whether connecting additional encoder layers to the language model can improve understanding without requiring a large increase in computation.

The proposed connector draws on visual features from multiple layers and is designed to fit into existing multimodal architectures. An additional Efficient Dense Connector variant reduces the visual token budget: it achieves performance comparable to LLaVA-v1.5 while using only 25% of its visual tokens. This makes the connection between visual encoding and language processing an explicit target for efficiency improvements.

The authors evaluate the approach across visual encoders, image resolutions, dataset scales, and language models ranging from 2.7 billion to 70 billion parameters. They report state-of-the-art results across 19 image and video benchmarks. The model also demonstrates zero-shot video understanding despite training only on images, providing evidence that the richer visual connection can support capabilities beyond the training modality's static-image setting.
summary.tldr: Dense Connector improves multimodal understanding by supplying language models with visual features from multiple encoder layers.

title: Dense Connector for MLLMs

abstract: When decisions are made at high frequency, traditional reinforcement learning (RL) methods struggle to accurately estimate action values. In turn, their performance is inconsistent and often poor. Whether the performance of distributional RL (DRL) agents suffers similarly, however, is unknown. In this work, we establish that DRL agents *are* sensitive to the decision frequency. We prove that action-conditioned return distributions collapse to their underlying policy's return distribution as the decision frequency increases. We quantify the rate of collapse of these return distributions and exhibit that their statistics collapse at different rates. Moreover, we define distributional perspectives on action gaps and advantages. In particular, we introduce the *superiority* as a probabilistic generalization of the advantage---the core object of approaches to mitigating performance issues in high-frequency value-based RL. In addition, we build a superiority-based DRL algorithm. Through simulations in an option-trading domain, we validate that proper modeling of the superiority distribution produces improved controllers at high decision frequencies.

paragraphs: Making decisions more frequently can make it harder for a reinforcement learning agent to distinguish good actions from bad ones. This paper investigates that problem for distributional reinforcement learning, which represents possible returns as distributions. The authors establish that this richer representation still suffers from sensitivity to decision frequency.

Their theoretical result shows that, as decision frequency increases, the return distribution associated with each action approaches the return distribution of the underlying policy. Action-specific differences therefore shrink. The paper quantifies this collapse and shows that different statistics of the distributions disappear at different rates, making the choice of what to model consequential.

The authors then develop distributional versions of action gaps and advantages, introducing a quantity called superiority that generalizes advantage probabilistically. They build an algorithm around it and evaluate it in option-trading simulations. Those experiments show that properly modeling the superiority distribution improves controllers at high decision frequencies, connecting the theoretical diagnosis to a concrete learning approach.
summary.tldr: The paper explains why distributional reinforcement learning struggles at high decision frequencies and introduces a superiority-based algorithm that improves simulated controllers.

title: Action Gaps and Advantages in Continuous-Time Distributional Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Aligning language models (LMs) to human preferences has emerged as a critical pursuit, enabling these models to better serve diverse user needs. Existing methods primarily focus on optimizing LMs for a single reward function, limiting their adaptability to varied objectives. Here, we propose $\textbf{multi-objective decoding~(MOD)}$, a decoding-time algorithm that outputs the next token from a linear combination of predictions of all base models, for any given weighting over different objectives.We exploit a common form among a family of $f$-divergence regularized alignment approaches (such as PPO, DPO, and their variants) to identify a closed-form solution by Legendre transform, and derive an efficient decoding strategy.Theoretically, we show why existing approaches can be sub-optimal even in natural settings and obtain optimality guarantees for our method.Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the algorithm. For example, compared to a parameter-merging baseline, MOD achieves 12.8\% overall reward improvement when equally optimizing towards $3$ objectives. Moreover, we experiment with MOD on combining three fully-finetuned LMs of different model sizes, each aimed at different objectives such as safety, coding, and general user preference. Unlike traditional methods that require careful curation of a mixture of datasets to achieve comprehensive improvement, we can quickly experiment with preference weightings using MOD to find the best combination of models. Our best combination reduces toxicity on Toxigen to nearly 0\% and achieves 7.9--33.3\% improvement across three other metrics ($\textit{i.e.}$, Codex@1, GSM-COT, BBH-COT).
