paragraphs: Sign-language models need features that capture relationships relevant to signing, beyond visual contours and textures. Graph-based approaches can connect regions within a frame and across time, but the paper highlights a tradeoff: strengthening those cross-region relationships may weaken the representations of individual regions. MixSignGraph is designed to preserve useful local detail alongside those broader connections.

The model combines local and temporal sign graphs with a hierarchical sign graph. After cross-region features are extracted, the hierarchical component gathers features for the same region from frame representations at different levels of granularity. This strengthens discriminative local information. For gloss-free tasks, the authors also introduce text-based CTC pretraining, generating pseudo gloss labels from text sequences to provide pretraining supervision.

Experiments span five sign-language datasets and multiple tasks. The authors report that MixSignGraph exceeds most current models across several datasets without additional cues. The results support combining cross-region modeling with explicit restoration of local representations, while the text-derived pretraining offers an additional route to improving gloss-free performance.
summary.tldr: MixSignGraph combines spatial, temporal, and hierarchical graphs to strengthen sign-language features, with text-derived pretraining for gloss-free tasks.

title: MixSignGraph: A Sign Sequence is Worth Mixed Graphs of Nodes

abstract: We study the problem of designing procurement auctions for the strategic uncapacitated facility location problem: a company needs to procure a set of facility locations in order to serve its customers and each facility location is owned by a strategic agent. Each owner has a private cost for providing access to their facility (e.g., renting it or selling it to the company) and needs to be compensated accordingly. The goal is to design truthful auctions that decide which facilities the company should procure and how much to pay the corresponding owners, aiming to minimize the total cost, i.e., the monetary cost paid to the owners and the connection cost suffered by the customers (their distance to the nearest facility). We evaluate the performance of these auctions using the \emph{frugality ratio}. We first analyze the performance of the classic VCG auction in this context and prove that its frugality ratio is exactly $3$. We then leverage the learning-augmented framework and design auctions that are augmented with predictions regarding the owners' private costs. Specifically, we propose a family of learning-augmented auctions that achieve significant payment reductions when the predictions are accurate, leading to much better frugality ratios. At the same time, we demonstrate that these auctions remain robust even if the predictions are arbitrarily inaccurate, and maintain reasonable frugality ratios even under adversarially chosen predictions. We finally provide a family of ``error-tolerant'' auctions that maintain improved frugality ratios even if the predictions are only approximately accurate, and we provide upper bounds on their frugality ratio as a function of the prediction error.

The result balances three requirements: incentives for honest cost reporting, benefit from useful predictions, and protection against misleading predictions. Prediction quality improves the economic outcome without being assumed perfect for the mechanism’s basic robustness.
summary.tldr: Predictions of facility-owner costs can reduce truthful-auction payments while retaining worst-case safeguards.

title: Procurement Auctions with Predictions: Improved Frugality for Facility Location

abstract: Calibrating blackbox machine learning models to achieve risk control is crucial to ensure reliable decision-making. A rich line of literature has been studying how to calibrate a model so that its predictions satisfy explicit finite-sample statistical guarantees under a _fixed_, _static_, and unknown data-generating distribution. However, prediction-supported decisions may influence the outcome they aim to predict, a phenomenon named _performativity_ of predictions, which is commonly seen in social science and economics. In this paper, we introduce _Performative Risk Control_, a framework to calibrate models to achieve risk control under performativity with provable theoretical guarantees. Specifically, we provide an iteratively refined calibration process, where we ensure the predictions are improved and risk-controlled throughout the process. We also study different types of risk measures and choices of tail bounds. Lastly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework by numerical experiments on the task of predicting credit default risk. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first one to study statistically rigorous risk control under performativity, which will serve as an important safeguard against a wide range of strategic manipulation in decision-making processes.

To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first one to study statistically rigorous risk control under performativity, which will serve as an important safeguard against a wide range of strategic manipulation in decision-making processes.

This feedback, called performativity, challenges calibration methods that assume a fixed data-generating distribution. The paper introduces Performative Risk Control to provide statistically grounded calibration in settings where deployment itself influences outcomes.

The framework uses an iteratively refined calibration process. The authors establish theoretical guarantees that predictions improve while remaining risk-controlled throughout that process. They also investigate different risk measures and tail bounds, examining how the statistical choices used to express and bound risk fit into the performative setting.

Numerical experiments on credit-default prediction demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness. The main contribution is to bring explicit risk control into a feedback-sensitive deployment setting, extending the usual focus on static distributions. The authors also position the framework as a safeguard against strategic manipulation in decision-making. That motivation follows from treating responses to model-driven decisions as part of calibration, rather than assuming deployment leaves the environment unchanged.
summary.tldr: Performative Risk Control iteratively calibrates models with theoretical risk guarantees when prediction-supported decisions influence subsequent outcomes.

title: Performative Risk Control: Calibrating Models for Reliable Deployment under Performativity

abstract: Humans rely on multisensory integration to perceive spatial environments, where auditory cues enable sound source localization in three-dimensional space. Despite the critical role of spatial audio in immersive technologies such as VR/AR, most existing multimodal datasets provide only monaural audio, which limits the development of spatial audio generation and understanding. To address these challenges, we introduce MRSAudio, a large-scale multimodal spatial audio dataset designed to advance research in spatial audio understanding and generation. MRSAudio spans four distinct components: MRSLife, MRSSpeech, MRSMusic, and MRSSing, covering diverse real-world scenarios. The dataset includes synchronized binaural and ambisonic audio, exocentric and egocentric video, motion trajectories, and fine-grained annotations such as transcripts, phoneme boundaries, lyrics, scores, and prompts.To demonstrate the utility and versatility of MRSAudio, we establish five foundational tasks: audio spatialization, and spatial text to speech, spatial singing voice synthesis, spatial music generation and sound event localization and detection. Results show that MRSAudio enables high-quality spatial modeling and supports a broad range of spatial audio research.Demos and dataset access are available at https://mrsaudio.github.io.

paragraphs: Understanding a sound includes understanding where it comes from. Yet many multimodal datasets provide only single-channel audio, limiting research on spatial sound understanding and generation. MRSAudio addresses this gap with recorded spatial audio linked to visual information, motion, and detailed annotations across a range of real-world scenarios.

It synchronizes binaural and ambisonic audio with both external-view and first-person video, as well as motion trajectories. Its fine-grained annotations include transcripts, phoneme boundaries, lyrics, musical scores, and prompts. This combination connects sound content with spatial and visual context.

Their results show that the dataset supports high-quality spatial modeling across these uses. The contribution is a coordinated resource for studying both where sounds occur and how to generate spatial audio, extending the research possibilities beyond those offered by monaural recordings.
summary.tldr: MRSAudio combines spatial recordings, synchronized video, motion trajectories, and detailed annotations to support spatial audio understanding and generation.

title: MRSAudio: A Large-Scale Multimodal Recorded Spatial Audio Dataset with Refined Annotations

abstract: Automated model discovery is the process of automatically searching and identifying the most appropriate model for a given dataset over a large combinatorial search space. Existing approaches, however, often face challenges in balancing the capture of fine-grained details with ensuring generalizability beyond training data regimes with a reasonable model complexity. In this paper, we present a multi-modal \& multi-step pipeline for effective automated model discovery. Our approach leverages two vision-language-based modules (VLM), AnalyzerVLM and EvaluatorVLM, for effective model proposal and evaluation in an agentic way. AnalyzerVLM autonomously plans and executes multi-step analyses to propose effective candidate models. EvaluatorVLM assesses the candidate models both quantitatively and perceptually, regarding the fitness for local details and the generalibility for overall trends. Our results demonstrate that our pipeline effectively discovers models that capture fine details and ensure strong generalizability. Additionally, extensive ablation studies show that both multi-modality and multi-step reasoning play crucial roles in discovering favorable models.

paragraphs: Automated model discovery searches a large space of possible models for one that explains a dataset well. The challenge is to capture small but meaningful details while also representing broader trends that extend beyond the training data. A model can fit observations closely without achieving this balance, particularly when complexity becomes excessive.

The paper proposes a pipeline with two vision-language modules that divide the work of proposing and assessing models. AnalyzerVLM plans and carries out several analysis steps before suggesting candidates. EvaluatorVLM then examines those candidates using both quantitative evidence and perceptual assessment. Its evaluation considers how well a model captures local details alongside how well it represents overall trends.

The reported results show that the pipeline discovers models combining detailed fit with strong generalization. Ablation studies also support the importance of both multimodal input and reasoning across multiple steps. The contribution is a coordinated discovery process: candidate generation and evaluation each explicitly address the tension between explaining observed detail and finding a model that remains useful beyond it.
summary.tldr: A two-module vision-language pipeline discovers models by combining multistep analysis with quantitative and perceptual evaluation.

title: Automated Model Discovery via Multi-modal & Multi-step Pipeline

abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) to aggregate multiple preferences has attracted considerable research attention. With aggregation algorithms advancing, a potential economic scenario arises where fine-tuning services are provided to agents with different preferences. In this context, agents may benefit from strategically misreporting their preferences, but this could harm the aggregation performance. This paper addresses such incentive issues by framing it as a mechanism design problem: an LLM provider determines the fine-tuning objective (training rule) and the pricing scheme (payment rule) for agents. We primarily focus on training rules that maximize social welfare subject to certain regularizations, referred to as SW-Max rules. First, we show that under most circumstances, truthful reporting is sub-optimal with simply a SW-Max rule, thereby highlighting the necessity of payments. Second, we extend the VCG payment to implement SW-Max rules in dominant-strategy incentive compatibility (DSIC). We characterize sufficient conditions for payment equivalence and derive the necessary conditions for a payment rule to implement a SW-Max rule in DSIC and other principles. Third, we demonstrate that our mechanism is approximately DSIC with perturbed input, showcasing its robustness against the inevitable errors in real-world applications. Experiments on real LLM training results further confirm the practical implications of our results.

paragraphs: When several customers contribute preferences to a shared language-model fine-tuning service, they may benefit from misrepresenting what they want. That strategic behavior can undermine preference aggregation. This paper treats the service as a mechanism design problem in which the provider chooses both a training objective and a payment rule.

The analysis focuses on training rules that maximize social welfare subject to regularization. The authors show that, under most circumstances, such a rule alone does not make truthful reporting optimal. They extend VCG payments so that truthful reporting becomes a dominant strategy: an agent benefits from honesty regardless of how others report their preferences.

The paper also establishes sufficient conditions for payment equivalence and necessary conditions for payment rules to implement the desired training rules under incentive and other principles. With perturbed inputs, the mechanism is approximately dominant-strategy incentive compatible, addressing errors that can arise in practice. Experiments using real language-model training results support the practical implications of coupling preference aggregation with carefully designed payments.
summary.tldr: Payment mechanisms can make honest preference reporting a dominant strategy for customers sharing an LLM fine-tuning service.

title: Mechanism Design for LLM Fine-tuning with Multiple Reward Models

abstract: Generating realistic time series data is critical for applications in healthcare, finance, and climate science. However, irregular sampling and missing values present significant challenges. While prior methods address these irregularities, they often yield suboptimal results and incur high computational costs. Recent advances in regular time series generation, such as the diffusion-based ImagenTime model, demonstrate strong, fast, and scalable generative capabilities by transforming time series into image representations, making them a promising solution. However, extending ImagenTime to irregular sequences using simple masking introduces ``unnatural'' neighborhoods, where missing values replaced by zeros disrupt the learning process. To overcome this, we propose a novel two-step framework: first, a Time Series Transformer completes irregular sequences, creating natural neighborhoods; second, a vision-based diffusion model with masking minimizes dependence on the completed values. This hybrid approach leverages the strengths of both completion and masking, enabling robust and efficient generation of realistic time series. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across benchmarks, delivering a relative improvement in discriminative score by 70% and in computational cost by 85%.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the problem of generating regularly sampled time series from data with missing values or irregular observations. Its starting point is an image-based approach to time series generation: represent sequences as images, then use a diffusion model. Simply filling missing entries with zeros creates artificial local patterns, disrupting the neighborhoods that the image model learns from.

The proposed framework separates this problem into two stages. A Time Series Transformer first completes the irregular sequences, giving the image representation more natural neighborhoods. A vision-based diffusion model then learns with masking that reduces its dependence on those completed values. Completion supplies a coherent local structure, while masking keeps the generated replacements from carrying too much influence.

The authors report state-of-the-art benchmark performance, including a 70% relative improvement in discriminative score and an 85% improvement in computational cost. The contribution is the combination of completion and masking: each addresses a different difficulty in adapting image-based generation to incomplete time series.
summary.tldr: Completing irregular sequences before masked diffusion improves the reported quality and computational efficiency of time series generation.

title: A Diffusion Model for Regular Time Series Generation from Irregular Data with Completion and Masking

abstract: Discovering the latent structure from many observed variables is an important yet challenging learning task. Existing approaches for discovering latent structures often require the unknown number of hidden states as an input. In this paper, we propose a quartet based approach which is agnostic to this number. The key contribution is a novel rank characterization of the tensor associated with the marginal distribution of a quartet. This characterization allows us to design a nuclear norm based test for resolving quartet relations. We then use the quartet test as a subroutine in a divide-and-conquer algorithm for recovering the latent tree structure. Under mild conditions, the algorithm is consistent and its error probability decays exponentially with increasing sample size. We demonstrate that the proposed approach compares favorably to alternatives. In a real world stock dataset, it also discovers meaningful groupings of variables, and produces a model that fits the data better.

paragraphs: Learning a latent tree means discovering how observed variables are connected through hidden ones. Many existing approaches require the number of hidden states to be supplied beforehand, even though that number is itself unknown. This paper develops a structure-learning method that does not need that input, using relationships among groups of four observed variables.

For each quartet, the authors study the tensor representing its marginal probability distribution. A new characterization of tensor rank supports a nuclear-norm-based test for deciding the quartet’s relationship within the tree. This local test becomes a subroutine in a divide-and-conquer algorithm that reconstructs the larger latent structure.

Under mild conditions, the algorithm is consistent, and its error probability decreases exponentially as the sample size grows. The paper also reports favorable comparisons with alternatives. On a real stock dataset, it discovers meaningful variable groupings and yields a better-fitting model. The contribution connects a local algebraic test to global structure recovery, with conditional theoretical guarantees and empirical evidence for its usefulness.
summary.tldr: Quartet tensor tests recover latent-tree structure without requiring the number of hidden states in advance.

title: Unfolding Latent Tree Structures using 4th Order Tensors

abstract: We consider nonparametric estimation of L_2, Renyi-αand Tsallis-αdivergences between continuous distributions. Our approach is to construct estimators for particular integral functionals of two densities and translate them into divergence estimators. For the integral functionals, our estimators are based on corrections of a preliminary plug-in estimator. We show that these estimators achieve the parametric convergence rate of n^-1/2 when the densities’ smoothness, s, are both at least d/4 where d is the dimension. We also derive minimax lower bounds for this problem which confirm that s > d/4 is necessary to achieve the n^-1/2 rate of convergence. We validate our theoretical guarantees with a number of simulations.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate differences between continuous probability distributions without selecting a parametric family for them. It considers L2, Renyi-alpha, and Tsallis-alpha divergences. The common strategy is to estimate particular integrals involving two densities and then translate those estimates into the desired divergence quantities.

The estimators start with a preliminary plug-in estimate and apply corrections. The authors prove a convergence rate of n^(-1/2), the parametric rate, when both densities have smoothness at least d/4, where d is the dimension. This connects estimation accuracy to the relationship between the smoothness of the distributions and the dimension of their space.

The paper also derives minimax lower bounds, described in the abstract as requiring smoothness strictly greater than d/4 for that rate. The upper and lower statements thus use different wording at the boundary, while both identify the quarter-dimension threshold as central. Simulations validate the theoretical guarantees and complement the analysis of achievable estimation accuracy.
summary.tldr: Corrected plug-in estimators achieve fast divergence estimation under smoothness conditions, with minimax bounds linking attainable rates to dimension.

title: Nonparametric Estimation of Renyi Divergence and Friends

abstract: We study the problem of aggregating the contributions of multiple contributors in a crowdsourcing setting. The data involved is in a form not typically considered in most crowdsourcing tasks, in that the data is structured and has a temporal dimension. In particular, we study the visual tracking problem in which the unknown data to be estimated is in the form of a sequence of bounding boxes representing the trajectory of the target object being tracked. We propose a factorial hidden Markov model (FHMM) for ensemble-based tracking by learning jointly the unknown trajectory of the target and the reliability of each tracker in the ensemble. For efficient online inference of the FHMM, we devise a conditional particle filter algorithm by exploiting the structure of the joint posterior distribution of the hidden variables. Using the largest open benchmark for visual tracking, we empirically compare two ensemble methods constructed from five state-of-the-art trackers with the individual trackers. The promising experimental results provide empirical evidence for our ensemble approach to "get the best of all worlds".

paragraphs: Combining multiple contributors becomes more complicated when their outputs are structured sequences rather than separate labels. This paper studies that problem through visual tracking. Each contributor supplies a sequence of bounding boxes, and the desired output is the unknown trajectory of the target object across time.

The authors propose a factorial hidden Markov model that jointly learns the target trajectory and the reliability of each tracker. Estimating these quantities together lets the aggregation account for differences among contributors while modeling the evolving target. For efficient online inference, the method uses a conditional particle filter designed around the structure of the joint posterior distribution of hidden variables.

The evaluation compares two ensemble methods built from five state-of-the-art trackers with the individual trackers on a large open visual tracking benchmark. The reported results provide encouraging empirical support for combining their strengths. The broader contribution is an aggregation method that treats contributor reliability and temporal structure as connected parts of the same estimation problem.
summary.tldr: A factorial hidden Markov model combines tracking sequences by jointly estimating the target trajectory and each tracker’s reliability.

title: Ensemble-Based Tracking: Aggregating Crowdsourced Structured Time Series Data

abstract: We frame max-margin learning of latent variable structured prediction models as a convex optimization problem, making use of scoring functions computed by input-output observable operator models. This learning problem can be expressed as an optimization involving a low-rank Hankel matrix that represents the input-output operator model. The direct outcome of our work is a new spectral regularization method for max-margin structured prediction. Our experiments confirm that our proposed regularization framework leads to an effective way of controlling the capacity of structured prediction models.

This learning problem can be expressed as an optimization involving a low-rank Hankel matrix that represents the input-output operator model. Our experiments confirm that our proposed regularization framework leads to an effective way of controlling the capacity of structured prediction models.

paragraphs: Sequence tagging requires predicting related outputs across a sequence, and latent-variable structured models can represent hidden relationships involved in those predictions. This paper develops a convex optimization formulation for training such models with a max-margin objective. The formulation makes the representation used to score input-output relationships central to the learning problem.

The scores come from input-output observable operator models. The authors express learning through an optimization problem involving a low-rank Hankel matrix that represents the operator model. This matrix view creates a direct connection between the structured predictor and a representation whose rank is part of the formulation.

The resulting contribution is a spectral regularization method for max-margin structured prediction. Its purpose is to control model capacity: how much complexity the predictor can express during learning. Experiments confirm that the proposed regularization framework provides an effective way to exercise that control. The paper therefore links a convex training formulation, an operator-based scoring model, and matrix-based regularization within one approach.
summary.tldr: A convex operator-model formulation yields spectral regularization that effectively controls capacity in max-margin structured prediction.

title: Spectral Regularization for Max-Margin Sequence Tagging

abstract: We present a new model for prediction markets, in which we use risk measures to model agents and introduce a market maker to describe the trading process. This specific choice of modelling approach enables us to show that the whole market approaches a global objective, despite the fact that the market is designed such that each agent only cares about its own goal. In addition, the market dynamic provides a sensible algorithm for optimising the global objective. An intimate connection between machine learning and our markets is thus established, such that we could 1) analyse a market by applying machine learning methods to the global objective; and 2) solve machine learning problems by setting up and running certain markets.

In addition, the market dynamic provides a sensible algorithm for optimising the global objective. paragraphs: This paper constructs a prediction-market model in which individually motivated trading has a shared mathematical interpretation. Agents are modeled using risk measures, and a market maker specifies the trading process. These modeling choices let the authors connect the behavior of the whole market to a global objective, even though each agent pursues its own goal.

The authors show that the market approaches this global objective and that its trading dynamics provide a sensible algorithm for optimizing it. The important connection is between local decisions and collective optimization: a sequence of trades can be studied as the operation of an optimization procedure. The result concerns the proposed model and its particular formulation of agents and trading.

This connection opens two directions of use. Machine learning methods can help analyze a market through its global objective. Conversely, certain machine learning problems can be approached by constructing and running a corresponding market. The paper therefore supplies a framework for translating between market dynamics and optimization, rather than assuming that arbitrary markets automatically solve arbitrary learning problems.
summary.tldr: A risk-based prediction-market model connects self-interested trading to optimization of a global objective and certain machine learning problems.

title: Multi-period Trading Prediction Markets with Connections to Machine Learning

abstract: A new framework for topic modeling is developed, based on deep graphical models, where interactions between topics are inferred through deep latent binary hierarchies. The proposed multi-layer model employs a deep sigmoid belief network or restricted Boltzmann machine, the bottom binary layer of which selects topics for use in a Poisson factor analysis model. Under this setting, topics live on the bottom layer of the model, while the deep specification serves as a flexible prior for revealing topic structure. Scalable inference algorithms are derived by applying Bayesian conditional density filtering algorithm, in addition to extending recently proposed work on stochastic gradient thermostats. Experimental results on several corpora show that the proposed approach readily handles very large collections of text documents, infers structured topic representations, and obtains superior test perplexities when compared with related models.

paragraphs: This paper builds a topic model that uses a deep hierarchy to represent interactions among topics. Its foundation is Poisson factor analysis, with topics selected by binary variables in the bottom layer of a deeper graphical model. The hierarchy supplies a flexible prior that helps reveal structure in topic usage.

The deep component can be a sigmoid belief network or a restricted Boltzmann machine. Topics remain at the bottom of the overall model; the layers above them describe latent binary structure influencing their selection. This separates the topics themselves from the deeper mechanism that captures relationships among them.

To make learning scalable, the authors derive inference algorithms using Bayesian conditional density filtering and extensions of stochastic gradient thermostats. Experiments across several text corpora show that the approach handles very large document collections and learns structured topic representations. It also obtains better test perplexities than related models in those evaluations, supporting the usefulness of the deep prior for modeling unseen text.
summary.tldr: Deep binary hierarchies guide topic selection in scalable Poisson factor analysis, improving reported test perplexity on several corpora.

title: Scalable Deep Poisson Factor Analysis for Topic Modeling

abstract: We study the K-armed dueling bandit problem, a variation of the standard stochastic bandit problem where the feedback is limited to relative comparisons of a pair of arms. The hardness of recommending Copeland winners, the arms that beat the greatest number of other arms, is characterized by deriving an asymptotic regret bound. We propose Copeland Winners Deterministic Minimum Empirical Divergence (CW-RMED), an algorithm inspired by the DMED algorithm (Honda and Takemura, 2010), and derive an asymptotically optimal regret bound for it. However, it is not known whether the algorithm can be efficiently computed or not. To address this issue, we devise an efficient version (ECW-RMED) and derive its asymptotic regret bound. Experimental comparisons of dueling bandit algorithms show that ECW-RMED significantly outperforms existing ones.

paragraphs: The paper considers learning from comparisons between pairs of options rather than observing a separate reward for each option. Its target is a Copeland winner: an option that beats the greatest number of other options. This defines success through the pattern of pairwise wins, making the problem one of discovering which comparisons matter for identifying strong candidates.

The authors characterize the difficulty through an asymptotic regret lower bound and introduce CW-RMED, an algorithm with an asymptotically optimal regret guarantee. Here, asymptotic optimality concerns behavior as learning continues. It does not settle the practical cost of choosing the algorithm’s next comparison, and the abstract explicitly leaves its efficient computability unresolved.

To address that issue, the paper develops ECW-RMED, a computationally efficient version, and derives an asymptotic regret bound for it. Experiments show that this version significantly outperforms existing dueling bandit algorithms in the reported comparisons. The contribution separates the best achievable learning performance from the computational challenge of implementing a strategy that pursues it.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes asymptotic limits for Copeland dueling bandits and develops both an optimal algorithm and an efficient variant.

title: Copeland Dueling Bandit Problem: Regret Lower Bound, Optimal Algorithm, and Computationally Efficient Algorithm

abstract: Hypothesis testing is a useful statistical tool in determining whether a given model should be rejected based on a sample from the population. Sample data may contain sensitive information about individuals, such as medical information. Thus it is important to design statistical tests that guarantee the privacy of subjects in the data. In this work, we study hypothesis testing subject to differential privacy, specifically chi-squared tests for goodness of fit for multinomial data and independence between two categorical variables.
originalAbstract: Hypothesis testing is a useful statistical tool in determining whether a given model should be rejected based on a sample from the population. Sample data may contain sensitive information about individuals, such as medical information. Thus it is important to design statistical tests that guarantee the privacy of subjects in the data. In this work, we study hypothesis testing subject to differential privacy, specifically chi-squared tests for goodness of fit for multinomial data and independence between two categorical variables.

paragraphs: The paper studies statistical hypothesis testing when the sample contains sensitive information about individuals. A hypothesis test uses observations to decide whether a proposed model should be rejected. The authors place this task under differential privacy, making protection of the people represented in the sample part of the statistical problem.

The first focus is chi-squared goodness-of-fit testing for multinomial data. Here, the observations belong to categories, and the question concerns whether their observed distribution is compatible with a proposed model. The second focus is testing independence between two categorical variables. This asks whether their observed relationship provides grounds to reject an independence assumption.

These two settings concern different statistical judgments, but both require drawing conclusions from data that may include private individual records. The paper’s contribution, as described in the abstract, is its study of these chi-squared testing problems subject to differential privacy. Its motivation is to make privacy guarantees part of hypothesis testing, including applications where the underlying observations contain sensitive medical information.
summary.tldr: The paper studies differentially private chi-squared tests for categorical goodness of fit and independence.

title: Differentially Private Chi-Squared Hypothesis Testing: Goodness of Fit and Independence Testing

abstract: We propose a simple yet effective technique for neural network learning. The forward propagation is computed as usual. In back propagation, only a small subset of the full gradient is computed to update the model parameters. The gradient vectors are sparsified in such a way that only the top-$k$ elements (in terms of magnitude) are kept. As a result, only $k$ rows or columns (depending on the layout) of the weight matrix are modified, leading to a linear reduction ($k$ divided by the vector dimension) in the computational cost. Surprisingly, experimental results demonstrate that we can update only 1–4\% of the weights at each back propagation pass. This does not result in a larger number of training iterations. More interestingly, the accuracy of the resulting models is actually improved rather than degraded, and a detailed analysis is given.

paragraphs: The paper proposes meProp, a neural-network training technique that keeps the usual forward computation but makes backpropagation sparse. During the backward pass, it uses only a small subset of the full gradient to update parameters. The selection rule keeps the k gradient-vector entries with the largest magnitudes.

This sparsity means that only k rows or columns of a weight matrix are modified, depending on how the matrix is arranged. The stated computational reduction scales with k divided by the gradient-vector dimension. The method therefore connects a simple rule for retaining gradient entries to a direct reduction in the corresponding backward computation.

In the reported experiments, updating only 1–4% of the weights per backward pass did not require more training iterations. The resulting models also achieved improved accuracy rather than an accuracy loss. These are empirical findings about the evaluated training settings. They show that aggressively reducing the information used in each update can save computation while still supporting effective learning, and in these experiments also improved the final predictions.
summary.tldr: meProp retains only large-magnitude gradient entries during backpropagation, reducing computation and improving accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: meProp: Sparsified Back Propagation for Accelerated Deep Learning with Reduced Overfitting

abstract: This paper investigates recently proposed approaches for defending against adversarial examples and evaluating adversarial robustness. We motivate adversarial risk as an objective for achieving models robust to worst-case inputs. We then frame commonly used attacks and evaluation metrics as defining a tractable surrogate objective to the true adversarial risk. This suggests that models may optimize this surrogate rather than the true adversarial risk. We formalize this notion as obscurity to an adversary , and develop tools and heuristics for identifying obscured models and designing transparent models. We demonstrate that this is a significant problem in practice by repurposing gradient-free optimization techniques into adversarial attacks, which we use to decrease the accuracy of several recently proposed defenses to near zero. Our hope is that our formulations and results will help researchers to develop more powerful defenses.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether defenses against adversarial examples are being evaluated against attacks strong enough to reveal their weaknesses. It uses adversarial risk to express the goal of performing well on worst-case inputs. Common attacks and evaluation measures provide a computationally manageable substitute for this objective, but that substitute can leave vulnerabilities undiscovered.

The authors formalize this mismatch as obscurity to an adversary. A model may perform well against the evaluation procedure because that procedure struggles to find damaging inputs. The paper develops tools and heuristics for recognizing such models and for designing models whose vulnerabilities are more accessible to evaluation.

To demonstrate the practical consequences, the authors adapt gradient-free optimization methods into attacks. These attacks reduce the accuracy of several proposed defenses to nearly zero. The findings show that success against the tested attack can give a misleading picture of robustness, and motivate evaluations that more faithfully probe the underlying worst-case objective.
summary.tldr: Defenses can appear robust because evaluations miss their vulnerabilities, as stronger gradient-free attacks demonstrate.

title: Adversarial Risk and the Dangers of Evaluating Against Weak Attacks

abstract: Variable selection is a classic problem in machine learning (ML), widely used to find important explanatory factors, and improve generalization performance and interpretability of ML models. In this paper, we consider variable selection for models where multiple responses are to be predicted based on the same set of covariates. Since each response is relevant to a unique subset of covariates, we desire the selected variables for different responses have small overlap. We propose a regularizer that simultaneously encourage orthogonality and sparsity, which jointly brings in an effect of reducing overlap. We apply this regularizer to four model instances and develop efficient algorithms to solve the regularized problems. We provide a formal analysis on why the proposed regularizer can reduce generalization error. Experiments on both simulation studies and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed regularizer in selecting less-overlapped variables and improving generalization performance.

paragraphs: The paper studies variable selection when several responses are predicted from the same pool of input variables. Its motivating setting is one where each response is relevant to its own subset of covariates. The authors therefore seek selections with little overlap across responses, aiming to identify distinct explanatory factors while improving generalization and interpretability.

They propose a regularizer that encourages sparsity and orthogonality together. Sparsity favors using fewer variables, while the combined regularization creates pressure for different responses to rely on less-overlapping selections. The goal is reduced overlap rather than a stated requirement that every response use an entirely disjoint set of inputs.

The regularizer is applied to four model instances, with efficient algorithms developed for the resulting optimization problems. A formal analysis explains why the proposed penalty can reduce generalization error. Simulation studies and real-world experiments show effective selection of less-overlapping variables and improved generalization. The findings support incorporating the desired relationship between response-specific selections directly into the learning objective.
summary.tldr: A regularizer combining sparsity and orthogonality selects less-overlapping predictors for multiple responses and improves generalization in experiments.

title: Nonoverlap-Promoting Variable Selection

abstract: We investigate quantum algorithms for classification, a fundamental problem in machine learning, with provable guarantees. Given $n$ $d$-dimensional data points, the state-of-the-art (and optimal) classical algorithm for training classifiers with constant margin by Clarkson et al. runs in $\tilde{O}(n +d)$, which is also optimal in its input/output model. We design sublinear quantum algorithms for the same task running in $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n} +\sqrt{d})$, a quadratic improvement in both $n$ and $d$. Moreover, our algorithms use the standard quantization of the classical input and generate the same classical output, suggesting minimal overheads when used as subroutines for end-to-end applications. We also demonstrate a tight lower bound (up to poly-log factors) and discuss the possibility of implementation on near-term quantum machines.

paragraphs: This paper develops quantum algorithms for training linear and kernel-based classifiers with provable guarantees. For n data points with d dimensions and a constant-margin requirement, the cited optimal classical approach takes approximately O(n + d) time, ignoring polylogarithmic factors. The quantum algorithms reduce that dependence to approximately O(sqrt(n) + sqrt(d)).

The improvement is quadratic in both the number of examples and the feature dimension. The algorithms use a standard quantum version of the classical input and produce the same classical output as the classical approach. The authors therefore suggest that they could serve as subroutines in larger applications with minimal overhead, linking the complexity result to a compatible output format.

A matching lower bound, up to polylogarithmic factors, shows that the runtime dependence is tight within the framework analyzed. The paper also discusses possible implementation on near-term quantum machines. The main established result is the algorithmic speedup and its lower bound; the hardware discussion concerns implementation possibilities.
summary.tldr: Quantum algorithms train constant-margin classifiers with square-root dependence on sample count and dimension, with a nearly matching lower bound.

title: Sublinear quantum algorithms for training linear and kernel-based classifiers

abstract: In this article we revisit the definition of Precision-Recall (PR) curves for generative models proposed by (Sajjadi et al., 2018). Rather than providing a scalar for generative quality, PR curves distinguish mode-collapse (poor recall) and bad quality (poor precision). We first generalize their formulation to arbitrary measures hence removing any restriction to finite support. We also expose a bridge between PR curves and type I and type II error (a.k.a. false detection and rejection) rates of likelihood ratio classifiers on the task of discriminating between samples of the two distributions. Building upon this new perspective, we propose a novel algorithm to approximate precision-recall curves, that shares some interesting methodological properties with the hypothesis testing technique from (Lopez-Paz & Oquab, 2017). We demonstrate the interest of the proposed formulation over the original approach on controlled multi-modal datasets.

paragraphs: A single score for a generative model can conceal different kinds of failure. Precision–recall curves separate the quality of generated samples from coverage of the target distribution. Poor precision reflects bad generated samples, while poor recall reflects missing modes. This paper revisits a formulation of those curves to broaden where it applies and how it can be estimated.

The authors generalize the definition to arbitrary probability measures, removing the restriction to distributions with finite support. They also connect the curves to the two kinds of error made by likelihood-ratio classifiers that distinguish samples from the generated and target distributions. This gives precision and recall a second interpretation through false detections and rejections in a discrimination problem.

Using that connection, they propose an algorithm for approximating precision–recall curves. The classifier perspective supplies a methodological basis for estimation, alongside the broader mathematical definition. Experiments on controlled datasets with multiple modes demonstrate the usefulness of the formulation relative to the original approach. The work thus develops both the meaning of generative precision–recall and a way to approximate it.
summary.tldr: A broader definition of generative precision–recall connects distribution quality and coverage to classification errors and yields a new approximation algorithm.

title: Revisiting precision recall definition for generative modeling

abstract: We propose a novel Bayesian nonparametric method to learn translation-invariant relationships on non-Euclidean domains. The resulting graph convolutional Gaussian processes can be applied to problems in machine learning for which the input observations are functions with domains on general graphs. The structure of these models allows for high dimensional inputs while retaining expressibility, as is the case with convolutional neural networks. We present applications of graph convolutional Gaussian processes to images and triangular meshes, demonstrating their versatility and effectiveness, comparing favorably to existing methods, despite being relatively simple models.

paragraphs: This paper introduces graph convolutional Gaussian processes for observations that are functions defined on graphs. The goal is to learn translation-invariant relationships on domains that need not have the ordinary geometry of a flat grid. This extends the modeling idea of convolution to inputs whose underlying structure is a general graph.

The proposed method is Bayesian and nonparametric. Its model structure is designed to accommodate high-dimensional inputs while retaining expressive power, a motivation shared with convolutional neural networks. The graph supplies the domain on which each observation is defined, allowing the same broad framework to address different kinds of structured input.

The authors apply the method to images and triangular meshes. These applications demonstrate versatility across the two domains, and the reported comparisons are favorable to existing methods despite the models' relative simplicity. The contribution is therefore both a model construction and evidence of its usefulness: convolutional structure can be incorporated into Gaussian processes for learning relationships on graph-based domains.
summary.tldr: Graph convolutional Gaussian processes bring expressive Bayesian modeling to high-dimensional observations defined on graphs.

title: Graph Convolutional Gaussian Processes

abstract: Recent developments on large-scale distributed machine learning applications, e.g., deep neural networks, benefit enormously from the advances in distributed non-convex optimization techniques, e.g., distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). A series of recent works study the linear speedup property of distributed SGD variants with reduced communication. The linear speedup property enables us to scale out the computing capability by adding more computing nodes into our system. The reduced communication complexity is desirable since communication overhead is often the performance bottleneck in distributed systems. Recently, momentum methods are more and more widely adopted by practitioners to train machine learning models since they can often converge faster and generalize better. However, it remains unclear whether any distributed momentum SGD possesses the same linear speedup property as distributed SGD and has reduced communication complexity. This paper fills the gap by considering a distributed communication efficient momentum SGD method and proving its linear speedup property.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization aims to make training faster by spreading computation across multiple machines. That benefit can be undermined by communication overhead, which is often a bottleneck. Previous analyses had established linear speedup for distributed SGD variants with reduced communication, leaving open whether a distributed method using momentum could enjoy the same combination of properties.

The paper studies a communication-efficient momentum SGD method for nonconvex optimization and proves its linear speedup property. This addresses the theoretical question of whether adding computing nodes can scale the method's optimization progress favorably while retaining its communication-efficient design. The focus is the analyzed method, rather than an assertion about every distributed momentum algorithm.

The result matters because momentum is widely used in practical machine learning, where it can often improve convergence and generalization. Those practical motivations make a theoretical account of distributed momentum valuable. The paper's stated contribution supplies that account for linear speedup, connecting a commonly used optimization ingredient with the scaling guarantees sought in distributed training.
summary.tldr: The paper proves linear speedup for a communication-efficient distributed momentum SGD method in nonconvex optimization.

title: On the Linear Speedup Analysis of Communication Efficient Momentum SGD for Distributed Non-Convex Optimization

abstract: Recently there has been increased interest in using machine learning techniques to improve classical algorithms. In this paper we study when it is possible to construct compact, composable sketches for weighted sampling and statistics estimation according to functions of data frequencies. Such structures are now central components of large-scale data analytics and machine learning pipelines. However, many common functions, such as thresholds and $p$th frequency moments with $p>2$, are known to require polynomial size sketches in the worst case. We explore performance beyond the worst case under two different types of assumptions. The first is having access to noisy \emph{advice} on item frequencies. This continues the line of work of Hsu et al. (ICLR 2019), who assume predictions are provided by a machine learning model. The second is providing guaranteed performance on a restricted class of input frequency distributions that are better aligned with what is observed in practice. This extends the work on heavy hitters under Zipfian distributions in a seminal paper of Charikar et al. (ICALP 2002). Surprisingly, we show analytically and empirically that "in practice" small polylogarithmic-size sketches provide accuracy for "hard" functions.

paragraphs: Large data pipelines often replace raw data with compact summaries called sketches. This paper studies sketches that support sampling and statistical estimation based on how frequently items occur. The summaries must also be composable, so information summarized separately can be combined. Some useful frequency functions, including thresholds and frequency moments above order two, require polynomial storage in the worst case.

The authors investigate whether smaller summaries become possible under two different kinds of additional information. One setting provides noisy advice about item frequencies, potentially supplied by a learned predictor. The other restricts the input frequency distributions to classes that better reflect patterns observed in practice. These are distinct ways of moving beyond guarantees that must accommodate every possible input.

Their analytical and empirical results show that small, polylogarithmic sketches can accurately handle functions considered difficult under worst-case analysis. The significance is conditional: predictions or distributional structure can make compact summaries effective without overturning the general worst-case storage requirements.
summary.tldr: Noisy frequency predictions or restrictions on input distributions can enable compact sketches for functions that require much larger summaries in the worst case.

title: Composable Sketches for Functions of Frequencies: Beyond the Worst Case

abstract: Incorporating symbolic reasoning into machine learning algorithms is a promising approach to improve performance on learning tasks that require logical reasoning. We study the problem of generating a programmatic variant of referring expressions that we call referring relational programs. In particular, given a symbolic representation of an image and a target object in that image, the goal is to generate a relational program that uniquely identifies the target object in terms of its attributes and its relations to other objects in the image. We propose a neurosymbolic program synthesis algorithm that combines a policy neural network with enumerative search to generate such relational programs. The policy neural network employs a program interpreter that provides immediate feedback on the consequences of the decisions made by the policy, and also takes into account the uncertainty in the symbolic representation of the image. We evaluate our algorithm on challenging benchmarks based on the CLEVR dataset, and demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms several baselines.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify a particular object through a small relational program. The input is a symbolic representation of an image and a target object. The desired program uses the object’s attributes and its relationships to other objects to distinguish it uniquely within the scene.

The authors combine a policy neural network with enumerative search in a neurosymbolic synthesis algorithm. A program interpreter supplies immediate feedback about the consequences of the policy’s decisions. The policy also accounts for uncertainty in the symbolic image representation, so the program-generation process incorporates both executable reasoning and uncertainty about the scene it describes.

Experiments on challenging benchmarks derived from CLEVR show significant improvements over several baselines. The approach matters because generating a reference is treated as constructing an executable object-selection procedure. Interpreter feedback connects generation decisions to their effects on the represented scene, while search and the neural policy work together to find programs that identify the intended target.
summary.tldr: A neural policy, program interpreter, and enumerative search jointly generate relational programs that uniquely identify objects in symbolic scenes.

title: Generating Programmatic Referring Expressions via Program Synthesis

abstract: The Transformer is widely used in natural language processing tasks. To train a Transformer however, one usually needs a carefully designed learning rate warm-up stage, which is shown to be crucial to the final performance but will slow down the optimization and bring more hyper-parameter tunings. In this paper, we first study theoretically why the learning rate warm-up stage is essential and show that the location of layer normalization matters. Specifically, we prove with mean field theory that at initialization, for the original-designed Post-LN Transformer, which places the layer normalization between the residual blocks, the expected gradients of the parameters near the output layer are large. Therefore, using a large learning rate on those gradients makes the training unstable. The warm-up stage is practically helpful for avoiding this problem. On the other hand, our theory also shows that if the layer normalization is put inside the residual blocks (recently proposed as Pre-LN Transformer), the gradients are well-behaved at initialization. This motivates us to remove the warm-up stage for the training of Pre-LN Transformers. We show in our experiments that Pre-LN Transformers without the warm-up stage can reach comparable results with baselines while requiring significantly less training time and hyper-parameter tuning on a wide range of applications.

paragraphs: Transformer training often begins with a learning-rate warm-up period. This paper explains why the need for that period depends on where layer normalization is placed. It connects an architectural choice to the size of gradients at initialization and, consequently, to the stability of early training.

Using mean field theory, the authors show that the original Post-LN arrangement, with normalization between residual blocks, produces large expected gradients near the output layer at initialization. For Pre-LN, which places normalization inside residual blocks, the theory instead finds well-behaved initial gradients.

This analysis motivates training Pre-LN Transformers without warm-up. Across the reported applications, that configuration achieves results comparable to the baselines while substantially reducing training time and hyperparameter tuning. The finding ties a practical simplification to a specific explanation of initialization behavior. It supports removing warm-up in the studied Pre-LN setting rather than treating warm-up as an unavoidable feature of Transformer training.
summary.tldr: Moving layer normalization inside Transformer residual blocks improves initial gradient behavior and enables effective training without learning-rate warm-up in experiments.

title: On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture

abstract: The safe operation of physical systems typically relies on high-quality models. Since a continuous stream of data is generated during run-time, such models are often obtained through the application of Gaussian process regression because it provides guarantees on the prediction error. Due to its high computational complexity, Gaussian process regression must be used offline on batches of data, which prevents applications, where a fast adaptation through online learning is necessary to ensure safety. In order to overcome this issue, we propose the LoG-GP. It achieves a logarithmic update and prediction complexity in the number of training points through the aggregation of locally active Gaussian process models. Under weak assumptions on the aggregation scheme, it inherits safety guarantees from exact Gaussian process regression. These theoretical advantages are exemplarily exploited in the design of a safe and data-efficient, online-learning control policy. The efficiency and performance of the proposed real-time learning approach is demonstrated in a comparison to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Physical systems need accurate models to operate safely, and their ongoing operation generates data that could improve those models. Gaussian process regression is attractive because it provides prediction-error guarantees. Its computational cost, however, makes rapid updates difficult when safe operation requires the model to adapt as new data arrive.

LoG-GP addresses this problem by combining locally active Gaussian process models. Its update and prediction costs grow logarithmically with the number of training points. This makes the accumulation of training data less costly computationally than an approach whose work rises rapidly with the full dataset. The aggregation is central to obtaining this efficiency.

Under weak assumptions on the aggregation scheme, LoG-GP inherits safety guarantees from exact Gaussian process regression. The authors use these theoretical properties to design an online-learning control policy that is safe and data-efficient. Comparisons with state-of-the-art methods demonstrate the approach's efficiency and performance. The result links faster model maintenance with safety analysis, while keeping the guarantee explicitly dependent on the stated aggregation assumptions.
summary.tldr: LoG-GP combines local Gaussian processes for logarithmic update and prediction costs while preserving safety guarantees under aggregation assumptions.

title: Gaussian Process-Based Real-Time Learning for Safety Critical Applications

abstract: Conveying complex objectives to reinforcement learning (RL) agents can often be difficult, involving meticulous design of reward functions that are sufficiently informative yet easy enough to provide. Human-in-the-loop RL methods allow practitioners to instead interactively teach agents through tailored feedback; however, such approaches have been challenging to scale since human feedback is very expensive. In this work, we aim to make this process more sample- and feedback-efficient. We present an off-policy, interactive RL algorithm that capitalizes on the strengths of both feedback and off-policy learning. Specifically, we learn a reward model by actively querying a teacher’s preferences between two clips of behavior and use it to train an agent. To enable off-policy learning, we relabel all the agent’s past experience when its reward model changes. We additionally show that pre-training our agents with unsupervised exploration substantially increases the mileage of its queries. We demonstrate that our approach is capable of learning tasks of higher complexity than previously considered by human-in-the-loop methods, including a variety of locomotion and robotic manipulation skills. We also show that our method is able to utilize real-time human feedback to effectively prevent reward exploitation and learn new behaviors that are difficult to specify with standard reward functions.

paragraphs: Specifying a useful reward function can be difficult when an agent's desired behavior is complex. Human preference feedback offers another way to communicate the objective, but repeatedly asking a person for judgments is expensive. PEBBLE aims to use both that feedback and the agent's collected experience more efficiently.

The algorithm actively asks a teacher to choose between two behavior clips and learns a reward model from those preferences. It then uses the model to train an off-policy agent. Whenever the reward model changes, all past experience is relabeled with the updated rewards, allowing earlier interactions to remain useful under the revised understanding of the task.

Unsupervised exploration before this interactive training further increases the usefulness of preference queries. The authors demonstrate locomotion and robotic manipulation tasks of greater complexity than previously considered by human-in-the-loop methods. They also show that real-time human feedback can effectively prevent reward exploitation and teach behaviors that are difficult to express through standard reward functions. These findings connect feedback efficiency with continued reuse of experience.
summary.tldr: PEBBLE combines preference learning, experience relabeling, and unsupervised exploration to make interactive reinforcement learning more feedback-efficient.

title: PEBBLE: Feedback-Efficient Interactive Reinforcement Learning via Relabeling Experience and Unsupervised Pre-training

abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) automates the design of deep neural networks. One of the main challenges in searching complex and non-continuous architectures is to compare the similarity of networks that the conventional Euclidean metric may fail to capture. Optimal transport (OT) is resilient to such complex structure by considering the minimal cost for transporting a network into another. However, the OT is generally not negative definite which may limit its ability to build the positive-definite kernels required in many kernel-dependent frameworks. Building upon tree-Wasserstein (TW), which is a negative definite variant of OT, we develop a novel discrepancy for neural architectures, and demonstrate it within a Gaussian process surrogate model for the sequential NAS settings. Furthermore, we derive a novel parallel NAS, using quality k-determinantal point process on the GP posterior, to select diverse and high-performing architectures from a discrete set of candidates. Empirically, we demonstrate that our TW-based approaches outperform other baselines in both sequential and parallel NAS.

This selects a batch of candidates that combines predicted quality with diversity. summary.tldr: Tree-Wasserstein kernels guide sequential architecture search and support parallel selection of diverse, promising networks.

title: Optimal Transport Kernels for Sequential and Parallel Neural Architecture Search

abstract: Historically, to bound the mean for small sample sizes, practitioners have had to choose between using methods with unrealistic assumptions about the unknown distribution (e.g., Gaussianity) and methods like Hoeffding’s inequality that use weaker assumptions but produce much looser (wider) intervals. In 1969, \citet{Anderson1969} proposed a mean confidence interval strictly better than or equal to Hoeffding’s whose only assumption is that the distribution’s support is contained in an interval $[a,b]$. For the first time since then, we present a new family of bounds that compares favorably to Anderson’s. We prove that each bound in the family has {\em guaranteed coverage}, i.e., it holds with probability at least $1-\alpha$ for all distributions on an interval $[a,b]$. Furthermore, one of the bounds is tighter than or equal to Anderson’s for all samples. In simulations, we show that for many distributions, the gain over Anderson’s bound is substantial.

paragraphs: Estimating a population mean from few observations creates a tension between strong distributional assumptions and wide confidence intervals. This paper studies bounds that require only that the distribution lie within a bounded interval. Its reference point is Anderson's bound, which is already at least as tight as Hoeffding's under that support assumption.

The authors introduce a family of bounds and prove guaranteed coverage for each member. At a chosen confidence level, each bound holds with at least the promised probability for every distribution supported on the specified interval. The guarantee therefore does not require assuming a Gaussian distribution or another particular distributional shape.

One member of the family is at least as tight as Anderson's bound for every sample. Simulations additionally show substantial improvements for many distributions. These are distinct claims: the universal comparison permits equality, while substantial gains are demonstrated empirically across many cases. The result offers more informative small-sample mean bounds while preserving a distribution-wide coverage guarantee under the bounded-support assumption.
summary.tldr: New mean bounds retain guaranteed coverage for bounded distributions, with one bound always at least as tight as Anderson's.

title: Towards Practical Mean Bounds for Small Samples

abstract: We study reinforcement learning for infinite-horizon discounted linear kernel MDPs, where the transition probability function is linear in a predefined feature mapping. Existing UCLK \citep{zhou2020provably} algorithm for this setting only has a regret guarantee, which cannot lead to a tight sample complexity bound. In this paper, we extend the uniform-PAC sample complexity from episodic setting to the infinite-horizon discounted setting, and propose a novel algorithm dubbed UPAC-UCLK that achieves an $\Tilde{O}\big(d^2/((1-\gamma)^4\epsilon^2)+1/((1-\gamma)^6\epsilon^2)\big)$ uniform-PAC sample complexity, where $d$ is the dimension of the feature mapping, $\gamma \in(0,1)$ is the discount factor of the MDP and $\epsilon$ is the accuracy parameter. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first $\tilde{O}(1/\epsilon^2)$ sample complexity bound for learning infinite-horizon discounted MDPs with linear function approximation (without access to the generative model).

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning in continuing environments where future rewards are discounted. It assumes a linear-kernel MDP: transition probabilities depend linearly on a predefined feature mapping. The question is how much interaction is needed to learn accurately, rather than only how much regret accumulates during learning.

The authors extend uniform-PAC sample-complexity analysis from episodic problems to this infinite-horizon setting and introduce UPAC-UCLK. Their bound is, up to logarithmic factors, the sum of d squared divided by ((1−γ) to the fourth power times ε squared) and one divided by ((1−γ) to the sixth power times ε squared). Here d is feature dimension, γ is the discount factor, and ε is the desired accuracy.

Both terms have inverse-square dependence on accuracy, while the discount factor contributes a substantial additional dependence. The authors identify this as the first such accuracy dependence for discounted infinite-horizon MDPs with linear approximation without access to a generative model. The contribution closes a gap left by an earlier regret guarantee, which did not yield a tight sample-complexity bound.
summary.tldr: UPAC-UCLK provides a uniform-PAC sample-complexity bound with inverse-square accuracy dependence for discounted linear-kernel MDPs without a generative model.

title: On the Sample Complexity of Learning Infinite-horizon Discounted Linear Kernel MDPs

abstract: Due to the over-smoothing issue, most existing graph neural networks can only capture limited dependencies with their inherently finite aggregation layers. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new kind of graph convolution, called Graph Implicit Nonlinear Diffusion (GIND), which implicitly has access to infinite hops of neighbors while adaptively aggregating features with nonlinear diffusion to prevent over-smoothing. Notably, we show that the learned representation can be formalized as the minimizer of an explicit convex optimization objective. With this property, we can theoretically characterize the equilibrium of our GIND from an optimization perspective. More interestingly, we can induce new structural variants by modifying the corresponding optimization objective. To be specific, we can embed prior properties to the equilibrium, as well as introducing skip connections to promote training stability. Extensive experiments show that GIND is good at capturing long-range dependencies, and performs well on both homophilic and heterophilic graphs with nonlinear diffusion. Moreover, we show that the optimization-induced variants of our models can boost the performance and improve training stability and efficiency as well. As a result, our GIND obtains significant improvements on both node-level and graph-level tasks.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often capture only limited-range relationships because repeated aggregation can make node representations overly similar. Graph Implicit Nonlinear Diffusion, or GIND, addresses this over-smoothing problem with an implicit graph convolution. It has access to arbitrarily many neighborhood hops while adapting feature aggregation through nonlinear diffusion.

The authors show that the resulting representation is the minimizer of an explicit convex optimization objective. This provides a mathematical description of the model’s equilibrium. It also creates a design mechanism: modifying the objective produces structural variants that can incorporate prior properties into the equilibrium or introduce skip connections to improve training stability.

Experiments show that GIND captures long-range dependencies and performs well on graphs whose connected nodes tend to be similar as well as graphs whose connected nodes tend to differ. The optimization-derived variants can further improve performance, stability, and efficiency. The reported gains cover both node-level and graph-level tasks, linking the equilibrium formulation to practical improvements across different graph prediction settings.
summary.tldr: GIND uses an optimization-defined nonlinear diffusion equilibrium to capture distant graph relationships while addressing over-smoothing.

title: Optimization-Induced Graph Implicit Nonlinear Diffusion

abstract: We study a variant of a recently introduced min-max optimization framework where the max-player is constrained to update its parameters in a greedy manner until it reaches a first-order stationary point. Our equilibrium definition for this framework depends on a proposal distribution which the min-player uses to choose directions in which to update its parameters. We show that, given a smooth and bounded nonconvex-nonconcave objective function, access to any proposal distribution for the min-player’s updates, and stochastic gradient oracle for the max-player, our algorithm converges to the aforementioned approximate local equilibrium in a number of iterations that does not depend on the dimension. The equilibrium point found by our algorithm depends on the proposal distribution, and when applying our algorithm to train GANs we choose the proposal distribution to be a distribution of stochastic gradients. We empirically evaluate our algorithm on challenging nonconvex-nonconcave test-functions and loss functions arising in GAN training. Our algorithm converges on these test functions and, when used to train GANs, trains stably on synthetic and real-world datasets and avoids mode collapse.

paragraphs: Min-max optimization involves two players pushing the same objective in opposite directions. This paper studies a particular version in which the maximizing player must make greedy updates until reaching a first-order stationary point. The minimizing player chooses update directions using a proposal distribution, which also helps define what counts as an equilibrium.

For a smooth, bounded objective that need be neither convex nor concave, the authors prove convergence to their approximate local equilibrium. The result assumes access to a proposal distribution for the minimizing player and stochastic gradients for the maximizing player. Its iteration bound does not depend on dimension. However, the equilibrium reached depends on the proposal distribution, so the guarantee concerns a specific, distribution-dependent solution concept.

The authors test the algorithm on difficult mathematical objectives and GAN training losses. For GANs, they propose directions using stochastic gradients. The reported experiments show convergence on the test functions and stable GAN training without mode collapse on the evaluated synthetic and real-world datasets.
summary.tldr: A min-max algorithm has a dimension-independent iteration guarantee for a proposal-dependent local equilibrium and shows stable GAN training in experiments.

title: A Convergent and Dimension-Independent Min-Max Optimization Algorithm

abstract: Deep learning models are able to approximate one specific dynamical system but struggle at learning generalisable dynamics, where dynamical systems obey the same laws of physics but contain different numbers of elements (e.g., double- and triple-pendulum systems). To relieve this issue, we proposed the Modular Lagrangian Network (ModLaNet), a structural neural network framework with modularity and physical inductive bias. This framework models the energy of each element using modularity and then construct the target dynamical system via Lagrangian mechanics. Modularity is beneficial for reusing trained networks and reducing the scale of networks and datasets. As a result, our framework can learn from the dynamics of simpler systems and extend to more complex ones, which is not feasible using other relevant physics-informed neural networks. We examine our framework for modelling double-pendulum or three-body systems with small training datasets, where our models achieve the best data efficiency and accuracy performance compared with counterparts. We also reorganise our models as extensions to model multi-pendulum and multi-body systems, demonstrating the intriguing reusable feature of our framework.
