paragraphs: A model that learns one physical system may struggle with another containing more elements, even when both obey the same laws. ModLaNet addresses this problem by organizing the model around reusable components. Its goal is to learn dynamics from simpler systems and extend that learning to more complex arrangements, such as pendulums with additional linked elements.

The framework models the energy of individual elements and combines them into a target system through Lagrangian mechanics. This physical structure gives the learned components a defined role in constructing the overall dynamics. Modularity also supports reusing trained networks and reducing network and dataset scale, making the organization of the model central to its generalization strategy.

The authors evaluate double-pendulum and three-body systems using small training datasets, reporting the best accuracy and data efficiency among the compared methods. They then reorganize trained models for multi-pendulum and multi-body systems to demonstrate reuse. These findings support transferring learned components across the tested system sizes, addressing a form of generalization that the relevant physics-informed networks discussed in the paper could not provide.
summary.tldr: ModLaNet combines reusable element-level energy models with Lagrangian mechanics to extend learned dynamics from simpler physical systems to more complex ones.

title: ModLaNets: Learning Generalisable Dynamics via Modularity and Physical Inductive Bias

abstract: In many online decision processes, the optimizing agent is called to choose between large numbers of alternatives with many inherent similarities; in turn, these similarities imply closely correlated losses that may confound standard discrete choice models and bandit algorithms. We study this question in the context of nested bandits, a class of adversarial multi-armed bandit problems where the learner seeks to minimize their regret in the presence of a large number of distinct alternatives with a hierarchy of embedded (non-combinatorial) similarities. In this setting, optimal algorithms based on the exponential weights blueprint (like Hedge, EXP3, and their variants) may incur significant regret because they tend to spend excessive amounts of time exploring irrelevant alternatives with similar, suboptimal costs. To account for this, we propose a nested exponential weights (NEW) algorithm that performs a layered exploration of the learner’s set of alternatives based on a nested, step-by-step selection method. In so doing, we obtain a series of tight bounds for the learner’s regret showing that online learning problems with a high degree of similarity between alternatives can be resolved efficiently, without a red bus / blue bus paradox occurring.

We study this question in the context of nested bandits, a class of adversarial multi-armed bandit problems where the learner seeks to minimize their regret in the presence of a large number of distinct alternatives with a hierarchy of embedded (non-combinatorial) similarities. paragraphs: An online learner may face many alternatives that differ only slightly from one another. Those similarities can make their losses closely related. Standard bandit algorithms may then spend too much effort exploring numerous versions of a poor choice. The paper studies this issue when alternatives have a nested hierarchy of similarities.

The proposed nested exponential weights algorithm organizes exploration into layers. It selects alternatives through a sequence of nested decisions, using the hierarchy in the selection process. This adapts the exponential-weights approach to the structure of the alternatives instead of allowing many similar, suboptimal options to consume excessive exploration.

The authors establish a series of tight regret bounds for this adversarial bandit setting. The bounds show that a high degree of similarity can be used to resolve these learning problems efficiently. The result also addresses the red-bus/blue-bus issue: closely related alternatives should not distort decision-making merely through their multiplicity. The contribution makes the organization of the choice set an explicit part of the learning algorithm and its guarantees.
summary.tldr: Nested exponential weights uses hierarchical similarities among alternatives to avoid redundant exploration and achieve tight regret bounds.

title: Nested Bandits

abstract: Reinforcement learning is a promising paradigm for solving sequential decision-making problems, but low data efficiency and weak generalization across tasks are bottlenecks in real-world applications. Model-based meta reinforcement learning addresses these issues by learning dynamics and leveraging knowledge from prior experience. In this paper, we take a closer look at this framework and propose a new posterior sampling based approach that consists of a new model to identify task dynamics together with an amortized policy optimization step. We show that our model, called a graph structured surrogate model (GSSM), achieves competitive dynamics prediction performance with lower model complexity. Moreover, our approach in policy search is able to obtain high returns and allows fast execution by avoiding test-time policy gradient updates.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can require substantial experience and may transfer poorly between tasks. Model-based meta reinforcement learning addresses these problems by learning how environments evolve and drawing on experience from previous tasks. This paper examines that framework with particular attention to identifying task dynamics and efficiently finding a useful policy.

The proposed approach uses posterior sampling and combines two components: a graph structured surrogate model, or GSSM, for task dynamics, and an amortized policy optimization step. The dynamics model provides predictions about the task, while the policy-search component is designed to support fast execution without performing policy gradient updates at test time.

The authors report that GSSM achieves competitive dynamics prediction with lower model complexity. Their policy-search approach also obtains high returns while avoiding those test-time updates. These findings address two distinct costs within the framework: the complexity of modeling an environment and the work needed to produce effective behavior when the learned approach is used.
summary.tldr: A graph structured dynamics model and amortized policy search support competitive prediction and high returns without test-time policy gradient updates.

title: Model-based Meta Reinforcement Learning using Graph Structured Surrogate Models and Amortized Policy Search

abstract: Gradient Descent (GD) is a powerful workhorse of modern machine learning thanks to its scalability and efficiency in high-dimensional spaces. Its ability to find local minimisers is only guaranteed for losses with Lipschitz gradients, where it can be seen as a ’bona-fide’ discretisation of an underlying gradient flow. Yet, many ML setups involving overparametrised models do not fall into this problem class, which has motivated research beyond the so-called ”Edge of Stability” (EoS), where the step-size crosses the admissibility threshold inversely proportional to the Lipschitz constant above. Perhaps surprisingly, GD has been empirically observed to still converge regardless of local instability and oscillatory behavior. The incipient theoretical analysis of this phenomena has mainly focused in the overparametrised regime, where the effect of choosing a large learning rate may be associated to a ‘Sharpness-Minimisation’ implicit regularisation within the manifold of minimisers, under appropriate asymptotic limits. In contrast, in this work we directly examine the conditions for such unstable convergence, focusing on simple, yet representative, learning problems, via analysis of two-step gradient updates. Specifically, we characterize a local condition involving third-order derivatives that guarantees existence and convergence to fixed points of the two-step updates, and leverage such property in a teacher-student setting, under population loss. Finally, starting from Matrix Factorization, we provide observations of period-2 orbit of GD in high-dimensional settings with intuition of its dynamics, along with exploration into more general settings.

Looking at two steps together makes it possible to study behavior that a single-step stability analysis does not capture.

The authors also apply this property in a teacher-student learning problem using population loss.

The paper supplements the analysis with observations of period-two behavior in high-dimensional problems, beginning with matrix factorization. Its contribution is a sufficient local explanation for particular forms of unstable-looking convergence. The theoretical condition and the high-dimensional observations play different roles: the former supplies a guarantee, while the latter illustrates related dynamics and motivates exploration of broader settings.
summary.tldr: Analyzing gradient descent two updates at a time reveals a sufficient local condition for convergence beyond ordinary stability thresholds.

title: Beyond the Edge of Stability via Two-step Gradient Updates

abstract: We study the incentivized information acquisition problem, where a principal hires an agent to gather information on her behalf. Such a problem is modeled as a Stackelberg game between the principal and the agent, where the principal announces a scoring rule that specifies the payment, and then the agent then chooses an effort level that maximizes her own profit and reports the information. We study the online setting of such a problem from the principal’s perspective, i.e., designing the optimal scoring rule by repeatedly interacting with the strategic agent. We design a provably sample efficient algorithm that tailors the UCB algorithm (Auer et al., 2002) to our model, which achieves a $\mathcal{O} (K^2\cdot T^{2/3})$ regret after $T$ iterations, where $K$ is the number of effort levels of the agent. Our algorithm features a delicate estimation procedure for the optimal profit of the principal, and a conservative correction scheme that ensures the desired agent’s actions are incentivized. Furthermore, a key feature of our regret bound is that it is independent of the number of states of the environment.

We study the online setting of such a problem from the principal’s perspective, i.e., designing the optimal scoring rule by repeatedly interacting with the strategic agent. paragraphs: This paper studies a principal who pays a strategic agent to collect information. The principal announces a scoring rule specifying payment, and the agent chooses an effort level to maximize its own profit before reporting information. The principal must learn how to set that rule through repeated interactions with the agent.

The authors model the interaction as a Stackelberg game and adapt an upper-confidence-bound algorithm to the online learning problem. The method estimates the principal's optimal profit and applies a conservative correction designed to ensure that the intended agent actions are actually incentivized. Learning the payment rule therefore has to account for how the agent responds to it.

The algorithm has a regret bound of order K squared times T to the two-thirds power, where K counts effort levels and T counts interactions. The bound is independent of the number of environmental states. This gives a sample-efficient guarantee whose stated dependence tracks the agent's effort choices and the interaction horizon without growing with that state count.
summary.tldr: An online algorithm learns scoring rules that incentivize information gathering, with regret independent of the environment's number of states.

title: Learning to Incentivize Information Acquisition: Proper Scoring Rules Meet Principal-Agent Model

abstract: In this paper, we introduce Latent Go-Explore (LGE), a simple and general approach based on the Go-Explore paradigm for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). Go-Explore was initially introduced with a strong domain knowledge constraint for partitioning the state space into cells. However, in most real-world scenarios, drawing domain knowledge from raw observations is complex and tedious. If the cell partitioning is not informative enough, Go-Explore can completely fail to explore the environment. We argue that the Go-Explore approach can be generalized to any environment without domain knowledge and without cells by exploiting a learned latent representation. Thus, we show that LGE can be flexibly combined with any strategy for learning a latent representation. Our results indicate that LGE, although simpler than Go-Explore, is more robust and outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of pure exploration on multiple hard-exploration environments including Montezuma’s Revenge. The LGE implementation is available as open-source at https://github.com/qgallouedec/lge.

That partition is consequential: if its cells fail to capture useful distinctions, exploration can fail entirely. Constructing informative cells from raw observations can also require substantial manual work.

Latent Go-Explore replaces this manually specified partition with a learned latent representation. The proposed approach removes the need for explicit cells and domain knowledge while retaining the Go-Explore paradigm. The authors also show that LGE can be combined flexibly with different strategies for learning the representation, making that learning component a replaceable part of the approach.

Results on multiple difficult exploration environments, including Montezuma's Revenge, indicate that LGE is more robust and achieves better pure exploration performance than state-of-the-art algorithms. The stated evaluation concerns exploration itself. Its significance is that a simpler, learned representation can support effective exploration without depending on a carefully engineered cell partition for each environment.
summary.tldr: Latent Go-Explore replaces hand-designed state cells with learned representations and improves pure exploration on several challenging environments.

title: Cell-Free Latent Go-Explore

abstract: A number of methods have been proposed for causal effect estimation, yet few have demonstrated efficacy in handling data with complex structures, such as images. To fill this gap, we propose Causal Multi-task Deep Ensemble (CMDE), a novel framework that learns both shared and group-specific information from the study population. We provide proofs demonstrating equivalency of CDME to a multi-task Gaussian process (GP) with a coregionalization kernel a priori. Compared to multi-task GP, CMDE efficiently handles high-dimensional and multi-modal covariates and provides pointwise uncertainty estimates of causal effects. We evaluate our method across various types of datasets and tasks and find that CMDE outperforms state-of-the-art methods on a majority of these tasks.

paragraphs: Estimating causal effects becomes difficult when the descriptive information about study participants has a complex structure, such as images. The paper introduces Causal Multi-task Deep Ensemble, or CMDE, to address this setting. Its design learns information shared across the study population alongside information specific to individual groups, preserving both kinds of structure in the estimation process.

The authors establish a theoretical connection to multi-task Gaussian processes: before observing data, CMDE is equivalent to a process with a coregionalization kernel. This links the ensemble to a model that represents relationships between tasks. Compared with the multi-task Gaussian process approach, CMDE efficiently handles high-dimensional covariates and combinations of different data modalities.

CMDE also provides pointwise uncertainty estimates, giving uncertainty information alongside causal-effect estimates for individual points. Across datasets and tasks, it outperforms state-of-the-art methods on a majority of the evaluated tasks. The result supports the framework’s usefulness for structurally complex data while retaining the reported qualification that its empirical advantage does not cover every task.
summary.tldr: CMDE combines shared and group-specific learning to estimate causal effects and pointwise uncertainty from complex, high-dimensional data.

title: Estimating Causal Effects using a Multi-task Deep Ensemble

abstract: Accelerating the discovery of novel and more effective therapeutics is an important pharmaceutical problem in which deep learning is playing an increasingly significant role. However, real-world drug discovery tasks are often characterized by a scarcity of labeled data and significant covariate shift—a setting that poses a challenge to standard deep learning methods. In this paper, we present Q-SAVI, a probabilistic model able to address these challenges by encoding explicit prior knowledge of the data-generating process into a prior distribution over functions, presenting researchers with a transparent and probabilistically principled way to encode data-driven modeling preferences. Building on a novel, gold-standard bioactivity dataset that facilitates a meaningful comparison of models in an extrapolative regime, we explore different approaches to induce data shift and construct a challenging evaluation setup. We then demonstrate that using Q-SAVI to integrate contextualized prior knowledge of drug-like chemical space into the modeling process affords substantial gains in predictive accuracy and calibration, outperforming a broad range of state-of-the-art self-supervised pre-training and domain adaptation techniques.

paragraphs: Drug-discovery prediction often combines two difficulties: few labeled examples and a mismatch between the chemical inputs available for training and those encountered later. This mismatch, called covariate shift, makes extrapolation challenging for standard deep-learning methods. The paper introduces Q-SAVI to incorporate relevant prior knowledge into predictions in this setting.

Q-SAVI is a probabilistic model that places a prior distribution over functions. This allows knowledge about the data-generating process to express preferences about the predictive relationships the model should consider plausible. The approach makes those preferences explicit and probabilistically grounded. In the reported application, the prior incorporates contextual knowledge about the space of drug-like chemicals.

The authors build a new bioactivity dataset and investigate ways to induce data shift, creating an evaluation focused on extrapolation. In that setup, Q-SAVI delivers substantial improvements in predictive accuracy and calibration over a broad range of self-supervised pretraining and domain-adaptation approaches. The results support using domain-informed priors to improve both predictions and their associated confidence when labeled data are scarce and inputs shift.
summary.tldr: Q-SAVI encodes chemical-domain knowledge in function priors to improve bioactivity prediction and calibration under data scarcity and covariate shift.

title: Drug Discovery under Covariate Shift with Domain-Informed Prior Distributions over Functions

abstract: We study how to train personalized models for different tasks on decentralized devices with limited local data. We propose "Structured Cooperative Learning (SCooL)", in which a cooperation graph across devices is generated by a graphical model prior to automatically coordinate mutual learning between devices. By choosing graphical models enforcing different structures, we can derive a rich class of existing and novel decentralized learning algorithms via variational inference. In particular, we show three instantiations of SCooL that adopt Dirac distribution, stochastic block model (SBM), and attention as the prior generating cooperation graphs. These EM-type algorithms alternate between updating the cooperation graph and cooperative learning of local models. They can automatically capture the cross-task correlations among devices by only monitoring their model updating in order to optimize the cooperation graph. We evaluate SCooL and compare it with existing decentralized learning methods on an extensive set of benchmarks, on which SCooL always achieves the highest accuracy of personalized models and significantly outperforms other baselines on communication efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/ShuangtongLi/SCooL.

paragraphs: Devices with limited local data can benefit from learning together, but different devices may need personalized models for different tasks. Structured Cooperative Learning, or SCooL, addresses how to organize that cooperation. It uses a graphical model prior to generate a graph describing mutual learning relationships among devices.

Different choices of graph-generating structure produce a family of decentralized learning algorithms through variational inference. The paper presents three versions based on a Dirac distribution, a stochastic block model, and attention. Their expectation-maximization-style procedures alternate between updating the cooperation graph and cooperatively training the local models.

The algorithms infer relationships between tasks by monitoring model updates, using that information to improve the cooperation graph. Across the extensive benchmarks reported in the abstract, SCooL achieves the highest personalized-model accuracy and significantly better communication efficiency than the compared methods. These results support learning the pattern of cooperation alongside the models themselves, so that the sharing structure reflects the relationships among devices' tasks.
summary.tldr: SCooL learns cooperation graphs alongside personalized device models, improving accuracy and communication efficiency on the evaluated benchmarks.

title: Structured Cooperative Learning with Graphical Model Priors

abstract: Recent studies have shown that paddings in convolutional neural networks encode absolute position information which can negatively affect the model performance for certain tasks. However, existing metrics for quantifying the strength of positional information remain unreliable and frequently lead to erroneous results. To address this issue, we propose novel metrics for measuring and visualizing the encoded positional information. We formally define the encoded information as Position-information Pattern from Padding (PPP) and conduct a series of experiments to study its properties as well as its formation. The proposed metrics measure the presence of positional information more reliably than the existing metrics based on PosENet and tests in F-Conv. We also demonstrate that for any extant (and proposed) padding schemes, PPP is primarily a learning artifact and is less dependent on the characteristics of the underlying padding schemes.

paragraphs: Padding in convolutional neural networks can encode absolute position information, which can harm performance on certain tasks. Understanding that effect requires reliable ways to measure how much position information the network contains. This paper argues that existing measurements are unreliable and can produce incorrect conclusions about its presence.

The authors formally define the relevant encoded information as Position-information Pattern from Padding, or PPP. They introduce metrics for measuring and visualizing it, then conduct experiments on its properties and formation. The proposed measurements detect positional information more reliably than existing approaches based on PosENet and tests used in F-Conv, giving the investigation a more dependable measurement basis.

The paper further finds that PPP is primarily an artifact of learning across existing and proposed padding schemes, with less dependence on the schemes’ underlying characteristics. This shifts the explanation toward what emerges during learning. The contribution therefore concerns both how positional information should be measured and how its emergence should be understood.
summary.tldr: New metrics measure padding-related position information more reliably and show that it is primarily a learning artifact.

title: Unveiling The Mask of Position-Information Pattern Through the Mist of Image Features

abstract: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) were recently proposed as a new paradigm for machine learning. Instead of training the network to an observed training set, a fixed model is pre-trained offline on small, simulated training sets from a variety of tasks. The pre-trained model is then used to infer class probabilities in-context on fresh training sets with arbitrary size and distribution. Empirically, PFNs achieve state-of-the-art performance on tasks with similar size to the ones used in pre-training. Surprisingly, their accuracy further improves when passed larger data sets during inference. This article establishes a theoretical foundation for PFNs and illuminates the statistical mechanisms governing their behavior. While PFNs are motivated by Bayesian ideas, a purely frequentistic interpretation of PFNs as pre-tuned, but untrained predictors explains their behavior. A predictor’s variance vanishes if its sensitivity to individual training samples does and the bias vanishes only if it is appropriately localized around the test feature. The transformer architecture used in current PFN implementations ensures only the former. These findings shall prove useful for designing architectures with favorable empirical behavior.

paragraphs: Prior-data fitted networks learn offline from many small simulated datasets, then use a fresh dataset as context for predicting class probabilities. The pretrained model stays fixed during this use. Empirically, these models perform strongly on tasks resembling their pretraining sizes, and their accuracy can improve further when given larger datasets at inference time.

This paper develops a statistical explanation for that behavior. Although these networks are motivated by Bayesian ideas, the authors interpret them in frequentist terms as predictors tuned beforehand but not trained on the newly observed dataset. This viewpoint separates how additional examples affect prediction variability from how they affect systematic prediction error.

The analysis shows that variance vanishes if sensitivity to individual training examples vanishes. Vanishing bias requires appropriate localization around the test feature. The Transformer architecture used in current implementations ensures only the former property. Thus, reduced sensitivity can explain one benefit of more data without establishing the condition needed for bias to disappear. The distinction offers guidance for designing architectures with better statistical behavior.
summary.tldr: A frequentist analysis explains how PFNs can reduce variance with more context data while requiring suitable localization for bias to vanish.

title: Statistical Foundations of Prior-Data Fitted Networks

abstract: Multi armed bandit (MAB) algorithms have been increasingly used to complement or integrate with A/B tests and randomized clinical trials in e-commerce, healthcare, and policymaking. Recent developments incorporate possible delayed feedback. While existing MAB literature often focuses on maximizing the expected cumulative reward outcomes (or, equivalently, regret minimization), few efforts have been devoted to establish valid statistical inference approaches to quantify the uncertainty of learned policies. We attempt to fill this gap by providing a unified statistical inference framework for policy evaluation where a target policy is allowed to differ from the data collecting policy, and our framework allows delay to be associated with the treatment arms. We present an adaptively weighted estimator that on one hand incorporates the arm-dependent delaying mechanism to achieve consistency, and on the other hand mitigates the variance inflation across stages due to vanishing sampling probability. In particular, our estimator does not critically depend on the ability to estimate the unknown delay mechanism. Under appropriate conditions, we prove that our estimator converges to a normal distribution as the number of time points goes to infinity, which provides guarantees for large-sample statistical inference. We illustrate the finite-sample performance of our approach through Monte Carlo experiments.

paragraphs: Bandit algorithms adapt their choices as they learn, but evaluating a policy also requires quantifying uncertainty about its outcomes. Delayed feedback complicates that evaluation, particularly when delays differ across treatment arms. This paper develops an inference framework that allows the policy being evaluated to differ from the policy that collected the data.

The proposed estimator uses adaptive weights to address two problems at once. It incorporates arm-dependent delays to achieve consistency and controls variance inflation when some choices become increasingly unlikely during data collection. The method does not critically rely on being able to estimate the unknown delay mechanism, an important feature of its design.

Under appropriate conditions, the authors prove that the estimator approaches a normal distribution as the number of time points grows. This provides a basis for large-sample uncertainty statements rather than an unconditional finite-sample guarantee. Monte Carlo experiments illustrate finite-sample behavior. The contribution extends bandit analysis beyond reward maximization to statistical evaluation under delayed and adaptively collected observations.
summary.tldr: An adaptively weighted estimator enables policy evaluation with arm-dependent delayed bandit feedback and conditional large-sample inference guarantees.

title: Statistical Inference on Multi-armed Bandits with Delayed Feedback

abstract: Slot attention has shown remarkable object-centric representation learning performance in computer vision tasks without requiring any supervision. Despite its object-centric binding ability brought by compositional modelling, as a deterministic module, slot attention lacks the ability to generate novel scenes. In this paper, we propose the Slot-VAE, a generative model that integrates slot attention with the hierarchical VAE framework for object-centric structured scene generation. For each image, the model simultaneously infers a global scene representation to capture high-level scene structure and object-centric slot representations to embed individual object components. During generation, slot representations are generated from the global scene representation to ensure coherent scene structures. Our extensive evaluation of the scene generation ability indicates that Slot-VAE outperforms slot representation-based generative baselines in terms of sample quality and scene structure accuracy.

paragraphs: Slot attention can organize an image into representations of individual objects without supervision. However, the deterministic module does not itself provide a way to generate new scenes. Slot-VAE combines that object-centered representation ability with a hierarchical variational autoencoder, turning structured scene understanding into a basis for scene generation.

For each image, the model infers two connected levels of representation. A global representation captures the scene’s high-level organization, while individual slots encode object components. During generation, the model produces the object slots from the global representation. This dependency is intended to keep the generated components consistent with an overall scene structure.

The evaluation reports better sample quality and scene-structure accuracy than generative baselines built around slot representations. The contribution is the coordination between scene-level and object-level generation: objects are modeled as components of a coherent scene, with their representations conditioned on its global structure. The reported results support this hierarchical design for the evaluated scene-generation tasks.
summary.tldr: Slot-VAE generates structured scenes by conditioning object-level slots on a shared global scene representation.

title: Slot-VAE: Object-Centric Scene Generation with Slot Attention

abstract: As a staple of data analysis and unsupervised learning, the problem of private clustering has been widely studied, under various privacy models. Centralized differential privacy is the first of them, and the problem has also been studied for the local and the shuffle variation. In each case, the goal is to design an algorithm that computes privately a clustering, with the smallest possible error. The study of each variation gave rise to new algorithm: the landscape of private clustering algorithm is therefore quite intricate. In this paper, we show that a 20 year-old algorithm can be slightly modified to work for any of those models. This provides a unified picture: while matching almost all previously known results, it allows us to improve some of them, and extend to a new privacy model, the continual observation setting, where the input is changing over time and the algorithm must output a new solution at each time step.

paragraphs: Private clustering aims to group data while protecting information about the individuals represented in it. Researchers have developed different algorithms for centralized, local, and shuffle models of differential privacy. This paper asks whether those separate lines of work can be brought together through a shared algorithmic approach while keeping clustering error competitive.

The authors show that a small modification to an algorithm developed twenty years earlier can make it work across these privacy models. Reusing one underlying method provides a unified account of a landscape that otherwise contains many distinct algorithms. Its significance lies in covering multiple privacy settings while retaining strong results within them.

The approach matches almost all previously known results and improves some of them. It also extends to continual observation, where the input changes over time and a new clustering solution must be released at every time step. This extension brings repeated, evolving outputs into the same broader framework, rather than limiting the contribution to a single clustering of static data.
summary.tldr: A lightly modified older algorithm unifies several private clustering settings, matches most prior results, and extends to continually changing data.

title: Making Old Things New: A Unified Algorithm for Differentially Private Clustering

abstract: We propose a new method called the N-particle underdamped Langevin algorithm for optimizing a special class of non-linear functionals defined over the space of probability measures. Examples of problems with this formulation include training mean-field neural networks, maximum mean discrepancy minimization and kernel Stein discrepancy minimization. Our algorithm is based on a novel spacetime discretization of the mean-field underdamped Langevin dynamics, for which we provide a new, fast mixing guarantee. In addition, we demonstrate that our algorithm converges globally in total variation distance, bridging the theoretical gap between the dynamics and its practical implementation.

In addition, we demonstrate that our algorithm converges globally in total variation distance, bridging the theoretical gap between the dynamics and its practical implementation.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an optimization algorithm for a special class of nonlinear objectives whose inputs are probability measures. In these problems, the quantity being optimized is a distribution. The abstract identifies training mean-field neural networks, minimizing maximum mean discrepancy, and minimizing kernel Stein discrepancy as examples that fit this formulation.

The proposed N-particle underdamped Langevin algorithm comes from a new discretization of mean-field underdamped Langevin dynamics in both space and time. This connects a continuous mathematical process to a finite-particle procedure that can be implemented. The authors also establish a new fast-mixing guarantee for the underlying dynamics, addressing how quickly the process approaches its limiting behavior.

A further result proves global convergence of the algorithm in total variation distance, a measure of discrepancy between probability distributions. This is important because a guarantee for continuous dynamics alone does not complete the analysis of a discretized implementation. The paper’s contribution covers both levels, linking the mathematical dynamics and the practical algorithm for the stated class of objectives.
summary.tldr: A new particle-based Langevin algorithm connects fast-mixing mean-field dynamics to a discretized implementation with global total-variation convergence.

title: Mean-field Underdamped Langevin Dynamics and its Spacetime Discretization

abstract: For Multivariate Time Series Forecasting (MTSF), recent deep learning applications show that univariate models frequently outperform multivariate ones. To address the deficiency in multivariate models, we introduce a method to Construct Auxiliary Time Series (CATS) that functions like a 2D temporal-contextual attention mechanism, which generates Auxiliary Time Series (ATS) from Original Time Series (OTS) to effectively represent and incorporate inter-series relationships for forecasting. Key principles of ATS—continuity, sparsity, and variability—are identified and implemented through different modules. Even with a basic 2-layer MLP as the core predictor, CATS achieves state-of-the-art, significantly reducing complexity and parameters compared to previous multivariate models, marking it as an efficient and transferable MTSF solution.

paragraphs: Forecasting several time series together should create opportunities to use relationships between them. Yet the paper starts from an empirical puzzle: recent models that handle each series individually frequently outperform multivariate models. CATS addresses how those relationships are represented and supplied to a forecasting model, rather than assuming that joint modeling automatically makes them useful.

The method constructs auxiliary time series from the original observations. These derived series serve as additional inputs that represent relationships across the original series. The construction behaves like an attention mechanism spanning time and context. Separate modules implement three principles the authors identify for useful auxiliary series: continuity, sparsity, and variability.

With this construction, even a basic predictor consisting of a two-layer multilayer perceptron achieves reported state-of-the-art forecasting performance. The authors also report substantially lower complexity and fewer parameters than previous multivariate models. The result points to the value of organizing cross-series information before prediction: a comparatively simple predictor can perform strongly when auxiliary inputs make those relationships more usable.
summary.tldr: CATS constructs auxiliary time series that help a simple predictor exploit relationships between series while reducing model complexity.

title: CATS: Enhancing Multivariate Time Series Forecasting by Constructing Auxiliary Time Series as Exogenous Variables

abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) have been shown effective to generate combinatorial objects with desired properties. We here propose a new GFlowNet training framework, with policy-dependent rewards, that bridges keeping flow balance of GFlowNets to optimizing the expected accumulated reward in traditional Reinforcement-Learning (RL). This enables the derivation of new policy-based GFlowNet training methods, in contrast to existing ones resembling value-based RL. It is known that the design of backward policies in GFlowNet training affects efficiency. We further develop a coupled training strategy that jointly solves GFlowNet forward policy training and backward policy design. Performance analysis is provided with a theoretical guarantee of our policy-based GFlowNet training. Experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets verify that our policy-based strategies provide advanced RL perspectives for robust gradient estimation to improve GFlowNet performance. Our code is available at: github.com/niupuhua1234/GFN-PG.

paragraphs: Generative Flow Networks generate combinatorial objects with desired properties. Their training involves maintaining flow balance, while traditional reinforcement learning commonly optimizes accumulated reward. This paper connects those perspectives through a training framework whose rewards depend on the policy. The connection makes it possible to derive policy-based training methods for GFlowNets.

The authors contrast these methods with existing GFlowNet approaches that resemble value-based reinforcement learning. They also address the backward policy, whose design affects training efficiency. Their coupled strategy learns the forward policy and designs the backward policy jointly, bringing two connected parts of the training problem into the same optimization process.

The paper supplies performance analysis and a theoretical guarantee for its policy-based framework. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets support using reinforcement-learning ideas for more robust gradient estimation and improved GFlowNet performance. The significance is both conceptual and practical: expressing flow balance through expected reward opens another route to training, while joint policy learning addresses an efficiency-sensitive design choice within that route.
summary.tldr: A policy-gradient framework connects GFlowNet flow balance to reward optimization and jointly trains forward and backward policies.

title: GFlowNet Training by Policy Gradients

abstract: While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used for program synthesis, they lack the global view needed to develop useful abstractions; they generally predict programs one at a time, often repeating the same functionality. Generating redundant code from scratch is both inefficient and error-prone. To address this, we propose Refactoring for Generalizable Abstraction Learning (ReGAL), a gradient-free method for learning a library of reusable functions via code refactorization, i.e., restructuring code without changing its execution output. ReGAL learns from a small set of existing programs, iteratively verifying and refining its abstractions via execution. We find that the shared function libraries discovered by ReGAL make programs easier to predict across diverse domains. On five datasets – LOGO graphics generation, Date reasoning, TextCraft (a Minecraft-based text-game) MATH, and TabMWP – both open-source and proprietary LLMs improve in accuracy when predicting programs with REGAL functions. For CodeLlama-13B, REGAL results in absolute accuracy increases of 11.5% on LOGO, 26.1% on date understanding, and 8.1% on TextCraft, out-performing GPT-3.5 in two of three domains. Our analysis reveals REGAL’s abstractions encapsulate frequently-used subroutines as well as environment dynamics.

Our analysis reveals REGAL’s abstractions encapsulate frequently-used subroutines as well as environment dynamics.

paragraphs: Language models often generate programs individually, repeatedly rebuilding functionality that could be shared. ReGAL addresses this by learning a library of reusable functions from a small collection of existing programs. Its organizing idea is refactoring: restructuring code while preserving what its execution produces.

The method works without gradient-based learning and repeatedly checks and refines proposed abstractions through execution. The resulting library gives subsequent program generation reusable building blocks. The authors find that these functions capture both frequently repeated subroutines and environment dynamics, allowing learned abstractions to represent recurring behavior as well as common code fragments.

Across five datasets covering graphics, date reasoning, a text game, and mathematical tasks, both open-source and proprietary language models improve their program-prediction accuracy using ReGAL functions. For CodeLlama-13B, the reported absolute gains are 11.5 percentage points on LOGO, 26.1 on date understanding, and 8.1 on TextCraft, exceeding GPT-3.5 in two of those three domains. The results show that execution-checked reuse can make programs easier for models to predict across diverse evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: ReGAL refactors existing programs into execution-checked reusable libraries that improve language models’ program-generation accuracy.

title: ReGAL: Refactoring Programs to Discover Generalizable Abstractions

abstract: In this paper, we propose R$^3$: Learning Reasoning through Reverse Curriculum Reinforcement Learning (RL), a novel method that employs only outcome supervision to achieve the benefits of process supervision for large language models. The core challenge in applying RL to complex reasoning is to identify a sequence of actions that result in positive rewards and provide appropriate supervision for optimization. Outcome supervision provides sparse rewards for final results without identifying error locations, whereas process supervision offers step-wise rewards but requires extensive manual annotation. R$^3$ overcomes these limitations by learning from correct demonstrations. Specifically, R$^3$ progressively slides the start state of reasoning from a demonstration’s end to its beginning, facilitating easier model exploration at all stages. Thus, R$^3$ establishes a step-wise curriculum, allowing outcome supervision to offer step-level signals and precisely pinpoint errors. Using Llama2-7B, our method surpasses RL baseline on eight reasoning tasks by $4.1$ points on average. Notably, in program-based reasoning, 7B-scale models perform comparably to larger models or closed-source models with our R$^3$.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for reasoning faces a supervision problem: a reward for the final answer says little about where an incorrect solution went wrong. Rewarding individual steps offers more guidance but requires substantial annotation. R³ uses correct demonstrations to extract step-level learning benefits while relying only on outcome supervision.

Training begins near the end of a correct demonstration, where the model has relatively little reasoning left to complete. The starting point then moves progressively toward the demonstration's beginning. This reverse curriculum makes exploration easier at successive stages and allows final-outcome feedback to provide signals about particular portions of the reasoning process, helping locate errors.

With Llama2-7B, the method exceeds the reported reinforcement-learning baseline by an average of 4.1 points across eight reasoning tasks. These results support using the structure of correct demonstrations to make sparse outcome rewards more informative, without introducing manually annotated rewards for every reasoning step.
summary.tldr: R³ starts reasoning practice near the end of correct demonstrations and works backward, making outcome-only rewards more useful for learning.

title: Training Large Language Models for Reasoning through Reverse Curriculum Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study the problem of classification with selectively labeled data, whose distribution may differ from the full population due to historical decision-making. We exploit the fact that in many applications historical decisions were made by multiple decision-makers, each with different decision rules. We analyze this setup under a principled instrumental variable (IV) framework and rigorously study the identification of classification risk. We establish conditions for the exact identification of classification risk and derive tight partial identification bounds when exact identification fails. We further propose a unified cost-sensitive learning (UCL) approach to learn classifiers robust to selection bias in both identification settings. Finally, we theoretically and numerically validate the efficacy of our proposed method.

paragraphs: Historical decisions can determine which examples receive labels, leaving the labeled dataset unrepresentative of the full population. A classifier trained on that subset may therefore face selection bias. This paper studies how variation among multiple historical decision-makers, each using a different decision rule, can help address the problem.

The authors use an instrumental variable framework to analyze whether classification risk can be recovered from the available data. They establish conditions for exact identification, meaning that the population risk can be determined within the framework. When those conditions do not yield exact identification, they derive tight bounds on the possible risk instead.

The proposed unified cost-sensitive learning approach handles both identification settings and aims to learn classifiers robust to selection bias. Theoretical and numerical results validate the method. The distinction between exact identification and bounded uncertainty is consequential: the learning procedure is designed to work with what the historical decision process permits researchers to infer, including cases where risk cannot be uniquely determined.
summary.tldr: The paper uses differences among historical decision-makers to identify or bound classification risk and learn classifiers robust to selective labeling.

title: Learning with Selectively Labeled Data from Multiple Decision-makers

abstract: Pre-training Transformers in FP4 precision is becoming a promising approach to gain substantial speedup, but it comes with a considerable loss of accuracy. Microscaling (MX) data format provides a fine-grained per-group quantization method to improve the representation ability of the FP4 format and is supported by the next-generation Blackwell GPU architecture. However, training with MXFP4 data format still results in significant degradation and there is a lack of systematic research on the reason. In this work, we propose a novel training method TetraJet for a more accurate FP4 training. We comprehensively evaluate all of the quantizers involved in the training, and identify the weight oscillation problem in the forward pass as the main source of the degradation in MXFP4 training. Therefore, we introduce two novel methods, EMA Quantizer (Q-EMA) and Adaptive Ramping Optimizer (Q-Ramping), to resolve the oscillation problem. Extensive experiments on Vision Transformers demonstrate that TetraJet consistently outperforms the existing 4-bit training methods, and Q-EMA & Q-Ramping can provide additional enhancement by effectively reducing oscillation. We decreased the accuracy degradation by more than 50% compared to the baseline, and can even achieve competitive performance compared to full precision training.

paragraphs: Training Transformers with four-bit floating-point values promises substantial speed improvements, but accuracy can suffer. Microscaling improves FP4 representation through fine-grained group quantization, yet MXFP4 training still shows significant degradation. This paper investigates the cause of that degradation and introduces TetraJet to make four-bit training more accurate.

The authors evaluate the quantizers involved throughout training and identify weight oscillation during the forward pass as the main source of the observed MXFP4 degradation. They introduce an EMA Quantizer, Q-EMA, and an Adaptive Ramping Optimizer, Q-Ramping, to reduce this oscillation. The approach therefore connects a diagnosis of training behavior to changes in quantization and optimization.

Experiments on Vision Transformers show that TetraJet consistently outperforms existing four-bit training methods, with additional gains from Q-EMA and Q-Ramping. The reported accuracy degradation falls by more than 50% relative to the baseline, and performance can be competitive with full-precision training. This is a reduction in the accuracy gap, supporting oscillation control as an effective intervention in the tested low-precision training setting.
summary.tldr: TetraJet reduces weight oscillation in MXFP4 Vision Transformer training, cutting reported accuracy degradation by more than half.

title: Oscillation-Reduced MXFP4 Training for Vision Transformers

abstract: Capability evaluations are required to understand and regulate AI systems that may be deployed or further developed. Therefore, it is important that evaluations provide an accurate estimation of an AI system’s capabilities. However, in numerous cases, previously latent capabilities have been elicited from models, sometimes long after initial release. Accordingly, substantial efforts have been made to develop methods for eliciting latent capabilities from models. In this paper, we evaluate the effectiveness of capability elicitation techniques by intentionally training model organisms – language models with hidden capabilities that are revealed by a password. We introduce a novel method for training model organisms, based on circuit-breaking, which is more robust to elicitation techniques than standard password-locked models. We focus on elicitation techniques based on prompting and activation steering, and compare these to fine-tuning methods. Prompting techniques can elicit the actual capability of both password-locked and circuitbroken model organisms in an MCQA setting, while steering fails to do so. For a code-generation task, only fine-tuning can elicit the hidden capabilities of our novel model organism. Additionally, our results suggest that combining techniques improves elicitation. Still, if possible, fine-tuning should be the method of choice to improve the trustworthiness of capability evaluations.

paragraphs: A capability evaluation can underestimate a language model if the evaluation fails to reveal skills the model already possesses. This paper studies elicitation methods using deliberately constructed models whose hidden capabilities can be unlocked with a password. Knowing that a capability exists creates a controlled setting for testing whether an evaluation method can uncover it.

The authors introduce a circuit-breaking method for building these models, producing hidden capabilities that resist elicitation more strongly than standard password locking. They compare prompting, activation steering, and fine-tuning. On multiple-choice question answering, prompting reveals the underlying capability in both kinds of model organisms, while activation steering fails to do so.

The result differs for code generation: only fine-tuning reveals the hidden capabilities of the new circuitbroken model in that task. Combining techniques also appears helpful. The authors consequently recommend fine-tuning when available to improve evaluation trustworthiness. The task-specific contrast is central to the findings: a technique that successfully reveals capability in one evaluation setting may still miss it in another.
summary.tldr: Tests on deliberately capability-hiding models favor fine-tuning for reliable elicitation, with prompting success varying by task.

title: The Elicitation Game: Evaluating Capability Elicitation Techniques

abstract: The discovery of new materials is essential for enabling technological advancements. Computational approaches for predicting novel materials must effectively learn the manifold of stable crystal structures within an infinite design space. We introduce Open Materials Generation (OMatG), a unifying framework for the generative design and discovery of inorganic crystalline materials. OMatG employs stochastic interpolants (SI) to bridge an arbitrary base distribution to the target distribution of inorganic crystals via a broad class of tunable stochastic processes, encompassing both diffusion models and flow matching as special cases. In this work, we adapt the SI framework by integrating an equivariant graph representation of crystal structures and extending it to account for periodic boundary conditions in unit cell representations. Additionally, we couple the SI flow over spatial coordinates and lattice vectors with discrete flow matching for atomic species. We benchmark OMatG’s performance on two tasks: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) for specified compositions, and de novo generation (DNG) aimed at discovering stable, novel, and unique structures. In our ground-up implementation of OMatG, we refine and extend both CSP and DNG metrics compared to previous works. OMatG establishes a new state of the art in generative modeling for materials discovery, outperforming purely flow-based and diffusion-based implementations. These results underscore the importance of designing flexible deep learning frameworks to accelerate progress in materials science. The OMatG code is available at https://github.com/FERMat-ML/OMatG.

paragraphs: Generating inorganic crystals requires learning which structures are stable within an effectively unlimited design space. OMatG approaches this with stochastic interpolants: tunable processes that connect a starting distribution to the distribution of crystal structures. This framework includes diffusion and flow matching as special cases, allowing a broader range of generative processes within one design.

The authors adapt the framework to crystals through an equivariant graph representation and explicit treatment of the periodic boundaries of unit cells. They also couple the evolution of spatial coordinates and lattice vectors with discrete flow matching for atomic species. The model therefore handles geometry and chemical identity through connected continuous and discrete processes.

Evaluation covers predicting structures for specified compositions and generating stable, novel, unique structures from scratch. The authors refine the metrics for both tasks and report state-of-the-art results, outperforming purely diffusion-based and purely flow-based implementations. The findings support the value of a flexible generative framework that accommodates the different mathematical properties of crystal geometry, periodicity, and atomic composition.
summary.tldr: OMatG combines stochastic interpolants with crystal-aware representations to improve structure prediction and new-material generation.

title: Open Materials Generation with Stochastic Interpolants

abstract: Fine-tuning Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in multi-task learning scenarios has emerged as an effective strategy for achieving cross-domain specialization. However, multi-task fine-tuning frequently induces performance degradation on open-response datasets. We posit that free-form answer generation primarily depends on language priors, and strengthening the integration of visual behavioral cues is critical for enhancing prediction robustness. In this work, we propose Noise Resilient Confidence Alignment to address the challenge of open-response overfitting during multi-task fine-tuning. Our approach prioritizes maintaining consistent prediction patterns in MLLMs across varying visual input qualities. To achieve this, we employ Gaussian perturbations to synthesize distorted visual inputs and enforce token prediction confidence alignment towards the normal visual branch. By explicitly linking confidence calibration to visual robustness, this method reduces over-reliance on language priors. We conduct extensive empirical evaluations across diverse multi-task downstream settings via popular MLLM architectures. The comprehensive experiment demonstrates the effectiveness of our method, showcasing its ability to alleviate open-response overfitting while maintaining satisfying multi-task fine-tuning performance.

paragraphs: Training a multimodal language model on several tasks can improve specialization while harming its ability to answer open-ended questions. The authors propose that free-form responses depend heavily on language priors: patterns the model has learned about what answers usually look like. They argue that stronger use of visual cues can make these predictions more robust.

Their method, Noise Resilient Confidence Alignment, trains the model to maintain consistent prediction patterns when image quality changes. It creates distorted visual inputs using Gaussian noise and aligns confidence in token predictions from that branch toward predictions made with the normal visual input. The objective connects prediction confidence with robustness to visual degradation, encouraging the model to reduce its dependence on language priors.

Experiments cover multiple downstream task combinations and popular multimodal architectures. The reported results show reduced overfitting on open-response tasks while retaining satisfactory performance across the tasks being tuned. The contribution is a training constraint that addresses how confidently the model responds under visual changes, rather than treating task performance alone as the tuning objective.
summary.tldr: Aligning prediction confidence across normal and noisy images reduces open-response overfitting during multimodal multitask tuning.

title: Be Confident: Uncovering Overfitting in MLLM Multi-Task Tuning

abstract: In this work, we study online convex optimization with a fixed constraint function $g : \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. Prior work on this problem has shown $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret and cumulative constraint satisfaction $\sum_{t=1}^{T} g(x_t) \leq 0$, while only accessing the constraint value and subgradient at the played actions $g(x_t), \partial g(x_t)$. Using the same constraint information, we show a stronger guarantee of anytime constraint satisfaction $g(x_t) \leq 0 \forall t \in [T]$, and matching $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret guarantees. These contributions are thanks to our approach of using Polyak feasibility steps to ensure constraint satisfaction, without sacrificing regret. Specifically, after each step of online gradient descent, our algorithm applies a subgradient descent step on the constraint function where the step-size is chosen according to the celebrated Polyak step-size. We further validate this approach with numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization involves choosing actions over time while controlling regret, a measure of performance relative to a comparator. This paper studies the setting with a fixed constraint function. Earlier work achieved regret growing as the square root of the number of rounds while ensuring that constraint values summed to a nonpositive total.

That cumulative guarantee can allow a violation at one round to be offset by slack at another. The authors establish the stronger property that every played action satisfies the constraint, while retaining the same order of regret. Their method uses the same kind of constraint information as prior work: the value and a subgradient at played actions.

The algorithm follows each online gradient descent step with a feasibility correction. This correction descends along a constraint subgradient using a Polyak step size. The analysis shows that this additional step can enforce constraints at every round without worsening the stated regret rate. Numerical experiments further validate the approach, linking the theoretical guarantee to its behavior in the tested problems.
summary.tldr: Polyak feasibility corrections enforce constraints at every round of online convex optimization while preserving square-root regret guarantees.

title: Constrained Online Convex Optimization with Polyak Feasibility Steps

abstract: Equalized odds, an important notion of algorithmic fairness, aims to ensure that sensitive variables, such as race and gender, do not unfairly influence the algorithm’s prediction when conditioning on the true outcome. Despite rapid advancements, current research primarily focuses on equalized odds violations caused by a single sensitive attribute, leaving the challenge of simultaneously accounting for multiple attributes under-addressed. We bridge this gap by introducing an in-processing fairness-aware learning approach, FairICP, which integrates adversarial learning with a novel inverse conditional permutation scheme. FairICP offers a flexible and efficient scheme to promote equalized odds under fairness conditions described by complex and multi-dimensional sensitive attributes. The efficacy and adaptability of our method are demonstrated through both simulation studies and empirical analyses of real-world datasets.

FairICP offers a flexible and efficient scheme to promote equalized odds under fairness conditions described by complex and multi-dimensional sensitive attributes. The efficacy and adaptability of our method are demonstrated through both simulation studies and empirical analyses of real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Equalized odds asks whether predictions depend on sensitive attributes after conditioning on the true outcome. Under this fairness criterion, the relevant comparison is between people with the same actual outcome. The paper focuses on the challenge of accounting for several sensitive attributes simultaneously, rather than studying violations associated with just one attribute.

FairICP incorporates fairness into model training through a combination of adversarial learning and inverse conditional permutation. The proposed scheme is designed to handle sensitive information with a complex, multidimensional structure. This matters because a fairness objective involving several attributes requires a method that can work with their combined information during learning.

The authors evaluate FairICP in simulations and on real-world datasets, reporting evidence of its effectiveness and adaptability. Its contribution is a flexible and efficient training approach for encouraging equalized odds in these more complex settings. The stated result is that the method promotes the fairness objective; the abstract does not claim that every trained model satisfies equalized odds exactly.
summary.tldr: FairICP combines adversarial learning and inverse conditional permutation to encourage equalized odds across multiple sensitive attributes.

title: FairICP: Encouraging Equalized Odds via Inverse Conditional Permutation

abstract: Orientation estimation is a fundamental task in 3D shape analysis which consists of estimating a shape’s orientation axes: its side-, up-, and front-axes. Using this data, one can rotate a shape into canonical orientation, where its orientation axes are aligned with the coordinate axes. Developing an orientation algorithm that reliably estimates complete orientations of general shapes remains an open problem. We introduce a two-stage orientation pipeline that achieves state of the art performance on up-axis estimation and further demonstrate its efficacy on full-orientation estimation, where one seeks all three orientation axes. Unlike previous work, we train and evaluate our method on all of Shapenet rather than a subset of classes. We motivate our engineering contributions by theory describing fundamental obstacles to orientation estimation for rotationally-symmetric shapes, and show how our method avoids these obstacles.

paragraphs: Estimating a three-dimensional shape’s orientation means finding its side, up, and front axes. Those axes allow the shape to be rotated into a common coordinate alignment. Reliably recovering the complete orientation across general shapes remains an open problem. This paper develops a two-stage pipeline and examines the particular difficulty introduced by rotational symmetry.

The authors provide theory describing fundamental obstacles to orientation estimation for rotationally symmetric shapes. That analysis motivates their engineering choices, and they show how the proposed method avoids those obstacles. The theoretical component gives a reason for the pipeline’s design rather than treating symmetry only as an empirical source of errors.

The method achieves state-of-the-art performance for estimating the up axis and also demonstrates effectiveness at recovering all three orientation axes. Training and evaluation cover all of ShapeNet, whereas previous work used subsets of classes. The results therefore assess the approach across the dataset’s full class range, while keeping the strongest performance claim specific to up-axis estimation.
summary.tldr: A theory-informed two-stage pipeline addresses rotational symmetry and achieves leading up-axis estimation results across all of ShapeNet.

title: Symmetry-Robust 3D Orientation Estimation

abstract: In this work, we investigate the merits of explicitly optimizing for inference time algorithmic performance during model training. We show how optimizing for inference time performance can improve overall model efficacy. We consider generic inference time objectives with $k$ samples, with focus on pass@$k$ and majority voting as two main applications. With language model training on reasoning datasets, we showcase the performance trade-off enabled by training with such objectives. When training on code generation tasks, we show that the approach significantly improves pass@$k$ objectives compared to the baseline method.

With language model training on reasoning datasets, we showcase the performance trade-off enabled by training with such objectives. When training on code generation tasks, we show that the approach significantly improves pass@$k$ objectives compared to the baseline method.

paragraphs: This paper studies training language models for the way their outputs will actually be used at inference time. Its focus is on procedures that draw multiple samples, so the relevant outcome depends on a collection of responses. The central question is whether explicitly optimizing that collection-level objective during training improves the eventual inference procedure.

The authors consider general objectives involving k samples, with particular attention to pass@k and majority voting. Pass@k concerns finding a successful response among the samples, while majority voting uses agreement among responses to choose an answer. These objectives evaluate sampled outputs differently, making the choice of training target consequential for the inference algorithm that follows.

Training on reasoning datasets demonstrates a performance trade-off enabled by these objectives. On code generation tasks, the approach significantly improves pass@k compared with the baseline method. The findings support matching training to a planned inference procedure and its success criterion. They also frame the improvement in terms of the selected objective: the paper reports trade-offs, rather than presenting one training objective as uniformly best for every use of multiple samples.
summary.tldr: Training language models for multi-sample inference objectives exposes performance trade-offs and improves reported code-generation pass@k.

title: Optimizing Language Models for Inference Time Objectives using Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Diffusion models, praised for their success in generative tasks, are increasingly being applied to robotics, demonstrating exceptional performance in behavior cloning. However, their slow generation process stemming from iterative denoising steps poses a challenge for real-time applications in resource-constrained robotics setups and dynamically changing environments. In this paper, we introduce the One-Step Diffusion Policy (OneDP), a novel approach that distills knowledge from pre-trained diffusion policies into a single-step action generator, significantly accelerating response times for robotic control tasks. We ensure the distilled generator closely aligns with the original policy distribution by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence along the diffusion chain, requiring only $2%$-$10%$ additional pre-training cost for convergence. We evaluated OneDP on 6 challenging simulation tasks as well as 4 self-designed real-world tasks using the Franka robot. The results demonstrate that OneDP not only achieves state-of-the-art success rates but also delivers an order-of-magnitude improvement in inference speed, boosting action prediction frequency from 1.5 Hz to 62 Hz, establishing its potential for dynamic and computationally constrained robotic applications. A video demo is provided at our project page, and the code will be publicly available.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies can learn strong robotic behavior from demonstrations, but generating an action through repeated denoising takes time. That delay matters when a robot must respond quickly or has limited computing resources. One-Step Diffusion Policy, or OneDP, compresses a pretrained diffusion policy into an action generator that uses a single step.

The distillation process aims to keep the new generator close to the original policy’s distribution. It does so by minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence along the diffusion chain. The authors report convergence with an additional cost equivalent to 2%–10% of pretraining, connecting the speed improvement to a relatively small additional training investment.

Evaluation includes six simulation tasks and four real-world tasks designed by the authors using a Franka robot. OneDP reports state-of-the-art success rates alongside much faster inference, with action prediction frequency increasing from 1.5 Hz to 62 Hz. These results support the possibility of retaining strong task performance while substantially reducing action-generation delay, which is particularly relevant for dynamic and computationally constrained robotic operation.
summary.tldr: OneDP distills diffusion-based robot policies into single-step action generators, reporting strong success rates and substantially faster inference.

title: One-Step Diffusion Policy: Fast Visuomotor Policies via Diffusion Distillation

abstract: Despite remarkable advances, existing incomplete multi-view clustering (IMC) methods typically leverage either perspective-shared or perspective-specific determinants to encode cluster representations. To address this limitation, we introduce a BACDL algorithm designed to explicitly capture both concurrently, thereby exploiting heterogeneous data more effectively. It chooses to bifurcate feature clusters and further alienate them to enlarge the discrimination. With distribution learning, it successfully couples view guidance into feature clusters to alleviate dimension inconsistency. Then, building on the principle that samples in one common cluster own similar marginal distribution and conditional distribution, it unifies the association between feature clusters and sample clusters to bridge all views. Thereafter, all incomplete sample clusters are reordered and mapped to a common one to formulate clustering embedding. Last, the overall linear overhead endows it with a resource-efficient characteristic.

paragraphs: Incomplete multi-view clustering groups samples described by several kinds of information when some views are missing. A central challenge is combining what the views share with what makes each view distinctive. BACDL is designed to capture both sources of information together, addressing methods that typically emphasize one or the other.

The algorithm first splits feature clusters and then increases their separation to make them more distinguishable. It uses distribution learning to incorporate guidance from individual views into those clusters, helping reconcile differences in feature dimensionality. This provides a way to connect heterogeneous descriptions without requiring their original feature spaces to have identical dimensions.

Its cross-view connection relies on the principle that samples belonging to a common cluster have similar marginal and conditional distributions. BACDL uses this relationship to associate feature clusters with sample clusters, then reorders and maps incomplete sample clusters into a shared clustering representation. The abstract also states that the method has linear overall overhead, making computational efficiency part of its proposed contribution.
summary.tldr: BACDL combines shared and view-specific information through distribution learning to cluster incomplete multi-view data with linear overhead.

title: Bifurcate then Alienate: Incomplete Multi-view Clustering via Coupled Distribution Learning with Linear Overhead

abstract: Neural networks adapt through first-order parameter updates, yet it remains unclear whether such updates preserve logical coherence. We investigate the geometric limits of the Linear Propagation Assumption (LPA), the premise that local updates coherently propagate to logical consequences. To formalize this, we adopt relation algebra and study three core operations on relations: negation flips truth values, converse swaps argument order, and composition chains relations. For negation and converse, we prove that guaranteeing direction-agnostic first-order propagation necessitates a tensor factorization separating entity-pair context from relation content. However, for composition, we identify a fundamental obstruction. We show that composition reduces to conjunction, and prove that any conjunction well-defined on linear features must be bilinear. Since bilinearity is incompatible with negation, this forces the feature map to collapse. These results suggest that failures in knowledge editing, the reversal curse, and multi-hop reasoning may stem from common structural limitations inherent to the LPA.
