paragraphs: When a neural network receives a small parameter update, should related logical conclusions change consistently? This paper examines the Linear Propagation Assumption, which treats such local updates as coherently propagating to their logical consequences. It formalizes the question using relations and three operations: negating a relation, reversing its arguments, and chaining relations together.

For negation and argument reversal, the authors prove that guaranteeing first-order propagation regardless of update direction requires a particular tensor factorization. That structure separates information about the entity pair from information about the relation. This is a necessary structural condition for the stated propagation guarantee, rather than a claim that arbitrary network representations already possess it.

Chaining relations produces a deeper obstruction. The analysis reduces composition to conjunction and proves that conjunction defined on linear features must be bilinear. Its incompatibility with negation then forces the feature map to collapse. These results identify limits within the Linear Propagation Assumption and suggest a possible shared explanation for knowledge-editing failures, the reversal curse, and difficulties with multi-hop reasoning.
summary.tldr: The paper proves structural obstacles to making local first-order updates propagate consistently through negation, relation reversal, and composition.

title: Dynamics Reveals Structure: Challenging the Linear Propagation Assumption

abstract: Domain adaptation typically follows a two-stage pipeline: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) then Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, does RL necessarily require a pre-SFT phase for domain adaptation? SFT confines the model to an imitation distribution, limiting RL exploration, while the two-stage transition causes capability regression and extra engineering. We propose One-stage Policy Optimization (OnePO), an SFT-free paradigm that adapts pretrained LLMs to target domains in a single RL stage. OnePO uses teacher outputs as transient guidance to overcome the slow convergence of pure RL, while avoiding two failures of naive teacher-output integration: gradient starvation for low-probability teacher tokens and distribution anchoring from persistent teacher signals. It introduces two mechanisms: (1) Adaptive Objective Evolution, reshaping the RL objective for rapid absorption of teacher-provided knowledge; and (2) Teacher Retirement, automatically discarding teacher outputs once the model surpasses them. On medical adaptation, OnePO achieves 67.2 on HealthBench with only 20K training samples, outperforming SFT+RL by +2.7 and pure RL by +7.4 points. Scaling the same recipe produces HuatuoGPT-3, an open-source medical LLM series whose 32B variant reaches 70.3 on HealthBench. Additional writing and legal-domain experiments show that OnePO extends beyond medicine. Models and code are available at https://github.com/FreedomIntelligence/HuatuoGPT-3.

Pure reinforcement learning, however, can converge slowly, motivating temporary help from a teacher.

Adaptive Objective Evolution reshapes the learning objective to absorb teacher knowledge quickly. Teacher Retirement removes those outputs once the model surpasses them.

summary.tldr: OnePO adapts language models in a single reinforcement-learning stage using teacher guidance that is retired once the model surpasses it.

title: OnePO: Direct One-stage Policy Optimization for SFT-free Domain Adaptation

abstract: Soft labels from teacher models are a de facto practice for knowledge transfer and large-scale dataset distillation (e.g., SRe$^2$L, LPLD). However, when we limit the number of crops per image to reduce the substantial cost of storing precomputed soft labels, these methods suffer severely from local semantic drift: visually ambiguous crops can cause soft supervision to deviate from the image-level ground-truth semantics, leading to persistent errors and a train–test distribution mismatch. We revisit the overlooked role of hard labels and show that, when properly integrated, they can act as a content-invariant semantic anchor that calibrates such drift. We theoretically analyze the emergence of drift under sparse soft-label supervision and demonstrate that hybridizing hard and soft labels restores alignment between visual content and semantic supervision. Building on this insight, we propose a new training paradigm, Hard Label for Alleviating Local Semantic Drift (HALD), which uses hard labels as intermediate corrective signals while preserving the fine-grained benefits of soft labels. Extensive experiments on dataset distillation and large-scale classification benchmarks show consistent generalization improvements. On ImageNet-1K, our method achieves 42.7% accuracy with only 285M soft-label storage (reduces by 100$\times$), outperforming prior state-of-the-art LPLD by 9.0%. Code is available at https://github.com/Jiacheng8/HALD.

paragraphs: Teacher-provided soft labels contain useful information about class relationships, but storing them for many image crops is costly. Reducing the number of stored crops introduces another problem: an ambiguous local crop can receive supervision that drifts away from the image’s ground-truth meaning. The paper studies this local semantic drift and the persistent errors it can create.

HALD uses hard labels as intermediate corrective signals while retaining the fine-grained information in soft labels. The image-level label provides a semantic anchor that does not change with crop content. The authors analyze how drift arises under sparse soft-label supervision and show how combining hard and soft supervision restores alignment between visual content and intended semantics.

Experiments on dataset distillation and large-scale classification report consistent generalization gains. On ImageNet-1K, the method reaches 42.7% accuracy with a reported soft-label storage amount of 285M, a 100-fold reduction, and outperforms LPLD by a reported 9.0%. The result shows that appropriately integrated hard labels can improve the accuracy–storage tradeoff in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: HALD uses hard labels to correct semantic drift from sparse crop-level soft supervision, improving reported accuracy while sharply reducing label storage.

title: Hard Labels In! Rethinking the Role of Hard Labels in Mitigating Local Semantic Drift

abstract: Audio deepfake detection (ADD) models are critical for countering the malicious use of text-to-speech (TTS) models. Evaluating and strengthening ADD models requires developing datasets that span the space of generated audio and highlight high-error regions. Existing dataset development strategies face two challenges: (i) manual collection, and (ii) inefficient discovery of blind spots in the ADD models. To address these challenges, we propose FoeGlass, the first black-box automated red-teaming method for ADDs, which effectively discovers ADD failure modes in the space of generated audio underexplored by state-of-the-art deepfake benchmarks. FoeGlass uses the in-context learning capabilities of an LLM to explore the input space of a TTS model, generating audio samples that fool the target ADD using only black-box access to all components. By using a carefully designed context based on diversity measurements, FoeGlass mitigates the common problem of mode collapse in automated red-teaming systems. Empirical evaluations on several open-source ADD and TTS models demonstrate that data generated from FoeGlass substantially improves the false negative rates over unconditional sampling baselines and recent spoofing datasets by up to 94%, while requiring no manual supervision. Furthermore, we show that the attacks generated by FoeGlass are transferable across different target ADDs, demonstrating its broad applicability and ease of use for the automated red teaming of ADD systems. Finally, fine-tuning ADD models on FoeGlass-generated samples notably enhances the robustness of the detectors (up 41%).

The discovered attacks also transfer across detectors. Separately, fine-tuning detectors on FoeGlass examples improves robustness by up to 41%, supporting their value for strengthening detection as well as evaluating it.
summary.tldr: FoeGlass uses black-box, diversity-guided language-model exploration to discover audio deepfake detector failures and generate data that improves detector robustness.

title: FoeGlass: Simple In-Context Learning Is Enough for Red Teaming Audio Deepfake Detectors

abstract: Estimating causal structure in the presence of latent variables is an important yet challenging problem. Recent works have shown that distributional constraints, such as rank deficiency constraints of the covariance matrices, can be exploited to recover the underlying causal structure involving latent variables. However, real-world data often exhibit heterogeneity/nonstationarity, which pose challenges to existing methods. In this work, we develop a principled approach for identifying the structure of partially observed linear causal models from heterogenous/nonstationary data. We first formulate a class of heterogenous/nonstationary, partially observed linear causal models and prove that their distributional constraints are equivalent to those in the homogeneous case. Building on this, we propose a novel rank deficiency test that can efficiently handle heterogenous/nonstationary data, and further establish identifiability results for recovering the causal structure involving latent variables. We also provide a method to identify which variables exhibit distribution shifts, i.e., whose causal mechanisms vary across domains. Experiments on simulated and real-world data validate our theoretical findings and the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Recovering causal structure is harder when some variables are hidden and the data distribution changes across domains or over time. Existing approaches can exploit rank deficiencies in covariance matrices to reveal structure involving latent variables. The paper investigates how to retain this source of information when observations are heterogeneous or nonstationary.

The authors formulate a class of partially observed linear causal models with such variation. For this class, they prove that the relevant distributional constraints are equivalent to those in the homogeneous setting. They then develop a rank-deficiency test that efficiently handles the changing distributions and establish identifiability results for recovering causal structure involving hidden variables.

The method also identifies which variables have causal mechanisms that vary across domains. This connects structure recovery with locating the mechanisms responsible for distribution shifts. Experiments using simulated and real-world data support the theoretical findings and the method’s effectiveness. The guarantees concern the formulated class of linear models, preserving a specific setting in which heterogeneous observations can still support causal identification.
summary.tldr: The paper develops rank-based causal identification for partially observed linear systems whose distributions change across domains or time.

title: Identifying Partially Observed Causal Models from Heterogeneous/Nonstationary Data

abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is a practical paradigm for question answering over long documents, but it remains brittle for multimodal reading where text, tables, and figures are interleaved across many pages. First, flat chunking breaks document-native structure and cross-modal alignment, yielding semantic fragments that are hard to interpret in isolation. Second, even iterative retrieval can fail in long contexts by looping on partial evidence or drifting into irrelevant sections as noise accumulates, since each step is guided only by the current snippet without a persistent global search state. We introduce $G^2$-Reader, a dual-graph system, to address both issues. It evolves a Content Graph to preserve document-native structure and cross-modal semantics, and maintains a Planning Graph, an agentic directed acyclic graph of sub-questions, to track intermediate findings and guide stepwise navigation for evidence completion. On VisDoMBench across five multimodal domains, $G^2$-Reader with Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct reaches 66.21% average accuracy, outperforming strong baselines and a standalone GPT-5 (53.08%). Code is available: https://github.com/DorothyDUUU/G2_Reader.

paragraphs: Answering questions over long documents requires connecting evidence spread across text, tables, figures, and pages. Ordinary chunk-based retrieval can break those relationships, leaving fragments that are difficult to interpret. Repeated retrieval also risks circling around incomplete evidence or drifting into irrelevant material when the system lacks a persistent record of its search.

G²-Reader addresses these problems with two evolving graphs. The Content Graph preserves the document's structure and relationships between different kinds of content. The Planning Graph organizes sub-questions into a directed acyclic graph and records intermediate findings. Together, they connect evidence organization with an explicit plan for finding what is still needed.

On VisDoMBench across five multimodal domains, the system using Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct achieves 66.21% average accuracy, outperforming strong baselines and standalone GPT-5 at 53.08%. The result supports the usefulness of combining structured document representations with persistent search planning in this evaluation. It shows how a reading system can improve evidence completion by remembering both document relationships and the progress of its reasoning.
summary.tldr: G²-Reader combines a document content graph with a persistent planning graph to improve multimodal question answering.

title: $G^2$-Reader: Dual Evolving Graphs for Multimodal Document QA

abstract: Addressing Constrained Online Convex Optimization (COCO), we introduce CLASP (Convex Losses And Squared Penalties), a framework that minimizes cumulative loss together with squared constraint violations. We propose two variants of CLASP, CLASP-I and CLASP-F, allowing for a joint or separate handling of the static decision set and the time-varying constraints, a decoupling flexibility that affords simpler implementations when projections onto the static decision set are easy. Our theoretical analysis departs from prior work by fully leveraging the variety of cutter operators, and contraction properties such as the strongly quasi-nonexpansiveness, a proof strategy not previously applied in this setting. For convex losses, both CLASP algorithms achieve regret $O\left(T^{\max{\beta,1-\beta}}\right)$ and cumulative squared penalty $O\left(T^{{1-\beta}}\right)$ for any $\beta \in (0,1)$. Most importantly, for strongly convex problems, we provide the first logarithmic guarantees on both regret and cumulative squared penalty: In the strongly convex case, both CLASP algorithms guarantee that the regret is upper bounded by $O( \log T )$ and the cumulative squared penalty is also upper bounded by $O( \log T )$.

paragraphs: Constrained online optimization requires making decisions repeatedly while managing both prediction or decision loss and violations of constraints. CLASP addresses these objectives together by penalizing squared violations. Its two variants, CLASP-I and CLASP-F, allow the fixed decision set and changing constraints to be handled jointly or separately. Separating them can simplify implementation when projection onto the fixed set is easy.

The analysis uses cutter operators and their contraction properties to control the learning process. For convex losses, both variants have regret bounded by O(T raised to max(beta, 1−beta)) and cumulative squared penalty bounded by O(T raised to 1−beta), for any beta between zero and one. The parameter therefore determines the theoretical balance between the two bounds as the number of rounds grows.

For strongly convex problems, the paper establishes logarithmic bounds on both regret and cumulative squared penalty, presenting these simultaneous guarantees as a first. The distinction matters: stronger curvature assumptions support substantially slower growth of both quantities than the general convex guarantees.
summary.tldr: CLASP controls online loss and squared constraint violations, achieving logarithmic bounds for both under strong convexity.

title: CLASP: Online learning algorithms for Convex Losses And Squared Penalties

abstract: Anchor-based multi-view clustering has garnered wide attention for its ability to reduce the computational complexity of large-scale spectral clustering. However, existing methods mostly adopt a unidirectional optimization paradigm confined to sample-anchor bipartite graphs, treating the construction of the consensus graph and discrete clustering assignments as separate sub-problems to be solved independently. This weakens the information exchange between continuous representation and discrete structure, confining the optimization process to iterative updates within local modules.To address these limitations, we propose a Discretely-Refined Multi-view Clustering(DRMC) via Aligned Anchor Learning. Unlike approaches that directly perform fusion in the anchor space, our method starts from the anchor graph, elevates sample-anchor associations to sample-level similarity graph representations, and thereby enhances both within-cluster similarity and between-cluster separation. Furthermore, we design a discrete feedback module that jointly conducts spectral embedding learning and discrete label assignment by orthogonally aligning the continuous embedding matrix with the discrete indicator matrix. The resulting discrete partition is then fed back into the consensus graph construction, continuously refining the graph structure. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method exhibits significant advantages over existing state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering combines different representations of the same samples to discover groups. Anchor-based approaches reduce the cost of spectral clustering by linking samples to representative anchors. The paper argues that existing methods weaken information exchange by handling the shared graph and final discrete cluster assignments as largely separate optimization problems.

DRMC first uses sample–anchor associations to construct similarity representations at the sample level, rather than directly combining views only in anchor space. This step is designed to strengthen similarity within clusters and separation between clusters. A discrete feedback module then learns the spectral embedding and cluster assignments together, aligning the continuous embedding with the discrete assignment matrix through an orthogonal transformation.

The resulting partition is fed back into construction of the shared graph, so assignments can refine the structure that helped produce them. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show significant advantages over existing state-of-the-art approaches. The central contribution is this feedback between continuous representations and discrete group membership, allowing clustering decisions to participate in graph refinement instead of appearing only at the end.
summary.tldr: DRMC improves multi-view clustering by feeding discrete cluster assignments back into the shared similarity graph through aligned embedding learning.

title: Discretely-Refined Multi-view Clustering via Aligned Anchor Learning

abstract: Recently, the rapid development of low-altitude aerial applications has driven the need for drone-based unified detectors. In contrast to task-specific detectors that suffer from poor scalability across diverse scenarios, existing unified detectors leverage the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to learn task-aware features from diverse datasets. However, the imbalanced multi-task data distribution leads to over-activation of experts for dominant tasks and under-activation for others. To enable balanced feature learning, this paper combines three detection paradigms (RGB, IR, and RGB-IR) into a unified framework termed DroneDINO. DroneDINO extends DINO by introducing heterogeneous routed MoEs that organize experts into three functional groups: shared, task-specific, and dynamic. Unlike conventional dynamic experts where the top-$k$ experts are activated for each input, the shared expert is activated for all inputs, while each task-specific expert is activated exclusively for the matching task. To ensure inputs are routed to appropriate experts and yield task-discriminative features, we propose a task-recognition auxiliary training strategy to penalize features with low task-discriminability. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of DroneDINO, which consistently outperforms state-of-the-art unified and task-specific detectors across multiple drone-based detection benchmarks.
originalAbstract: Recently, the rapid development of low-altitude aerial applications has driven the need for drone-based unified detectors. In contrast to task-specific detectors that suffer from poor scalability across diverse scenarios, existing unified detectors leverage the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to learn task-aware features from diverse datasets. However, the imbalanced multi-task data distribution leads to over-activation of experts for dominant tasks and under-activation for others. To enable balanced feature learning, this paper combines three detection paradigms (RGB, IR, and RGB-IR) into a unified framework termed DroneDINO. DroneDINO extends DINO by introducing heterogeneous routed MoEs that organize experts into three functional groups: shared, task-specific, and dynamic. Unlike conventional dynamic experts where the top-$k$ experts are activated for each input, the shared expert is activated for all inputs, while each task-specific expert is activated exclusively for the matching task. To ensure inputs are routed to appropriate experts and yield task-discriminative features, we propose a task-recognition auxiliary training strategy to penalize features with low task-discriminability. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of DroneDINO, which consistently outperforms state-of-the-art unified and task-specific detectors across multiple drone-based detection benchmarks.

paragraphs: Drone detection systems may need to work with visible-light images, infrared images, or both together. A unified detector can share learning across these tasks, but uneven training data can cause its experts to specialize disproportionately in the most common tasks. DroneDINO addresses that imbalance within a single detection framework built on DINO.

Its mixture-of-experts architecture divides experts into shared, task-specific, and dynamic groups. The shared expert processes every input, while each task-specific expert activates only for its corresponding task. This gives common information and task-dependent information designated places in the architecture, alongside dynamically selected expertise. An auxiliary task-recognition objective penalizes features that fail to distinguish the tasks.

Experiments across multiple drone detection benchmarks report consistent improvements over leading unified detectors and detectors tailored to individual tasks. The stated contribution is therefore both architectural and empirical: organizing experts by distinct roles supports balanced feature learning, and the evaluated system generalizes effectively across the tested detection settings.
summary.tldr: DroneDINO combines shared, task-specific, and dynamic experts to improve unified visible-light and infrared drone detection.

title: DroneDINO: Towards Heterogeneous Routed Mixture of Experts for Drone-based Unified Object Detection

abstract: Training with quantized weights can reduce costs but often results in degraded accuracy, especially when optimization is carried out in low precision, without storing high-precision copies. We identify a key failure mode: under low precision, standard optimizers can get stuck and not make progress, especially at large weight magnitudes due to coarse mantissa resolution. To overcome this, multiplicative updates have been previously proposed, in place of additive updates in standard optimizers. While successful under extremely low precision, such as under the logarithmic number system, they suffer from failures near zero and across sign changes. The failure modes of additive and multiplicative updates are therefore complementary. To exploit this, we propose M+Adam, which combines both update types: additive steps handle sign changes and small magnitudes, while multiplicative steps ensure progress at large magnitudes when additive updates are zeroed out under rounding. We prove monotone descent for M+Adam under standard smoothness assumptions. Across LLaMA-style pretraining with 60M–1B models, $1$–$8\times$ Chinchilla budgets, and using only BF16, FP8, and FP4 master weights, M+Adam consistently improves low-precision training.

paragraphs: Training directly with low-precision weights can save resources, but rounding can prevent an optimizer from changing a weight at all. This is especially problematic for large weight magnitudes, where representable values are spaced farther apart. The paper identifies this stalled progress as a key failure mode when high-precision weight copies are not retained.

M+Adam combines two complementary update mechanisms. Additive updates handle small magnitudes and changes of sign, where multiplicative methods can struggle. Multiplicative updates maintain progress at larger magnitudes when rounding would erase additive steps. The combination addresses weaknesses in each update type by assigning them complementary roles in low-precision optimization.

The authors prove monotone descent under standard smoothness assumptions. Their experiments cover LLaMA-style pretraining with 60 million to one billion parameters and budgets from one to eight times Chinchilla, using only BF16, FP8, or FP4 master weights. M+Adam consistently improves training across those reported settings. The theoretical result remains conditional on its assumptions, while the experiments show the benefit of combining update types across several precision and scale choices.
summary.tldr: M+Adam combines additive and multiplicative updates to prevent complementary rounding-related failures in low-precision training.

title: M+Adam: Low-Precision Training via Additive–Multiplicative Optimization

abstract: Unified multimodal models capable of both understanding and generation have achieved remarkable strides. However, despite their unified designs, existing evaluations typically assess understanding and generation capabilities in isolation, overlooking the synergy between comprehension and generation. To bridge this gap, we introduce Unison, a comprehensive benchmark comprising 2,169 high-quality unified task samples, designed to evaluate joint understanding and generation in unified multimodal models. Unison offers three key strengths: 1) Comprehensive Dimensions: Unison encompasses internal consistency, understanding-guided generation, generation-guided understanding, and mutual enhancement to enable holistic evaluation. 2) Diagnostic Evaluation: it provides both unified and decoupled tracks for understanding and generation, allowing fine-grained attribution of failure modes and quantitative analysis of the gains from unified modeling. 3) Human Alignment: we also train Unison-Judge, an evaluation model well aligned with human judgments to achieve reliable assessment. Based on systematic evaluations of state-of-the-art models on Unison, we uncover critical limitations in current unified multimodal systems and highlight promising directions for future research. Unison will be publicly available at https://github.com/FudanCVL/Unison.

paragraphs: A multimodal model may both understand and generate content, yet separate tests of those abilities do not show whether they work well together. Unison addresses this evaluation gap with 2,169 unified task samples. Its focus is the interaction between comprehension and generation, including whether either ability helps improve the other.

The benchmark covers internal consistency, generation guided by understanding, understanding guided by generation, and mutual enhancement. It provides unified and decoupled evaluation tracks, allowing researchers to examine failures more closely and quantify benefits associated with combining the capabilities. This makes the evaluation useful for diagnosing coordination problems that isolated task scores can overlook.

The authors also train Unison-Judge, an evaluation model reported to align well with human judgments. Systematic testing of state-of-the-art models reveals limitations in current unified systems and points toward further research. The benchmark’s contribution is a way to assess whether unified modeling produces useful cooperation between capabilities, alongside tools for attributing where that cooperation succeeds or breaks down.
summary.tldr: Unison evaluates whether multimodal understanding and generation work together effectively, using unified tasks, diagnostic tracks, and a human-aligned judge.

title: Unison: Benchmarking Unified Multimodal Models via Synergistic Understanding and Generation

abstract: Fine-grained cross-modal alignment is pivotal for multimodal reasoning yet remains limited by Semantic Sparsity Bias—a fundamental asymmetry where dense visual signals are under-represented by sparse textual captions. This disparity leads to the inadvertent suppression of contextually vital visual regions (patch redundancy) and hinders precise concept grounding (patch ambiguity). While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer rich descriptive capabilities, their naive integration often induces semantic drift due to inconsistencies with sparse ground-truth captions. To systematically resolve these challenges, we present the Semantic-Enhanced Patch Slimming (SEPS) framework. Central to SEPS is a novel Dual-Granularity Semantic Calibration mechanism, which synthesizes a Holistic Visual-Linguistic Anchor from MLLMs to synergize with original sparse queries. This mechanism transforms patch selection into a semantic consensus process, ensuring that retained patches satisfy both local discriminability and global contextual integrity. Furthermore, we propose a Salience-Guided Metric Aggregation strategy to mitigate the similarity dilution effect inherent in global mean pooling, thereby amplifying highly-relevant patch-word correspondences. Extensive experiments on Flickr30K and MS-COCO datasets demonstrate that SEPS surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches across diverse backbones, delivering significant performance gains in text-to-image retrieval tasks. The complete implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SEPS/.

paragraphs: Images contain more visual detail than short captions typically describe. The paper argues that this imbalance can cause image–text alignment systems to suppress useful image regions or associate concepts ambiguously. Adding richer descriptions from multimodal language models can help, but inconsistencies with the original captions can also shift the intended meaning.

SEPS addresses this through a calibration mechanism that combines an overall visual-language description from a multimodal model with the original sparse query. Patch selection becomes a process of finding agreement between detailed local distinctions and the broader image context. This is intended to retain image regions that are informative without losing the meaning established by the query.

A second component emphasizes salient patch–word matches when combining similarity scores. It addresses the dilution that can occur when strong local matches are averaged together with less relevant information. Experiments on Flickr30K and MS-COCO report significant text-to-image retrieval gains over existing state-of-the-art approaches across multiple backbones. The results support combining calibrated descriptions, selective visual patches, and relevance-sensitive aggregation.
summary.tldr: SEPS calibrates richer image descriptions against sparse queries and emphasizes salient local matches to improve text-to-image retrieval.

title: SEPS: Semantic-Enhanced Patch Slimming Framework for Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Alignment

abstract: Data-efficient learning aims to eliminate redundancy in large training datasets by training models on smaller subsets of the most informative examples. While data selection has been extensively explored for vision models and large language models (LLMs), it remains underexplored for Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). Notably, none of existing methods can outperform random selection at different subset sizes. In this work, we propose the first principled method for data-efficient instruction tuning of LVLMs. We prove that examples with similar cross-modal attention matrices during instruction tuning have similar gradients. Thus, they influence model parameters in a similar manner and convey the same information to the model during training. Building on this insight, we propose XMAS, which clusters examples based on the trajectories of the top singular values of their attention matrices obtained from fine-tuning a small proxy LVLM. By sampling a balanced subset from these clusters, XMAS effectively removes redundancy in large-scale LVLM training data. Extensive experiments across 4 target models, 2 proxy models, and 2 datasets show that XMAS consistently outperforms 10 baseline methods. Moreover, XMAS can discard 50% of the LLaVA-665k dataset and 85% of the Vision-Flan dataset while fully preserving performance of LLaVA-1.5-7B on 10 downstream benchmarks and speeding up its training by 1.2$\times$. This is 30% more data reduction compared to the best baseline for LLaVA-665k. The project’s website can be found at https://bigml-cs-ucla.github.io/XMAS-project-page/.

paragraphs: Selecting a smaller training set is useful only if it preserves the information a model needs. For large vision-language models, the paper connects redundancy to cross-modal attention: it proves that examples with similar attention matrices during instruction tuning have similar gradients. Such examples therefore influence parameter updates in similar ways.

XMAS uses this connection to select data through a smaller proxy vision-language model. During proxy fine-tuning, it tracks the leading singular values of cross-modal attention matrices, producing trajectories that summarize their evolution. It clusters examples using those trajectories and samples a balanced subset across clusters, reducing repeated training information while retaining coverage of different groups.

Experiments across four target models, two proxies, and two datasets show consistent improvements over ten selection baselines. For LLaVA-1.5-7B, XMAS removes 50% of LLaVA-665k or 85% of Vision-Flan while preserving performance across ten downstream benchmarks, with a reported 1.2-fold training speedup. The findings support using attention dynamics from a smaller model to guide data selection for larger models.
summary.tldr: XMAS selects diverse training examples using cross-modal attention trajectories, substantially reducing vision-language tuning data while preserving tested performance.

title: Data Selection for Fine-tuning Vision Language Models via Cross Modal Alignment Trajectories

abstract: Adapting large pre-trained models to downstream tasks often produces task-specific parameter updates that are expensive to relearn for every model variant. While recent work has shown that such updates can be transferred between models with identical architectures, transferring them across models of different widths remains unexplored. In this work, we introduce Theseus, a training-free method for transporting task updates across heterogeneous-width models. Rather than matching parameters, we characterize a task update by the functional effect it induces on intermediate representations. We formalize task-vector transport as a functional matching problem on observed activations and show that, after aligning representation spaces via orthogonal Procrustes analysis, it admits a stable closed-form solution that preserves the geometry of the update. We evaluate Theseus on vision and language models across different widths, showing consistent improvements over baselines without additional training or backpropagation. Our results show that task updates can be meaningfully transferred across architectures when task identity is defined functionally rather than parametrically. Code is available at https://github.com/apanariello4/merge-and-rebase.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning produces task-specific changes to model parameters, but learning those changes again for every model variant can be expensive. This paper studies transferring such updates between models of different widths. Its method, Theseus, identifies an update through what it does to intermediate representations rather than through a direct correspondence between weights.

The authors formulate transfer as matching the update’s functional effect on observed activations. They first align representation spaces using orthogonal Procrustes analysis. In that aligned setting, they derive a stable closed-form solution that preserves the geometry of the update. This provides a transfer procedure without additional training or backpropagation.

Experiments on vision and language models of different widths show consistent improvements over the evaluated baselines. The results indicate that useful task information can survive differences in parameter dimensions when transfer is organized around representation changes. The supported scope is cross-width transfer: the method demonstrates how functional matching can connect these heterogeneous models without relearning the task update.
summary.tldr: Theseus transfers task updates between different-width models by matching their effects on representations, without additional training.

title: Transporting Task Vectors across Different Architectures without Training

abstract: Reliable evaluation of large language model (LLM) agents depends critically on benchmark validity, yet modern agent benchmarks often contain hidden flaws arising from interactions among user instructions, environments, tools, ground-truth trajectories, and evaluation protocols. These flaws confound model errors with benchmark artifacts and undermine leaderboard-based comparisons. We propose COBA (COmponent-based Benchmark Auditing), an automated pipeline for diagnosing and filtering validity issues in agent benchmarks. COBA decomposes agent tasks into four standardized components—User, Environment, Ground Truth, and Evaluation—and operationalizes a component-level issue taxonomy using hybrid rule-based detectors and taxonomy-guided LLM evaluation. Across six widely used agent benchmarks, COBA achieves strong alignment with expert judgments, with F1 scores between 0.791 and 0.874. It complements manual verification of $\tau^2$-bench by identifying issues missed due to benchmark complexity, and generalizes to previously unseen benchmarks with minimal adaptation. Our analysis shows that benchmark flaws are widespread and materially affect evaluation outcomes, demonstrating that component-based auditing provides a scalable foundation for more reliable and interpretable agent evaluation. We release AgentSuite, a unified benchmark-running platform that includes the COBA auditing pipeline and audited benchmark variants: https://github.com/Agent-Suite/AgentSuite.

paragraphs: An agent can appear to fail because its benchmark contains a flaw in the instructions, environment, expected solution, or scoring procedure. Such problems make it difficult to distinguish model weaknesses from defects in the test itself. This paper introduces COBA, an automated auditing pipeline designed to identify and filter these validity issues.

COBA separates each task into four components: User, Environment, Ground Truth, and Evaluation. It then applies a component-level classification of possible issues using both rule-based checks and language-model assessments guided by that classification. This organization makes the audit more specific: a questionable result can be traced to a particular part of the benchmark and its interactions with other parts.

Across six benchmarks, COBA agrees strongly with expert judgments, with F1 scores from 0.791 to 0.874. It also finds issues missed during manual verification of τ²-bench and transfers to previously unseen benchmarks with little adaptation. The authors release the pipeline and audited benchmark variants through AgentSuite. Their findings show that benchmark defects materially influence evaluation outcomes, making auditing important for interpreting agent comparisons.
summary.tldr: COBA audits agent benchmarks component by component to identify flaws that can distort model evaluations.

title: AgentSuite: Toward More Reliable Agent Evaluation with a Component-Based Benchmark Auditing Pipeline

abstract: This paper presents WorldPlay, a streaming video diffusion model that enables real-time, interactive world modeling with long-term geometric consistency, resolving the trade-off between speed and memory that limits current methods. WorldPlay draws power from three key ingredients. 1) We use a Dual Action Representation to enable robust action control in response to the user’s keyboard and mouse inputs. 2) To enforce long-term consistency, our Reconstituted Context Memory dynamically rebuilds context from past frames and uses temporal reframing to keep geometrically important but long-past frames accessible, effectively alleviating memory attenuation. 3) We also propose Context Forcing, a novel distillation method designed for memory-aware model. Aligning memory context between the teacher and student preserves the student’s capacity to use long-range information, enabling real-time speeds while preventing error drift. Taken together, WorldPlay generates long-horizon streaming 720p video at 24 FPS with superior consistency, comparing favorably with existing techniques and showing strong generalization across diverse scenes. Project page and online demo can be found: https://3d-models.hunyuan.tencent.com/world/ and https://3d.hunyuan.tencent.com/sceneTo3D.

paragraphs: WorldPlay is a streaming video diffusion model for interactive world modeling. Its goal is to respond to user actions in real time while maintaining consistent geometry over long sequences. The paper addresses the tension between fast generation and retaining enough past information to keep the generated world coherent.

A Dual Action Representation supports control through keyboard and mouse inputs. Reconstituted Context Memory dynamically rebuilds context from previous frames, while temporal reframing keeps geometrically important older frames accessible. These mechanisms address the fading influence of past observations, allowing long-past visual information to remain relevant to current generation.

The third component, Context Forcing, distills the model while aligning memory context between teacher and student. This is designed to preserve the student’s ability to use long-range information as generation becomes faster, helping prevent error drift. Together, the components produce long-horizon 720p streaming video at 24 frames per second. Reported comparisons show stronger consistency and strong generalization across diverse scenes, supporting the combined approach to interactive control, memory, and speed.
summary.tldr: WorldPlay combines action control, reconstructed visual memory, and memory-aware distillation for geometrically consistent interactive video at 24 FPS.

title: WorldPlay: Towards Long-Term Geometric Consistency for Real-Time Interactive World Modeling

abstract: Deep neural networks often generalize well despite heavy over-parameterization, challenging classical parameter-based analyses. We study generalization from a representation-centric perspective and analyze how the geometry of learned embeddings is associated with generalization performance for a fixed trained model. We derive a post-hoc generalization bound that relates the gap between population risk and held-out empirical risk to two factors: (i) the intrinsic dimension of the embedding, which determines the convergence rate of the empirical embedding distribution to its population counterpart in Wasserstein distance, and (ii) the sensitivity of the downstream mapping from embeddings to predictions, characterized by Lipschitz constants. Together, these provide a post-hoc explanation of generalization for trained models. At the final embedding layer, architectural sensitivity disappears and the bound is dominated by embedding dimension, explaining its strong empirical correlation with generalization performance. Experiments across architectures and datasets validate the theory and demonstrate the utility of embedding-based diagnostics.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can generalize well even when their parameter counts suggest substantial capacity to overfit. This paper studies a fixed, already-trained model through the geometry of its learned embeddings. Its goal is to explain the gap between performance on held-out examples and performance over the underlying population.

The derived bound depends on two ingredients. The intrinsic dimension of the embedding determines how quickly its empirical distribution approaches the population distribution in Wasserstein distance. Lipschitz constants describe how sensitive the downstream prediction mapping is to changes in those embeddings. Together, these connect the representation’s distributional behavior to the model’s generalization gap.

At the final embedding layer, the architectural sensitivity contribution disappears, leaving embedding dimension as the dominant part of the bound. This provides a post-training explanation for the strong empirical association between embedding dimension and generalization. Experiments across architectures and datasets support the theory and the usefulness of embedding-based diagnostics. The analysis concerns trained models, making learned representations central to its explanation.
summary.tldr: A post-training generalization bound connects embedding dimension and prediction sensitivity to the gap between held-out and population risk.

title: Understanding Generalization from Embedding Dimension and Distributional Convergence

abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) has been proposed as an auxiliary objective to improve next-token prediction (NTP) in language model training but shows inconsistent improvements, underperforming in standard NLP benchmarks. We found MTP’s exact future token prediction to be too difficult as an auxiliary loss. Instead, we propose token order prediction (TOP), which trains models to order upcoming tokens by their proximity using a learning-to-rank loss. TOP requires only a single additional unembedding layer compared to MTP’s multiple transformer layers. We pretrain models of 340M, 1.8B, and 7B parameters using NTP, MTP, DeepSeek MTP (DS-MTP) and TOP objectives. The results of nine standard NLP benchmarks show that TOP overall outperforms NTP, MTP, and DS-MTP even at scale. TOP models with continued training on math and code also perform better on 4 relevant benchmarks. On the synthetic star graph task, TOP enables pathfinding on graphs where NTP, MTP, and DS-MTP fail. Our implementation and training code is available at https://github.com/zaydzuhri/token-order-prediction.

paragraphs: Predicting several future tokens has been proposed as an extra training objective for language models, but its benefits have been inconsistent. The authors find that identifying exact future tokens is too difficult as an auxiliary task. They instead introduce token order prediction, which trains a model to rank upcoming tokens by how soon they appear.

This ranking objective provides a different way to learn from future context alongside next-token prediction. It requires one additional unembedding layer, compared with the multiple transformer layers used by multi-token prediction. The paper compares training objectives across models with 340 million, 1.8 billion, and 7 billion parameters.

Across nine standard language benchmarks, token order prediction performs better overall than next-token prediction, multi-token prediction, and DeepSeek multi-token prediction. Benefits also appear on four math and code benchmarks after continued training. On a synthetic star-graph task, it enables pathfinding where the compared objectives fail. These results support relative token order as an effective auxiliary signal across the evaluated scales and tasks.
summary.tldr: Training models to rank upcoming tokens by proximity improves language modeling overall across the evaluated model sizes and benchmarks.

title: Predicting the Order of Upcoming Tokens Improves Language Modeling

abstract: Over-aligning image generation models to a generalized aesthetic preference conflicts with user intent, particularly when "anti-aesthetic" outputs are requested for artistic or critical purposes. This adherence prioritizes developer-centered values, compromising user autonomy and aesthetic pluralism. We test this bias by constructing a wide-spectrum aesthetics dataset and evaluating state-of-the-art generation and reward models. This position paper finds that aesthetic-aligned generation models frequently default to conventionally beautiful outputs, failing to respect instructions for low-quality or negative imagery. Crucially, reward models penalize anti-aesthetic images even when they perfectly match the explicit user prompt. We confirm this systemic bias through image-to-image editing and evaluation against real abstract artworks.

This adherence prioritizes developer-centered values, compromising user autonomy and aesthetic pluralism. We test this bias by constructing a wide-spectrum aesthetics dataset and evaluating state-of-the-art generation and reward models. paragraphs: This position paper examines what happens when image generators are strongly aligned to a generalized idea of visual appeal. Artistic or critical intentions can call for deliberately unattractive, low-quality, or negative imagery. The authors argue that a system’s preference for conventional beauty can override those intentions and narrow the range of expression available to users.

To investigate, they construct a dataset spanning a broad range of aesthetics and evaluate leading generation and reward models. They find that aesthetically aligned generators frequently produce conventionally beautiful images despite instructions seeking contrary qualities. Reward models also penalize anti-aesthetic images even when those images fully satisfy the explicit prompt.

The paper argues that this pattern prioritizes developer-centered values and compromises user autonomy and aesthetic pluralism, particularly when the intended work deliberately challenges conventional beauty.
summary.tldr: Generation and reward models can favor conventional beauty even when users explicitly request anti-aesthetic imagery.

abstract: We investigate how to learn a kernel matrix for high dimensional data thatlies on or near a low dimensional manifold. Noting that the kernel matriximplicitly maps the data into a nonlinear feature space, we show how todiscover a mapping that "unfolds" the nderlying manifold from which the datawas sampled. The kernel matrix is constructed by maximizing the variance infeature space subject to local constraints that preserve the angles anddistances between nearest neighbors. The main optimization involves aninstance of semidefinite programming---a fundamentally different computationthan previous algorithms for manifold learning, such as Isomap and locallylinear embedding. The optimized kernels perform better than polynomial andGaussian kernels for problems in manifold learning, but worse for problems inlarge margin classification. We explain these results in terms of thegeometric properties of different kernels and comment on variousinterpretations of other manifold learning algorithms as kernel methods.

paragraphs: The paper considers high-dimensional observations that lie on or near a low-dimensional manifold. It learns a kernel matrix whose implicit feature-space mapping unfolds that underlying structure. Instead of selecting a standard kernel in advance, the method constructs one around a geometric objective and constraints derived from neighboring data points.

The objective maximizes variance in feature space while preserving angles and distances between nearest neighbors. This combines global spreading with local geometric preservation. The optimization is formulated as a semidefinite program, making its central computation fundamentally different from those used by Isomap and locally linear embedding, the manifold-learning methods named in the abstract.

The optimized kernels outperform polynomial and Gaussian kernels on the manifold-learning problems studied, but perform worse on large-margin classification problems. This distinction matters because a geometry useful for unfolding data need not be equally useful for separating classes. The paper explains the results through kernel geometry and discusses interpretations of other manifold-learning algorithms as kernel methods.
summary.tldr: A semidefinite program learns kernels that unfold manifolds while preserving local geometry, with stronger reported manifold-learning than classification results.

title: Learning a kernel matrix for nonlinear dimensionality reduction

abstract: This paper presents a search algorithm for finding functions that are highly correlated with an arbitrary set of data. The functions found by the search can be used to approximate the unknown function that generated the data. A special case of this approach is a method for learning Fourier representations. Empirical results demonstrate that on typical real-world problems the most highly correlated functions can be found very quickly, while combinations of these functions provide good approximations of the unknown function.
originalAbstract: This paper presents a search algorithm for finding functions that are highly correlated with an arbitrary set of data. The functions found by the search can be used to approximate the unknown function that generated the data. A special case of this approach is a method for learning Fourier representations. Empirical results demonstrate that on typical real-world problems the most highly correlated functions can be found very quickly, while combinations of these functions provide good approximations of the unknown function.

paragraphs: The paper approaches learning as a search for functions that closely track the observed data. The data are treated as observations generated by an unknown function, and the goal is to build an approximation of that function. Highly correlated candidate functions provide useful pieces from which that approximation can be assembled.

The main contribution is a search algorithm for finding these correlated functions for an arbitrary dataset. Learning a Fourier representation is a special case of the approach, so the proposed framework extends beyond that particular form of representation. Its central idea is to identify useful component functions through their relationship with the data and then combine them.

The empirical results address both the search and the resulting approximation. On the typical real-world problems studied, the most highly correlated functions are found very quickly, and combinations of those functions approximate the unknown function well. These findings support the practical value of the search strategy, while the reported speed remains an empirical observation about the studied problems.
summary.tldr: A search algorithm finds functions strongly correlated with data and combines them into useful approximations, generalizing Fourier-based learning.

title: A practical generalization of Fourier-based learning

abstract: In this work we take a novel view of nonlinear manifold learning. Usually, manifold learning is formulated in terms of finding an embedding or ‘unrolling’ of a manifold into a lower dimensional space. Instead, we treat it as the problem of learning a representation of a nonlinear, possibly non-isometric manifold that allows for the manipulation of novel points. Central to this view of manifold learning is the concept of generalization beyond the training data. Drawing on concepts from supervised learning, we establish a framework for studying the problems of model assessment, model complexity, and model selection for manifold learning. We present an extension of a recent algorithm, Locally Smooth Manifold Learning (LSML), and show it has good generalization properties. LSML learns a representation of a manifold or family of related manifolds and can be used for computing geodesic distances, finding the projection of a point onto a manifold, recovering a manifold from points corrupted by noise, generating novel points on a manifold, and more.

We present an extension of a recent algorithm, Locally Smooth Manifold Learning (LSML), and show it has good generalization properties. paragraphs: Manifold learning is often framed as placing observed data into a lower-dimensional space. This paper instead emphasizes learning a representation that can support operations on new points. It considers nonlinear manifolds, including those for which a distance-preserving unrolling is not assumed, and places generalization beyond the training data at the center of the task.

Drawing on supervised-learning ideas, the authors establish a framework for assessing models, controlling model complexity, and selecting among manifold representations. They also extend Locally Smooth Manifold Learning, or LSML, and show that it has good generalization properties. The learned representation can describe either one manifold or a family of related manifolds.

The representation supports several operations: computing distances along a manifold, projecting points onto it, recovering it from noisy observations, and generating new points on it. These capabilities explain why learning a reusable model matters beyond producing an embedding of an existing dataset. The paper connects the geometry of a learned manifold with questions about how well that representation works on previously unseen points.
summary.tldr: The paper treats manifold learning as reusable representation learning and extends LSML to support generalization and operations on novel points.

title: Non-isometric manifold learning: analysis and an algorithm

abstract: Kernel-based Bayesian methods for Reinforcement Learning (RL) such as Gaussian Process Temporal Difference (GPTD) are particularly promising because they rigorously treat uncertainty in the value function and make it easy to specify prior knowledge. However, the choice of prior distribution significantly affects the empirical performance of the learning agent, and little work has been done extending existing methods for prior model selection to the online setting. This paper develops Replacing-Kernel RL, an online model selection method for GPTD using population-based search. Replacing-Kernel RL is compared to standard GPTD and tile-coding on several RL domains, and is shown to yield significantly better asymptotic performance for many different kernel families. Furthermore, the resulting kernels capture an intuitively useful notion of prior state covariance that may nevertheless be difficult to capture manually.

However, the choice of prior distribution significantly affects the empirical performance of the learning agent, and little work has been done extending existing methods for prior model selection to the online setting. Replacing-Kernel RL is compared to standard GPTD and tile-coding on several RL domains, and is shown to yield significantly better asymptotic performance for many different kernel families. Furthermore, the resulting kernels capture an intuitively useful notion of prior state covariance that may nevertheless be difficult to capture manually.

paragraphs: Kernel-based Bayesian reinforcement learning methods such as Gaussian Process Temporal Difference represent uncertainty in value functions and allow prior knowledge to be specified. Their empirical performance, however, depends strongly on the chosen prior. The paper addresses selecting this model online, as the learning process proceeds.

The proposed Replacing-Kernel RL method uses population-based search to perform online model selection for GPTD. Kernel selection matters because the kernel expresses prior covariance between states: it determines how the model initially relates their values. Searching over kernels gives the agent a way to obtain useful relationships that may be difficult to specify manually.

The authors compare the method with standard GPTD and tile-coding across several reinforcement learning domains. They report significantly better asymptotic performance for many kernel families. The resulting kernels also express an intuitively useful notion of state covariance. These findings support online prior selection as a practical contributor to the performance of the evaluated Bayesian learning agents.
summary.tldr: Replacing-Kernel RL searches for GPTD kernels online, improving reported asymptotic performance and learning useful relationships between states.

title: Online kernel selection for Bayesian reinforcement learning

abstract: We address the problem of evaluating the risk of a given model accurately at minimal labeling costs. This problem occurs in situations in which risk estimates cannot be obtained from held-out training data, because the training data are unavailable or do not reflect the desired test distribution. We study active risk estimation processes in which instances are actively selected by a sampling process from a pool of unlabeled test instances and their labels are queried. We derive the sampling distribution that minimizes the estimation error of the active risk estimator when used to select instances from the pool. An analysis of the distribution that governs the estimator leads to confidence intervals. We empirically study conditions under which the active risk estimate is more accurate than a standard risk estimate that draws equally many instances from the test distribution.
originalAbstract: We address the problem of evaluating the risk of a given model accurately at minimal labeling costs. This problem occurs in situations in which risk estimates cannot be obtained from held-out training data, because the training data are unavailable or do not reflect the desired test distribution. We study active risk estimation processes in which instances are actively selected by a sampling process from a pool of unlabeled test instances and their labels are queried. We derive the sampling distribution that minimizes the estimation error of the active risk estimator when used to select instances from the pool. An analysis of the distribution that governs the estimator leads to confidence intervals. We empirically study conditions under which the active risk estimate is more accurate than a standard risk estimate that draws equally many instances from the test distribution.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to measure the risk of an existing model while paying for as few labels as possible. Ordinary evaluation using held-out training data may be unavailable or inappropriate when those data do not represent the intended test population. The authors instead start with a pool of unlabeled test examples and choose which examples to label.

Their approach makes sampling an active part of evaluation. Rather than treating every candidate as equally useful, it asks which sampling distribution minimizes the estimation error of the active risk estimator. The paper derives that distribution and analyzes the distribution governing the estimator to obtain confidence intervals. These intervals express uncertainty around the resulting risk estimate.

The empirical comparison holds the number of labeled examples equal between active estimation and standard sampling from the test distribution. The authors study conditions under which active selection produces a more accurate estimate. The contribution therefore concerns efficient assessment of a given model, with an advantage that depends on the conditions examined rather than a universal improvement.
summary.tldr: Active risk estimation selects test examples to label and derives an error-minimizing sampling distribution and confidence intervals for evaluating a given model.

title: Active Risk Estimation

abstract: A sparse representation of Support vector Machines (SVMs) with respect to input features is desirable for many applications. In this paper, by introducing a 0-1 control variable to each input feature, $l_0$-norm Sparse SVM (SSVM) is converted to a mixed integer programming (MIP) problem. Rather than directly solving this MIP, we propose an efficient cutting plane algorithm combining with multiple kernel learning to solve its convex relaxation. A global convergence proof for our method is also presented. Comprehensive experimental results on one synthetic and 10 real world datasets show that our proposed method can obtain better or competitive performance compared with existing SVM-based feature selection methods in term of sparsity and eneralization performance. Moreover, our proposed method can effectively handle large-scale and extremely high dimensional problems.

Rather than directly solving this MIP, we propose an efficient cutting plane algorithm combining with multiple kernel learning to solve its convex relaxation. A global convergence proof for our method is also presented. Comprehensive experimental results on one synthetic and 10 real world datasets show that our proposed method can obtain better or competitive performance compared with existing SVM-based feature selection methods in term of sparsity and eneralization performance. Moreover, our proposed method can effectively handle large-scale and extremely high dimensional problems.

paragraphs: A support vector machine can be easier to use when its prediction depends on only a small subset of input features. This paper tackles feature selection through an explicit sparsity objective. It introduces a binary control variable for each feature, turning the sparse SVM problem into a mixed integer optimization problem.

The authors solve a convex relaxation of that formulation using a cutting-plane algorithm combined with multiple kernel learning. This creates a tractable route to handling feature-selection decisions without directly solving the mixed integer problem. They also provide a global convergence proof for their method; the optimization target remains the stated convex relaxation.

Experiments on one synthetic dataset and ten real-world datasets show better or competitive results relative to existing SVM-based feature-selection methods in both sparsity and generalization. The method also handles large-scale, extremely high-dimensional problems effectively in the reported evaluation. These findings matter because selecting fewer features is useful only if the resulting model also predicts well and the selection procedure remains computationally manageable.
summary.tldr: A cutting-plane and multiple-kernel-learning method solves a convex relaxation of sparse SVM feature selection with competitive empirical results.

title: Learning Sparse SVM for Feature Selection on Very High Dimensional Datasets

abstract: Precision-recall (PR) curves and the areas under them are widely used to summarize machine learning results, especially for data sets exhibiting class skew. They are often used analogously to ROC curves and the area under ROC curves. It is already known that PR curves vary as class skew varies. What was not recognized before this paper is that there is a region of PR space that is completely unachievable, and the size of this region varies only with the skew. This paper precisely characterizes the size of that region and discusses its implications for empirical evaluation methodology in machine learning.
originalAbstract: Precision-recall (PR) curves and the areas under them are widely used to summarize machine learning results, especially for data sets exhibiting class skew. They are often used analogously to ROC curves and the area under ROC curves. It is already known that PR curves vary as class skew varies. What was not recognized before this paper is that there is a region of PR space that is completely unachievable, and the size of this region varies only with the skew. This paper precisely characterizes the size of that region and discusses its implications for empirical evaluation methodology in machine learning.

paragraphs: Precision-recall curves and their areas are widely used to summarize machine learning performance, especially when class proportions are uneven. Their behavior is often interpreted by analogy with ROC curves. This paper examines a structural feature of precision-recall space that affects how those summaries should be understood.

It was already known that precision-recall curves change when class skew changes. The paper identifies an additional fact: an entire region of precision-recall space is impossible to achieve, and the size of that region depends only on class skew. The authors precisely characterize its size, separating a constraint imposed by class proportions from differences attributable to the evaluated method.

This matters for empirical evaluation because the space in which performance is measured changes with the class balance. A curve or area therefore sits within a feasible region whose geometry is partly determined by the dataset. The paper discusses the methodological implications of this constraint, providing a more precise basis for interpreting precision-recall results in settings with different class proportions.
summary.tldr: Precision-recall space contains an impossible region whose size depends only on class skew, affecting interpretation of evaluation results.

title: Unachievable Region in Precision-Recall Space and Its Effect on Empirical Evaluation
